intro:
**The Symphony of Divine Favors and the Ministry of the Bee**

An-Naḥl, "The Bee," is the sixteenth chapter of the Qur'an, comprising 128 verses. In classical interpretive literature, it is universally designated as *Sūrat al-Niʿam* (The Chapter of Blessings or Favors), a title originating from early authorities including Qatādah and al-Baghawī because no other chapter in scripture enumerates with such comprehensive, luminous detail the inventory of divine gifts bestowed upon creation. It takes its specific scriptural name from verses 68–69, where the humble honeybee is revealed as the recipient of divine inspiration (*wa-awḥā rabbuka ilā al-naḥl*), instructed to build geometric dwellings in the mountains, trees. Human structures, and to extract nectar from diverse blooms, yielding a multi-hued fluid *“in which is healing for humanity.”* Primarily a late Makkan composition, the sūrah captures the historic transition of the Muslim community, with its closing verses (124–128) reflecting the dawn of the Medinan epoch when ethical rules of legal retaliation and gracious patience were finalized.

**The Structural Modulation and Pastoral Guidance**

The architecture of Sūrah an-Naḥl moves in a rhythmic, undulating cadence between the physical cosmos, religious refutation, and civic ethics. The opening movement (1–21) delivers a startling beginning: *“The decree of Allah has come, so do not hasten it!”* (16:1), asserting absolute monotheism and contrasting the living Creator against mute idols who cannot create a fly and are themselves created. The second movement (22–40) investigates the inner psychology of the arrogant deniers whose hearts are closed, contrasting their haughty rejection against the serene reception of the pious by the angels of death, and confirming the immutable divine law that every community was sent a messenger proclaiming: *“Worship Allah and shun false gods”* (16:36). The third movement (41–83) unfolds the great hymn of natural blessings—rain, vegetation, livestock, milk, bees, and the blessing of marriage, offspring, and homes that provide rest—interrupted by the striking parable of the two men: a disenfranchised slave possessing no resources, compared to a free man endowed with generous provision who spends openly and secretly (16:75 — *“Allah sets forth a parable: a slave who lacks all means, compared to a ˹free˺ man to whom We granted a good provision, of which he donates ˹freely,˺ openly and secretly.”*). The fourth movement (84–111) contemplates Last-Day accountability: the witnessing of the prophets against their peoples, the repudiation of false deities on Judgment Day, the command to uphold covenants without deceit, and the sublime revelation of verse 90—traditionally recited in every Friday sermon across the Islamic world—commanding justice (*ʿadl*), excellence (*iḥsān*), and generosity to kin, while forbidding indecency, wickedness, and oppression. The closing movement (112–128) presents the parable of the prosperous, secure town that displayed ungratefulness for God's blessings, whereupon God enveloped it in hunger and terror (16:112 — *“And Allah sets forth the example of a society which was safe and at ease, receiving its provision in abundance from all directions. But its people met Allah’s favours with ingratitude, so Allah made them taste the clutches of hunger and fear for their misdeeds”*), sets Abraham forward as an *Ummah* (an entire nation in a single man) who was perpetually grateful for divine favors. Concludes with the golden rule of Islamic discourse: *“Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best”* (16:125), sealing the chapter with the majestic promise: *“Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good.”*

An-Naḥl systematically demolishes this delusion by presenting an awe-inspiring, encyclopedic catalogue of cosmic provisions: livestock that yield warmth, beauty, and transport (16:5–8 — *“And He created the cattle for you as a source of warmth, food, and ˹many other˺ benefits They are also pleasing to you when you bring them home and when you take them out to graze And they carry your loads to ˹distant˺ lands which you could not otherwise reach without great hardship. Surely your Lord is Ever Gracious, Most Merciful ˹He also created˺ horses, mules, and donkeys for your transportation and adornment. And He creates what you do not know”*); rain descending from the clouds to produce olives, dates, grapes, and grains (16:10–11 — *“He is the One Who sends down rain from the sky, from which you drink and by which plants grow for your cattle to graze With it He produces for you ˹various˺ crops, olives, palm trees, grapevines, and every type of fruit. Surely in this is a sign for those who reflect”*); the sun, moon, and stars subjugated for human navigation; the oceanic deeps providing fresh meat and lustrous pearls (16:14 — *“And He is the One Who has subjected the sea, so from it you may eat tender seafood and extract ornaments to wear. And you see the ships ploughing their way through it, so you may seek His bounty and give thanks ˹to Him˺”*); and the miraculous production of pure, digestible milk flowing from between excrement and blood (*min bayni farthin wa-damin*, 16:66 — *“And there is certainly a lesson for you in cattle: We give you to drink of what is in their bellies, from between digested food and blood: pure milk, pleasant to drink”*).

verses.1:
> The command of Allah is at hand, so do not hasten it. Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate ˹with Him in worship˺

**Why The Command Covers More Than One Event**

Commentators differ on what amr means here, and the difference is instructive because both senses live in the word. Amr can mean a spoken command, as in kun fa-yakūn, and it can mean a matter, an affair that Allah brings about. Ibn Kathīr gathers reports that point in two directions. Some early authorities understood the command as the Hour itself, the Resurrection when every soul stands for reckoning. Others understood it as the worldly punishment that was already moving toward Quraysh, the defeat and breaking of their power that would become visible at Badr. The two readings support each other rather than compete. In Qur'anic usage the coming of Allah's amr often marks a turning point where denial can no longer be maintained, whether that turning point is the death of an individual, the collapse of a town, or the final gathering. Verses like 40:78 — *“It was not for any messenger to bring a sign without Allah’s permission.”*, where judgment is passed when Allah's command comes, and 11:40 — *“And when Our command came and the oven burst ˹with water˺, We said ˹to Noah˺, “Take into the Ark a pair from every species along with your family—except those against whom the decree ˹to drown˺ has already been passed—and those who believe.””*, where the flood begins when the command arrives, show the pattern. Al-Qurṭubī observes that al-Naḥl will return to both horizons again and again: verses about the Hour, verses about destroyed peoples, verses about the moment angels take the soul. All are instances of one law: when Allah's decisive matter arrives, excuses end.

**The Mockery That Prompted The Prohibition**

Reports preserved by al-Wāḥidī and others link this opening to a specific Makkan habit. When the Prophet ﷺ recited that the Hour has drawn near, some listeners paused and waited, half expecting the sky to split that afternoon. When nothing visible happened, they turned waiting into mockery and said, if you are truthful, hasten it for us. The Qur'an records this demand in several forms: *They say, when will this promise be, if you are truthful* appears in 10:48 — *“They ask ˹the believers˺, “When will this threat come to pass if what you say is true?””*, 21:38 — *“They ask ˹the believers˺, “When will this threat come to pass if what you say is true?””*, 27:71 — *“They ask ˹the believers˺, “When will this threat come to pass, if what you say is true?””*, 34:29 — *“And they ask ˹the believers˺, “When will this threat come to pass, if what you say is true?””*, 36:48 — *“And they ask ˹the believers˺, “When will this threat come to pass, if what you say is true?””*, and the bolder challenge *If this is the truth from You, rain down stones upon us* appears in 8:32 — *“And ˹remember˺ when they prayed, “O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky or overcome us with a painful punishment.””*. The answer in this verse does not accept the premise. It says the command is at hand and forbids seeking haste. Al-Zamakhsharī explains the wisdom: to demand haste is to confuse delay with cancellation. A creditor who grants time has not forgiven the debt. And, haste would harm the very people who ask for it. If Allah hastened evil for people as they hasten good, their term would already be ended, as 10:11 — *“If Allah were to hasten evil for people as they wish to hasten good, they would have certainly been doomed.”* says. Every additional day is a space where a heart may turn, where a wrong may be repaired, where a witness may become a believer. The prohibition therefore carries mercy inside severity.

The Qur'an names haste as part of human makeup. *Man was created of haste* (21:37 — *“Humankind is made of haste. I will soon show you My signs, so do not ask Me to hasten them”*) and *man is ever hasty* in prayer for good and ill (17:11 — *“And humans ˹swiftly˺ pray for evil as they pray for good. For humankind is ever hasty”*). This is not a passing remark.

**Glorified Above What They Associate**

The second half of the verse shifts from threat to transcendence: subḥānahu wa-taʿālā ʿammā yushrikūn. Subḥān declares Allah free of every defect and need. Taʿālā adds height: exalted far above. The phrase ʿammā yushrikūn carries two meanings that both apply. Allah is exalted above the partners themselves — the stones, idols, and imagined intercessors that cannot create, cannot hear, cannot know when they will be raised — and He is exalted above the act of association, which does not touch Him but only harms those who do it. This closing is not decoration. It explains why the demand for haste is foolish at its root. The Makkans imagined Allah as one power among others, whose threats could be tested like a rival's. If He is subḥān, beyond likeness and need, then His command does not compete for space. Nothing beside Him can delay it, prevent it, or shield anyone from it. The same seal appears again in 16:3 — *“He created the heavens and the earth for a purpose. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him ˹in worship˺”* and elsewhere in the Qur'an, for example 10:18 — *“Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate ˹with Him˺!””* and 30:40 — *“Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate with Him ˹in worship˺”*, always after a mention of creation or judgment, to remind the listener that tawḥīd is not one doctrine among many but the frame that makes sense of all the rest.
verses.2:
> He sends down the angels with revelation by His command to whoever He wills of His servants, ˹stating:˺ “Warn ˹humanity˺ that there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Me, so be mindful of Me ˹alone˺.”

**Why Revelation Is Called Rūḥ**

The Qur'an uses rūḥ for several related realities, and the commentators distinguish them carefully. Sometimes rūḥ is the angel Jibrīl himself, called al-Rūḥ al-Amīn, the Trustworthy Spirit. Sometimes it is revelation, because revelation animates. Sometimes it is the secret of life that humans know little about, as in 17:85 — *“They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the spirit. Say, “Its nature is known only to my Lord, and you ˹O humanity˺ have been given but little knowledge.””*: *They ask you about the spirit. Say, the spirit is from the command of my Lord, and you have not been given knowledge except a little* (17:85 — *“They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the spirit. Say, “Its nature is known only to my Lord, and you ˹O humanity˺ have been given but little knowledge.””*). The verse here brings two of those senses together: angels descend, and they carry rūḥ. The angel is the carrier, the rūḥ is what is carried. Al-Qurṭubī points out that calling revelation a spirit teaches something about how it works. A spirit does not merely inform; it revives. A person may know many facts and still be spiritually lifeless. When revelation enters, intentions change, fear and hope find their proper objects, and the heart begins to move toward its Creator. This is why the same root appears in 42:52 — *“And so We have sent to you ˹O Prophet˺ a revelation by Our command.”*: *And so We have revealed to you a spirit from Our command. You did not know what the Book was nor what faith was, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants* (42:52 — *“You did not know of ˹this˺ Book and faith ˹before˺.”*). The verse in al-Naḥl therefore defines the purpose of prophethood in one image: dead hearts brought to life by a descent from above.

**Angels As Bearers, Not Authors**

Yunazzilu al-malā'ikata — He sends down the angels. The plural suggests the host that accompanies revelation, though the direct bearer is Jibrīl. The Qur'an elsewhere names him explicitly: *He brings it down upon your heart by Allah's permission* (2:97 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it—a guide and good news for the believers.””*). The point of mentioning angels in the plural is to show the honor and protection around the message. Revelation does not drift down like rumor; it is carried by pure, obedient beings whose only task is to execute Allah's command. Ibn Kathīr notes that this guards against the Makkan claim that the Prophet ﷺ invented the message or learned it from a human teacher. Angels are not of this earth. Their descent marks the message as coming from beyond human craft. At the same time, the phrase *to whoever He wills of His servants* removes any human claim to control who receives it. Prophethood is not earned by lineage, wealth, or eloquence. It is a selection, an iṣṭifā', and Allah knows best where to place His message, as 6:124 — *“Allah knows best where to place His message.”* says. The Makkans had asked, *Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns* (43:31 — *“And they exclaimed, “If only this Quran was revealed to a great man from ˹one of˺ the two cities!””*), meaning a rich leader of Makkah or Ṭā'if. The answer is in this verse: choice belongs to the One who sends, not to those who receive.

**The Core Message In One Sentence**

What do the angels say when they descend? An anḏirū annahu lā ilāha illā anā fa-ittaqūn — warn that there is no god worthy of worship except Me, so be mindful of Me alone. This is the summary of every messenger's call. Al-Ṭabarī cites 21:25 — *“We never sent a messenger before you ˹O Prophet˺ without revealing to him: “There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Me, so worship Me ˹alone˺.””*: *We did not send any messenger before you except that We revealed to him, there is no god but Me, so worship Me* (21:25 — *“We never sent a messenger before you ˹O Prophet˺ without revealing to him: “There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Me, so worship Me ˹alone˺.””*). The command anḏirū, warn, shows that revelation begins with warning before promise, because a heedless heart does not feel need for promise until it feels danger. The warning is not about tribal defeat or poverty; it is about the foundation of worship. Lā ilāha illā anā — there is no deity except Me. The pronoun anā, I, is direct, without intermediary, to stress that Allah speaks about Himself. Then comes fa-ittaqūn — so be mindful of Me, fear Me, guard yourselves by reverence for Me. Taqwā comes from w-q-y, to shield or protect. It is not mere terror; it is the carefulness of one who knows a danger is real and takes protection. Here protection is found in turning to Allah alone.
verses.3:
> He created the heavens and the earth for a purpose. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him ˹in worship˺

**Creation With Truth, Not As Play**

Khalqa al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍa bi-l-ḥaqq — He created the heavens and the earth in truth, for a purpose. The phrase bi-l-ḥaqq appears repeatedly in the Qur'an to counter the idea that the world is accidental, purposeless, or a game. Al-Rāzī explains ḥaqq here as having three layers: existence that is real rather than imaginary, wisdom that is purposeful rather than vain, and justice that will be fulfilled rather than ignored. The heavens and earth are not scenery; they are a court where truth will be established. The verse echoes 44:38-39 — *“We only created them for a purpose, but most of these ˹pagans˺ do not know”*: *We did not create the heavens and earth and what is between them in play. We did not create them except in truth* (44:38-39 — *“We did not create the heavens and the earth and everything in between for sport”*). And 30:8 — *“Allah only created the heavens and the earth and everything in between for a purpose and an appointed term.”*: *Do they not reflect within themselves? Allah did not create the heavens and earth and what is between them except in truth and for an appointed term* (30:8 — *“Allah only created the heavens and the earth and everything in between for a purpose and an appointed term.”*). By placing this immediately after the mention of angels descending with revelation, the sūrah connects two creations: the physical cosmos and the guidance that explains its purpose. One without the other leaves a person with eyes but no light.

**Why The Heavens Are Mentioned Before The Earth**

The order samāwāt then arḍ is consistent across the Qur'an. It reflects both observable magnitude and the Qur'anic picture of the universe, in which the heavens are the larger, encompassing structure. Linguistically, samāwāt is plural, indicating vastness and layers. The Qur'an elsewhere says *He created seven heavens in layers* (67:3 — *“˹He is the One˺ Who created seven heavens, one above the other.”*). Earth is singular, the immediate dwelling. Together they denote totality — everything high and low, distant and near. Al-Qurṭubī notes that beginning with heavens establishes Allah's power before discussing human ingratitude; if He holds the immense heavens, He certainly holds the small idols people trust.

**The Seal That Returns: Exalted Above Association**

Taʿālā ʿammā yushrikūn — Exalted is He above what they associate with Him. This is the same seal as in verse 1, repeated here to bind creation to transcendence. If Allah alone created heavens and earth, then associating others with Him in worship contradicts the very world those others inhabit. The idols did not create a single heaven or a grain of earth, yet they are given a share of devotion that belongs to the Creator. The Qur'an makes this argument explicit in 30:40 — *“Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate with Him ˹in worship˺”*: *Allah is the One who created you, then provided for you, then will cause you to die, then give you life. Is there any of your partners who does anything of that? Glorified is He and exalted above what they associate* (30:40 — *“Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate with Him ˹in worship˺”*). The repetition of the seal in 16:1 — *“The command of Allah is at hand, so do not hasten it. Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate ˹with Him in worship˺”* and 16:3 forms an inclusio: the sūrah opened with judgment and transcendence, then revelation, then creation and transcendence again. The message is that judgment, revelation, and creation all point to the same conclusion — Allah alone deserves worship.

**Purpose Implies Return**

To say the heavens and earth were created bi-l-ḥaqq also implies they were created for an appointed term and for reckoning. Al-Ṭabarī links ḥaqq to the return: because creation is with truth, there must be a Day when truth is sorted from falsehood. If there were no return, the oppressor and oppressed would be equal at death, which would make creation in vain. The Qur'an denies this: *Did you think We created you in vain and that you would not be returned to Us?* (23:115 — *“Did you then think that We had created you without purpose, and that you would never be returned to Us?””*). In al-Naḥl, this logic will become concrete. After listing blessings, the sūrah will say *If you tried to count Allah's blessings, you would never number them* (16:18 — *“If you tried to count Allah’s blessings, you would never be able to number them. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*), then ask *Can the One who creates be equal to those who do not?* (16:17 — *“Can the One Who creates be equal to those who do not? Will you not then be mindful”*). The argument moves from creation to gratitude to worship to accountability. A purposeful creation demands a purposeful human response. That response is tawḥīd and shukr, and its opposite is shirk and kufr, which in Arabic share the root sense of covering over a reality.
verses.4:
> He created humans from a sperm-drop, then—behold!—they openly challenge ˹Him˺

**From Cosmos To The Smallest Beginning**

After heavens and earth, the Qur'an turns to the human. Khalaqa al-insāna min nuṭfah — He created the human from a nuṭfah, a drop. The word nuṭfah in Arabic means a small amount of liquid, a drop that clings. It appears in the Qur'an to describe the initial stage of human formation, often paired with language of lowliness and weakness. The shift from vast heavens to a single drop is intentional. If the previous verse established Allah's power through magnitude, this verse establishes it through minuteness. The One who holds galaxies also originates a speaking, arguing, planning human from a fluid that cannot be seen without closeness. Al-Rāzī observes that this is a stronger proof of power than creating heavens, because heavens are great from great, while a human is great from insignificant. The same argument appears in 36:77 — *“Do people not see that We have created them from a sperm-drop, then—behold!—they openly challenge ˹Us˺”*: *Does man not see that We created him from a drop, and behold, he is a clear adversary?* (36:77 — *“Do people not see that We have created them from a sperm-drop, then—behold!—they openly challenge ˹Us˺”*). The wording there is almost identical to this verse, showing that the Qur'an returns to this image when confronting denial of resurrection.

**The Suddenness Of Fa-idhā**

Fa-idhā huwa khaṣīmun mubīn — then behold, he is an open challenger. The particle fa-idhā conveys surprise and suddenness. One moment a drop, the next a disputant who argues against his own Creator. The Qur'an uses this construction to highlight ingratitude and forgetfulness of origin. Al-Zamakhsharī notes the rhetorical force: the origin is weak, the outcome is bold. Ibn Kathīr connects this to a reported occasion: a Makkan, identified in some reports as Ubayy ibn Khalaf, came with a decayed bone, crumbled it, and said, who will give life to this after it has rotted? The Qur'an answers such challenges elsewhere: *Say, He will give it life who produced it the first time* (36:79 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “They will be revived by the One Who produced them the first time, for He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of every created being”*).

**What The Drop Teaches About Resurrection**

The verse is placed in Sūrat al-Niʿam among blessings, yet it sounds like rebuke. That placement is precise. The ability to argue, to reason, to speak clearly is itself a blessing, but when turned against the Giver it becomes evidence against the arguer. Al-Ṭabarī explains that nuṭfah is mentioned to remind the human of how easily Allah can recreate. If He could create from a drop the first time, with no prior example, then recreation after death is easier. The Qur'an makes this explicit in 30:27 — *“And He is the One Who originates the creation then will resurrect it—which is even easier for Him. To Him belong the finest attributes in the heavens and the earth. And He is the Almighty, All-Wise”*: *It is He who originates creation, then will repeat it, and that is even easier for Him* (30:27 — *“And He is the One Who originates the creation then will resurrect it—which is even easier for Him.”*). The Makkan deniers did not doubt that Allah created them; they doubted that He would bring them back. The verse answers by pointing to their own origin: you already were brought from nothing like this, and you already know it, because you see children born. To deny the second creation while affirming the first is inconsistent. The word insān is generic, but the lesson is personal. Each reader knows his origin was a drop; each reader knows he now argues.

**The Psychology Of The Open Challenger**

Khaṣīmun mubīn describes a character type that appears throughout al-Naḥl. Later verses will mention those who argue that Allah forced them into shirk (16:35 — *“The polytheists argue, “Had Allah willed, neither we nor our forefathers would have worshipped anything other than Him, nor prohibited anything without His command.””*), those who say revelation is fables of ancients (16:24 — *“And when it is said to them, “What has your Lord revealed?” They say, “Ancient fables!””*), those who attribute daughters to Allah while disliking daughters for themselves (16:57-59 — *“And they attribute ˹angels as˺ daughters to Allah—glory be to Him!—the opposite of what they desire for themselves”*). All are forms of khaṣm, argument that defends desire rather than seeks truth. Al-Qurṭubī notes that khaṣīm here does not mean a skilled debater in a praiseworthy sense, but a contentious opponent who uses speech to push away truth. The Qur'an distinguishes between jidāl that is good, as in *argue with them in the best way* (16:125 — *“Surely your Lord ˹alone˺ knows best who has strayed from His Way and who is ˹rightly˺ guided”*), and jidāl that is blameworthy, which is argument for falsehood. The same tongue can do either. The drop that became a tongue is tested by how it uses speech. This is why gratitude in this sūrah includes speech: acknowledging blessings, not arguing them away. The human who was created to be ʿabd, servant, becomes khaṣīm, adversary, when he forgets.
verses.5:
> And He created the cattle for you as a source of warmth, food, and ˹many other˺ benefits

**The First Blessing After The Rebuke**

After describing the human as a contentious challenger, the Qur'an immediately says: wa-l-anʿāma khalaqahā — and the cattle He created for you. The pronoun lakum, for you, is placed early to stress purpose and favor. Despite contention, provision continues. Anʿām in Qur'anic usage means grazing livestock: camels, cattle, sheep, and goats, as detailed in 6:142-144 — *“˹Allah has created˺ four pairs: a pair of sheep and a pair of goats—ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Has He forbidden ˹to you˺ the two males or the two females or what is in the wombs of the two females?”* where eight pairs are listed. These four kinds were the core wealth of Arabian society, providing transport, milk, meat, wool, leather, and social standing. By naming them right after the drop, the sūrah moves from origin to sustenance, showing that the One who created from a drop also sustains that creation with other creations. Al-Ṭabarī notes that khalaqahā stresses that even these familiar animals are not self-existing; they were created, assigned, and subjected. The human did not invent the camel's endurance or the sheep's wool.

**The Social World Of Anʿām**

For the first Makkan audience, anʿām were not abstract. They were currency, status, and survival. A man's wealth was counted in camels. A tribe's strength was measured by its herds. When the Qur'an says these were created for you, it touches the core of that economy and says, your wealth is a gift, not an achievement. This is why the sūrah later mentions that cattle bear burdens to lands you could not reach except with hardship (16:7 — *“And they carry your loads to ˹distant˺ lands which you could not otherwise reach without great hardship. Surely your Lord is Ever Gracious, Most Merciful”*). The same animal that gives warmth also makes trade possible, connecting distant markets. The mention of difʾ first also subtly refutes the idea that the world is purely for the strong. The weak, the cold, the hungry are considered first: warmth for those who shiver, food for those who hunger. In a society where the strong often seized grazing lands, this emphasis matters. The One who created cattle assigned them for all of you, not only for chiefs.

**Why The Verse Ends Without A Seal**

Unlike verses 1, 3, and 7, verse 5 does not end with a divine name or transcendence formula. It ends with benefits and eating, leaving the thought open. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that this openness invites the reader to continue to the next verses where beauty, transport, and mercy are added. The catalogue is cumulative. Each verse adds a layer: warmth and food, then beauty when returning and grazing, then burden-bearing, then riding and adornment, then unknown creations. The absence of a seal here is therefore rhetorical; it keeps the list moving. The reader is not allowed to stop at one blessing and say enough; he is led through an inventory that will later be summarized as uncountable (16:18 — *“If you tried to count Allah’s blessings, you would never be able to number them. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*).
verses.6:
> They are also pleasing to you when you bring them home and when you take them out to graze

**Beauty As A Recognized Blessing**

Verse 5 mentioned warmth, benefits, and food. Verse 6 adds jamāl — beauty. Wa-lakum fīhā jamālun ḥīna turīḥūna wa-ḥīna tasraḥūn — and for you in them is beauty when you bring them home in the evening and when you send them out to pasture in the morning. This is the only place in the Qur'an where cattle are explicitly described as a source of aesthetic pleasure. Elsewhere they are described as useful, but here they are pleasing to look at. Al-Rāzī highlights this as evidence that the Qur'an does not reduce creation to mere utility. Beauty is itself a benefit, a gift that nourishes the eye and heart. The Makkan who owned herds knew this beauty firsthand: the sight of camels returning at dusk, full, slow, dust rising, is a scene of prosperity and calm. The Qur'an validates that feeling and attributes it to Allah. Your pleasure when you see them is part of what He created for you. This reframes aesthetics as part of gratitude, not vanity.

**Why Beauty Matters In An Argument For Tawḥīd**

Sūrat al-Naḥl is arguing against shirk, association of partners with Allah. Why mention beauty? A purely utilitarian animal could be ugly and still provide milk and meat. Al-Rāzī argues that jamāl cannot be explained by material necessity; it points to a Creator who is Himself beautiful and loves beauty, as in the prophetic saying *Allah is beautiful and loves beauty* (Muslim 91).

**Linguistic Note On Jamāl And The Daily Cycle**

Jamāl in Arabic means beauty that is pleasing in appearance and proportion, distinct from ḥusn which can include inner goodness, and from zīnah which often means added adornment. The Qur'an uses jamāl only twice, here and in 15:16 — *“Indeed, We have placed constellations in the sky, and adorned it for all to see”* where it describes stars as beautiful. Both uses connect beauty to creation that guides or sustains. Turīḥūna and tasraḥūna are both in the form IV with plural address, indicating a habitual, collective action. The pronouns lakum and fīhā anchor the blessing: for you, in them. The benefit is not abstract; it is located in the animals themselves and directed to you. The verse's brevity — a single sentence — mirrors the simplicity of the scene it describes: evening, morning, herds, pleasure. No religious term is needed. The image does the work.
verses.7:
> And they carry your loads to ˹distant˺ lands which you could not otherwise reach without great hardship. Surely your Lord is Ever Gracious, Most Merciful

**Trade, Migration, And The Making Of Society**

For Makkans, this verse was not poetry but economics. Quraysh were traders. Their two annual journeys, to Yemen in winter and Syria in summer, mentioned in Sūrat Quraysh (106:2 — *“secure in their trading caravan ˹to Yemen˺ in the winter and ˹Syria˺ in the summer”*), depended completely on camels bearing athqāl. Without camels, there is no trade; without trade, there is no Makkan prosperity. By saying these animals carry your loads to distant lands, the Qur'an reminds Quraysh that their wealth, which they attributed to their own skill and to the protection of their idols, in fact rides on the backs of animals Allah created and subjected. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the verse also applies to migration, hijrah, which would soon become central to the Muslim community. Those who would leave Makkah for Abyssinia and later Madinah would do so with camels carrying their families and goods. The verse so anticipates the very experience of its listeners: the loads they would soon carry as emigrants are made possible by the same Creator they are being called to trust.

**The Concept Of Taskhīr Behind The Scene**

Though the word taskhīr, subjection, does not appear in this verse, the idea underlies it. Animals that are stronger than humans — a camel can kill a man — still allow themselves to be loaded, led, and directed. This obedience is not natural in the sense of automatic; it is a subjection placed by Allah. The Qur'an makes this explicit later: *And We have subjected them to them, so some they ride and some they eat* (36:72 — *“And We have subjected these ˹animals˺ to them, so they may ride some and eat others”*). Al-Qurṭubī points out that a child can lead a camel that could crush him, which shows that its docility is a divine gift, not a human achievement. The verse invites reflection on this: why does a powerful animal submit to a weaker human? The answer in the sūrah is that Allah subjected it for you. Gratitude therefore requires acknowledging the Subjugator, not merely using the subjected. When the Makkans loaded their caravans and thanked their idols for protection, they misdirected thanks. The camel's submission came from Allah, not from Hubal.
verses.8:
> ˹He also created˺ horses, mules, and donkeys for your transportation and adornment. And He creates what you do not know

**Why Mules And Donkeys Are Named**

Mentioning bighāl and ḥamīr alongside khayl shows the Qur'an's attention to the full range of society. Not everyone owned a horse; horses were expensive and required skill. Donkeys were the transport of the common person, the student, the farmer, the woman carrying water. Mules, offspring of horse and donkey, were valued for strength and endurance in mountainous terrain. By naming all three, the verse includes all classes. The poor man's donkey and the chief's horse are both created by Allah for human use. Al-Qurṭubī adds that this naming also has legal implications. The fact that anʿām were mentioned separately as food, while these three are mentioned for riding and adornment without mention of eating, was used by many jurists to argue that horse, mule, and donkey meat is not intended as food. The Prophet ﷺ explicitly forbade eating domestic donkeys on the day of Khaybar, as reported in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4216 and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1801, and most schools extend the prohibition to mules. Horse meat is treated differently; some schools permit it, others discourage it because horses are more valuable alive for riding and defense.

**Adornment That Is More Than Vanity**

Wa-zīnah — and as adornment. The word zīnah in the Qur'an can mean both natural beauty and added decoration. Here it refers to the dignity and splendor that riding confers. Al-Rāzī explains that riding a horse, especially a well-kept one, gives the rider a sense of elevation, visibility, and honor. In a society where leaders were recognized by their mounts, this was not superficial. A rider could be seen, heard, and followed. The Qur'an does not dismiss this human desire to appear well; it places it within divine creation. You want to ride and look dignified — Allah created the means for that. This is consistent with the sūrah's broader method: it does not tell people to suppress natural desires but to see them as gifts that point to the Giver. Later the sūrah will mention garments for protection and garments for adornment (16:81 — *“And Allah has provided you shade out of what He created, and has given you shelter in the mountains.”*), repeating the same pair: protection and beauty, necessity and delight. The pairing guards against two extremes: asceticism that rejects beauty and materialism that worships it.
verses.9:
> It is upon Allah ˹alone˺ to ˹clearly˺ show the Straight Way. Other ways are deviant. Had He willed, He would have easily imposed guidance upon all of you

**Other Ways Are Deviant**

Wa-minhā jā'ir — and among them, from those ways, are deviant ones. Jā'ir comes from j-w-r, to deviate, to turn aside unjustly. It describes a path that does not lead to the destination but veers off. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that the pronoun minhā refers to subul, paths, implied though not explicitly stated, meaning among paths there are those that are crooked. The Qur'an often contrasts one straight way with many crooked ways, as in 6:153 — *“So follow it and do not follow other ways, for they will lead you away from His Way.”*: *This is My straight path, so follow it, and do not follow other paths, for they will separate you from His path* (6:153 — *“So follow it and do not follow other ways, for they will lead you away from His Way.”*). The image is of a main road with side tracks that lead into desert or danger. The sūrah will later give examples of such deviant paths: attributing partners to Allah, saying Allah willed their shirk as excuse, calling revelation fables. Each is a jā'ir path. By mentioning deviant ways immediately after affirming that Allah shows the straight way, the verse makes clear that guidance is available but not automatic; people may still choose crooked tracks. The existence of deviation does not mean guidance failed; it means humans have choice.

**Had He Willed, He Could Have Forced Guidance**

Wa-law shā'a la-hadākum ajmaʿīn — had He willed, He would have guided you all together. This clause answers a hidden objection. If Allah alone shows the way, why are not all guided? The answer is that He could have forced guidance, but He willed to allow choice. Al-Rāzī explains that hadā here means compelled guidance, making everyone follow truth without option, which Allah is able to do but does not do because the purpose of creation includes testing. The same idea appears in 6:149 — *“Say, “Allah has the most conclusive argument. Had it been His Will, He would have easily imposed guidance upon all of you.””*: *Had He willed, He would have guided you all* (6:149 — *“Say, “Allah has the most conclusive argument. Had it been His Will, He would have easily imposed guidance upon all of you.””*) and 13:31 — *“Have the believers not yet realized that had Allah willed, He could have guided all of humanity?”* and 32:13 — *“Had We willed, We could have easily imposed guidance on every soul. But My Word will come to pass: I will surely fill up Hell with jinn and humans all together”*. Ashʿarī theologians cite this to show that guidance is by Allah's will, not by human merit alone, while Muʿtazilī thinkers emphasize that Allah wills to leave room for human earning, so that reward has meaning. Both agree on the outcome: diversity of response to guidance is part of divine wisdom, not inability. The verse therefore preserves both divine power and human responsibility. Allah is able to guide all, He has shown the straight way clearly, yet He leaves the walking to you.

The placement after transport and before rain is not random. Verses 5-8 gave mounts, verse 15-16 will give landmarks and stars, and this verse gives direction for the heart. Without qaṣd al-sabīl, even the best mount goes astray. The Makkan audience understood travel. They knew that a caravan with strong camels but no guide perishes. The verse says, for your ultimate journey, Allah Himself is the guide who shows qaṣd, the straight aim. This also reframes the earlier prohibition against hastening Allah's command. The one who hastens judgment wants to skip the road; the one who follows qaṣd walks it patiently. The sūrah will close with *Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom* (16:125 — *“Invite ˹all˺ to the Way of your Lord with wisdom and kind advice, and only debate with them in the best manner.”*), echoing this same sabīl.

**A Verse That Guards Against Two Errors**

This verse guards against two opposite errors that still divide people. The first error is to think guidance is not from Allah, that humans find it alone by reason. The verse says wa-ʿalā Allāhi qaṣdu al-sabīl — upon Allah is the showing, not upon reason alone. The second error is to think that since Allah could guide all, those who are not guided are excused. In practical terms, the believer is taught to ask Allah for guidance constantly, as in al-Fātiḥah *Guide us to the straight path* (1:6 — *“Guide us along the Straight Path”*), while also striving to walk, because the path has been shown.
verses.10:
> He is the One Who sends down rain from the sky, from which you drink and by which plants grow for your cattle to graze

**The Descent That Makes Life Possible**

Huwa al-ladhī anzala min al-samā'i mā'an — He is the One who sends down water from the sky. The pronoun huwa is emphatic: He, not any partner, not any idol, not any force of nature independent of Him. Anzala indicates sending down from above, a descent that humans cannot produce. In Arabian context, rain was not a minor blessing; it was life itself. Without it, wells dry, pastures die, cattle perish, trade stops. Al-Ṭabarī notes that samā' here means the sky or the direction above, not only clouds, to stress that the source is beyond human control. The Qur'an repeats this gift throughout, as in 15:22 — *“We send fertilizing winds, and bring down rain from the sky for you to drink. It is not you who hold its reserves”* and 23:18 — *“We send down rain from the sky in perfect measure, causing it to soak into the earth. And We are surely able to take it away”*, always with the same emphasis: you do not send it down. The verse then divides the water's use into two immediate benefits: lakum minhu sharābun wa-minhu shajarun fīhi tusīmūn — from it you have drink and from it comes vegetation in which you pasture your cattle. Sharāb is drink for humans directly, shajar here means plants, trees, herbage generally, not only trees, and tusīmūn means to pasture, to let cattle graze freely. The same rain serves both you and your animals, linking human and animal dependence on one source.

**Shajar As All Vegetation**

Shajar is usually translated as trees, but commentators explain that here it means all plants, herbage, and shrubs that cattle graze, including what Arabs call hashīsh and kalā'. Al-Qurṭubī cites linguistic usage where shajar can mean any plant with a stalk, not only tall trees. The phrase fīhi tusīmūn, in which you pasture, uses sāma, to graze freely, distinct from raʿā which can mean to tend. Tusīmūn suggests letting animals roam in pasture, a scene of abundance where herbage is plentiful enough that cattle can be left to eat. This implies rain that is not scant but enough to produce pasture. In a desert, such pasture appears suddenly after rain, transforming barren land into green within days. Those who witnessed this transformation knew it as a resurrection in miniature, which is why the Qur'an often links rain to resurrection: *And We send down from the sky blessed water and give growth and so to gardens and grain* (50:9 — *“And We send down blessed rain from the sky, bringing forth gardens and grains for harvest”*) and *Look at the traces of Allah's mercy, how He gives life to the earth after its death. Indeed He will give life to the dead* (30:50 — *“See then the impact of Allah’s mercy: how He gives life to the earth after its death! Surely That ˹same God˺ can raise the dead. For He is Most Capable of everything”*). The pasture that appears after rain is therefore both provision and proof.
verses.11:
> With it He produces for you ˹various˺ crops, olives, palm trees, grapevines, and every type of fruit. Surely in this is a sign for those who reflect

**From Water To Crops To Fruits**

Yunbitu lakum bihi al-zarʿa wa-l-zaytūna wa-l-nakhīla wa-l-aʿnāba wa-min kulli al-thamarāt — with it He produces for you crops, olives, palm trees, grapevines, and from every fruit. The pronoun bihi refers back to the water in verse 10. One water, many outputs. Zarʿ is general crops, grains like wheat and barley that are staple food. Zaytūn, olives, provide oil, food, and light. Nakhīl, palm trees, provide dates, shade, building material, and fiber. Aʿnāb, grapevines, provide fruit, drink, and raisins. Then the summary wa-min kulli al-thamarāt — and from every type of fruit — widens beyond the four named to include all fruits known and unknown.

**Why Olives, Palms, And Grapevines Are Singled Out**

These three trees have special status in Qur'anic imagery. Zaytūn is mentioned in Sūrat al-Nūr as the blessed olive tree whose oil gives light: *lit from a blessed olive tree* (24:35 — *“His light is like a niche in which there is a lamp, the lamp is in a crystal, the crystal is like a shining star, lit from ˹the oil of˺ a blessed olive tree, ˹located˺ neither to the east nor the west, whose oil would almost glow, even without being touched by fire.”*). It was central to Mediterranean economy, providing oil for food, lamp, soap, and medicine. Nakhīl, palms, are called *like clustered columns* and are praised for their resilience in desert, providing shade where no other tree grows. Dates were staple food that could be stored for months, crucial for travel. Aʿnāb, grapevines, were the fruit of highlands and gardens, requiring trellising and care, symbolizing cultivation and settlement. By naming these three, the Qur'an covers different ecologies: olives for hills, palms for desert oases, grapes for valleys and terraces. It shows that Allah's provision adapts to different lands and climates, not only one. Al-Qurṭubī adds that these three are also mentioned together in 6:99 — *“And from palm trees come clusters of dates hanging within reach.”* and 13:4 — *“And on the earth there are ˹different˺ neighbouring tracts, gardens of grapevines, ˹various˺ crops, palm trees—some stemming from the same root, others standing alone.”* as examples of diverse fruits from one water, indicating they were recognized as a set representing agricultural diversity.

**The Connection To Gratitude And Ingratitude**

In the context of Sūrat al-Niʿam, this verse deepens the argument against ingratitude. If Allah produces for you crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit, then to attribute this to idols or to one's own effort alone is to cover the favor, which is the literal meaning of kufr. The verse says lakum — for you — twice in verses 10-11, stressing that the production is for human benefit. The appropriate response is shukr, gratitude, which in the Qur'an includes acknowledging the Giver, using the gift in obedience, and not giving the gift's credit to others. The seal li-qawmin yatafakkarūn suggests that ingratitude is a failure of reflection. Those who do not reflect see only crops, not the One who grew them. Those who reflect see through crops to the Creator. The sūrah will later say *If you tried to count Allah's blessings, you would never number them* (16:18 — *“If you tried to count Allah’s blessings, you would never be able to number them. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*), and this verse gives a taste of why counting fails: even from one water, the types of fruit are too many to list.
verses.12:
> And He has subjected for your benefit the day and the night, the sun and the moon. And the stars have been subjected by His command. Surely in this are signs for those who understand

**Stars Subjected By His Command**

Wa-l-nujūmu musakhkharātun bi-amrihi — and the stars have been subjected by His command. Nujūm, stars, includes all stars, planets, and constellations. The construction musakhkharātun bi-amrihi stresses that their subjection is by His command, His amr, the same word that opened the sūrah. The stars follow orbits, appear and disappear, guide travelers, yet they do so by command, not by independent will. The Qur'an says elsewhere *And He made the stars for you to be guided and so in darkness of land and sea* (6:97 — *“And He is the One Who has made the stars as your guide through the darkness of land and sea. We have already made the signs clear for people who know”*). In pre-Islamic Arabia, star lore was advanced; Arabs navigated by stars and attributed rain to star positions, saying *we were given rain by such-and-such star*.

**Day And Night As Mercy And Measure**

The Qur'an often pairs night and day as two mercies: *And among His signs is your sleep by night and by day and your seeking of His bounty* (30:23 — *“And one of His signs is your sleep by night and by day ˹for rest˺ as well as your seeking His bounty ˹in both˺. Surely in this are signs for people who listen”*). Night is not absence of mercy but a mercy itself: it provides rest, coolness, cover, and a time for reflection. Day is mercy for work, seeking provision, and seeing. Together they create a rhythm that matches human biology. Modern science confirms that human circadian rhythm depends on light-dark cycles, but the Qur'an noted the benefit long before: night for sukūn, tranquility, day for movement. Al-Qurṭubī adds that without night, humans would be exhausted by constant light and heat; without day, they could not farm or travel. The subjection includes both the existence and the alternation. Allah did not create only day or only night; He created both and made them alternate in measure, as in 73:20 — *“Allah ˹alone˺ keeps a ˹precise˺ measure of the day and night.”*: *Allah measures night and day*. This measurement is itself a sign of wisdom, not randomness.

**Sun And Moon: Two Lights With Different Roles**

Al-shamsa wa-l-qamara — sun and moon — are mentioned together throughout the Qur'an as two lights with different functions. Sun is diyā', intense light and heat; moon is nūr, reflected gentle light, as in 10:5 — *“He is the One Who made the sun a radiant source and the moon a reflected light, with precisely ordained phases, so that you may know the number of years and calculation ˹of time˺.”*: *He made the sun a radiant light and the moon a reflected light and measured for it stages that you might know number of years and calculation* (10:5 — *“He is the One Who made the sun a radiant source and the moon a reflected light, with precisely ordained phases, so that you may know the number of years and calculation ˹of time˺.”*). Sun ripens crops mentioned in previous verse; moon marks months for fasting, pilgrimage, and trade. Both are subjected, meaning they follow fixed courses that humans can rely on. Al-Rāzī notes that their subjection includes that they do not collide, do not deviate, do not need rest. They serve continuously. This continuous service, without wage or complaint, is presented as evidence that they are commanded, not divine. A god does not serve without ceasing for the benefit of others; a subjected creature does. The verse uses their very usefulness to disprove their divinity.

Verse 9 said upon Allah is to show the straight way. Verse 12 shows that He also shows the physical way via stars and celestial bodies. The link is subtle: just as stars guide travelers in darkness of land and sea, revelation guides hearts in darkness of ignorance. Both are subjected by His command. The sūrah will make this explicit in 16:16 — *“Also by landmarks and stars do people find their way”*: *and landmarks, and by the stars they are guided*. The same verb hadā, to guide, is used for stars and for revelation. The reader is being taught to see guidance everywhere: in sky and in Book, both from same Commander.
verses.13:
> And ˹He subjected˺ for you whatever He has created on earth of varying colours. Surely in this is a sign for those who are mindful

**Why Color Is Mentioned**

Color is a powerful sign because it is immediately visible and deeply tied to recognition and enjoyment. A world in one color would be functional but monotonous. Allah created a world where even of the same species, individuals differ: no two human faces identical, no two leaves exactly alike, yet all from same soil and water. Al-Rāzī argues that difference in colors with unity of origin is proof of a Wise Creator who intends beauty and distinction. If matter alone produced things, one would expect uniformity from uniform material. Instead, from one earth come black soil, white salt, red clay, green plants, blue water, yellow fruits. The Qur'an draws attention to this elsewhere: *And among His signs is the creation of heavens and earth and the diversity of your languages and colors. Surely in that are signs for those who know* (30:22 — *“And one of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the diversity of your languages and colours.”*) and *Do you not see that Allah sends down water from sky, then We bring forth fruits of varying colors, and in mountains are streaks white and red of varying colors and intensely black* (35:27 — *“And in the mountains are streaks of varying shades of white, red, and raven black”*). The present verse condenses that whole argument into one clause: varying colors on earth, for you.

**A Sign For Those Who Are Mindful**

Inna fī dhālika la-āyatan li-qawmin yadhakkarūn — surely in this is a sign for those who are mindful, who remember, who take heed. Yadhakkarūn comes from dh-k-r, to remember, to be reminded. The seal changes again: verse 11 for those who reflect, verse 12 for those who understand, now for those who are mindful. Al-Zamakhsharī explains the progression: reflection is needed for crops from one water, understanding for celestial systems, remembrance for the obvious diversity under your feet that you see every day but forget to consider. This fits Sūrat al-Niʿam's method: it does not introduce strange miracles; it asks you to notice the ordinary with new eyes.
verses.14:
> And He is the One Who has subjected the sea, so from it you may eat tender seafood and extract ornaments to wear. And you see the ships ploughing their way through it, so you may seek His bounty and give thanks ˹to Him˺

**Tender Meat From A Salty Source**

Li-ta'kulū minhu laḥman ṭariyyan — so that you may eat from it tender meat. Laḥm ṭarī is fresh, tender seafood, mainly fish. The Qur'an describes sea food as ṭarī, tender, to contrast with land meat that requires slaughtering, skinning, and often aging. Sea food is ready, soft, easily digestible. Al-Qurṭubī notes the legal implication: sea food is lawful without ritual slaughter, and can be eaten even in iḥrām, the state of pilgrimage where land hunting is forbidden, as in 5:96 — *“But hunting on land is forbidden to you while on pilgrimage.”*: *Lawful to you is game of the sea and its food as provision for you and travelers* (5:96 — *“But hunting on land is forbidden to you while on pilgrimage.”*). The tenderness also hints at mercy: from salty, bitter water comes soft, palatable meat. The same water that could kill from thirst if drunk produces food that sustains. Al-Rāzī sees this as a sign of divine power to bring opposite from opposite: fresh from salty, soft from harsh, life from a realm that can cause death. The phrase minhu, from it, indicates the sea itself is source, not only its shore.

**Ornaments Extracted From Depths**

Wa-tastakhrijū minhu ḥilyatan talbasūnahā — and you extract from it ornaments that you wear. Ḥilyah means ornament, jewelry, adornment, specifically pearls and coral, as clarified in 55:22 — *“Out of both ˹waters˺ come forth pearls and coral”*: *From both seas come forth pearl and coral* (55:22 — *“Out of both ˹waters˺ come forth pearls and coral”*). The verb tastakhrijū, you extract, indicates effort: diving, gathering, crafting. Yet the material is created by Allah, not by humans. Pearls form inside oysters, coral grows as living colonies, both hidden in depths that humans cannot make. Their extraction as adornment shows that the sea's benefits are not only nutritional but aesthetic, parallel to earlier mention of jamāl in cattle and zīnah in horses. The sea, which looks uniform from surface, contains hidden beauty that becomes visible only when brought up. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that ḥilyah that you wear includes both men and women, though in Arabian custom pearls were worn by women; the verse includes all who adorn themselves. The fact that ornaments come from sea, not only from earth mines, expands the idea of earth's varying colors to sea's hidden colors.

**Seeking Bounty And Giving Thanks**

Wa-li-tabtaghū min faḍlihi wa-laʿallakum tashkurūn — and so that you may seek His bounty and so that you may give thanks. Two purposes are given for sea subjection. First, seeking faḍl, bounty, which includes trade, travel, fishing, and profit. The Qur'an uses faḍl for provision sought through effort, especially via sea trade, as in 17:66 — *“It is your Lord Who steers the ships for you through the sea, so that you may seek His bounty. Surely He is ever Merciful to you”*: *Your Lord is He who drives the ship for you through the sea that you may seek of His bounty* (17:66 — *“It is your Lord Who steers the ships for you through the sea, so that you may seek His bounty. Surely He is ever Merciful to you”*).
verses.15:
> He has placed into the earth firm mountains, so it does not shake with you, as well as rivers, and pathways so you may find your way

**Mountains As Stabilizers**

Wa-alqā fī al-arḍi rawāsiya a tamīda bikum — and He cast into the earth firm mountains, so it does not shake with you. Alqā means to cast, to place, to throw down firmly, indicating a deliberate act of setting. Rawāsī is plural of rāsiyah, firm, anchored, from r-s-w, to be firm, to be anchored like a ship. An tamīda bikum — so that it does not sway, shake, or tilt with you — explains purpose. Al-Ṭabarī reports that early commentators understood mountains as pegs that stabilize the earth, preventing it from shaking with its inhabitants. The image appears elsewhere: *And We made in the earth firm mountains lest it shake with them* (21:31 — *“And We have placed firm mountains upon the earth so it does not shake with them, and made in it broad pathways so they may find their way”*) and *And the mountains as stakes* (78:7 — *“and ˹made˺ the mountains as ˹its˺ pegs”*). Al-Rāzī discusses two kinds of stability: physical, preventing earthquakes and excessive movement, and ecological, anchoring soil, storing water, and providing climate regulation. Modern geology notes that mountains have deep roots that stabilize tectonic plates, a meaning that aligns with the Qur'anic image of mountains as awtād, stakes, though the verse speaks in terms accessible to its first audience: you feel stable underfoot because mountains were cast.

**Rivers And The Gift Of Moving Water**

Wa-anhāran — and rivers. The word is added without verb, governed by alqā, He cast rivers as well. Anhār is plural of nahr, river, stream, flowing water. In Arabia, rivers in the sense of permanent large rivers were rare; the term includes streams, wadis that flow after rain, and underground channels that surface as springs. Al-Qurṭubī notes that rivers are mentioned after mountains because most rivers originate in mountains, from snowmelt and springs. The pairing is natural: mountains store water as snow and release it as rivers, providing continuous flow. This is a second stabilization: mountains stabilize earth, rivers stabilize life by ensuring water does not remain stagnant in one place but moves to where needed. The Qur'an often pairs mountains and rivers as in 13:3 — *“And He is the One Who spread out the earth and placed firm mountains and rivers upon it, and created fruits of every kind in pairs.”* and 27:61 — *“Or ˹ask them,˺ “Who made the earth a place of settlement, caused rivers to flow through it, placed firm mountains upon it, and set a barrier between ˹fresh and salt˺ bodies of water?”*, showing a system: firm heights and flowing waters together make land habitable. Without mountains, earth would shake; without rivers, it would be barren.
verses.16:
> Also by landmarks and stars do people find their way

**The Grammar Of Guidance**

Yahtadūn is from h-d-y, to be guided, to find way. The same root appears in verse 9 for Allah showing straight way and in verse 15 for finding way via paths. Here it is used for physical navigation, but the spiritual resonance remains. Al-Zamakhsharī points out that the verse uses bi- for both landmarks and star, indicating means: by means of landmarks and by means of star they are guided. The means are created, but guidance itself is from Allah who created means. This subtle grammar prevents attributing guidance to landmarks or stars themselves. They are instruments, not independent guides. The Qur'an elsewhere says *And He made stars for you to be guided and so in darkness of land and sea* (6:97 — *“And He is the One Who has made the stars as your guide through the darkness of land and sea. We have already made the signs clear for people who know”*), making explicit that stars are made for guidance, not that they guide by themselves. The verse so continues the argument against shirk: even guidance via stars is from Allah, not from stars as deities.

**Why The Translation Adds A Question**

The translation provided for this verse includes an extra sentence: *Almighty Allah or Powerless Gods?* The translation's added heading is an interpretive gloss; the Arabic of the verse itself reads: *and by landmarks, and by the stars they are guided*. The added question reflects the context of verses 17-22 which contrast Allah who creates with idols who create nothing. Many translations insert such headings or rhetorical questions to link verses, but the Arabic of 16:16 does not contain it. Therefore the blockquote must include *Almighty Allah or Powerless Gods?* exactly as in translation file, even though it is not Qur'anic text. verses.17:
> Can the One Who creates be equal to those who do not? Will you not then be mindful

**A Question That Answers Itself**

A-fa-man yakhluqu ka-man lā yakhluqu — is then He who creates like one who does not create? The particle a-fa introduces a rhetorical question that expects a negative answer: of course not. Man yakhluqu refers to Allah, the Creator established in previous verses through heavens, earth, humans, cattle, rain, crops, night, day, sun, moon, stars, earth colors, sea, mountains, rivers, paths, landmarks. Man lā yakhluqu refers to idols and false gods that create nothing. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the idols did not create anything, not even a fly, as 22:73 — *“And if a fly were to snatch anything away from them, they cannot ˹even˺ retrieve it from the fly.”* says: *Those you call upon besides Allah will never create a fly even if they gathered together for it* (22:73 — *“O humanity! A lesson is set forth, so listen to it ˹carefully˺: those ˹idols˺ you invoke besides Allah can never create ˹so much as˺ a fly, even if they ˹all˺ were to come together for that.”*). The comparison is not between two creators of different power, but between Creator and non-creator. The Qur'an uses this argument repeatedly because it appeals to basic reason: how can you give equal devotion to one who gives everything and to one who gives nothing? The question is short but it gathers the entire blessings catalogue and turns it into a proof.

**The Logic Of Creation As Proof Of Divinity**

The argument from creation to Creator is central to al-Naḥl. This is the Qur'anic definition of shirk's irrationality: giving what belongs to Creator to non-creator. Al-Rāzī formalizes the argument: premise one, Allah creates all these things; premise two, idols create nothing; conclusion, they are not equal and should not be treated equally in worship. The Makkans knew Allah was Creator; they said so when asked, as 29:61 — *“If you ask them ˹O Prophet˺ who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon ˹for your benefit˺, they will certainly say, “Allah!””* says: *If you ask them who created heavens and earth, they will say Allah* (29:61 — *“If you ask them ˹O Prophet˺ who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon ˹for your benefit˺, they will certainly say, “Allah!””*).

**The Psychological Power Of Comparison**

The Qur'an often uses comparison to expose shirk's absurdity, as in 13:16 — *“Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?””*: *Are the blind and seeing equal, or are darkness and light equal?* (13:16 — *“Or can darkness and light be equal?””*). Here the comparison is between creating and not creating. The human mind naturally values the maker over the non-maker. If two people claim your gratitude, one who built your house and one who did nothing, you would thank the builder. The verse applies this natural judgment to worship. Al-Qurṭubī points out that the verse does not say *is the Creator like the non-creator* in abstract terms; it says *is He who creates like one who does not create*, using active verbs to make the action vivid. Yakhluqu is present tense, indicating ongoing creation, not only initial. Allah continues to create: rain now, crops now, humans now. Idols continue to create nothing, now and ever.

**From Mindfulness To Counting Blessings**

The call a-fa-lā tadhakkarūn — will you not be mindful — is answered in the next verse: *If you tried to count Allah's blessings, you would never number them* (16:18 — *“If you tried to count Allah’s blessings, you would never be able to number them. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*). Mindfulness leads to counting, and counting leads to realizing uncountability, which leads to gratitude and humility. The verse serves as a hinge between the catalogue and its summary. It says, you have heard the list; now ask yourself, can the One who does all this be equal to those who do none of it?
verses.18:
> If you tried to count Allah’s blessings, you would never be able to number them. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**A Number Nobody Can Reach**

The verse says that if a person set out to count the blessings of God, he would not be able to number them. The claim is not a figure of speech but a fact of the human position: the health of the body alone, the air, the water, the food, the family, the guidance — each one opens into more than the person holding it can see. Al-Ṭabarī noted that even a single blessing, like sight, contains a chain of gifts inside it: the eye, the light to see by, the mind that reads what the eye sees, and the names the mind gives to things. The Book states the same conclusion in another sūrah and adds what the human being does with the total: you will not be able to count it, and man is indeed unjust and ungrateful (14:34 — *“If you tried to count Allah’s blessings, you would never be able to number them.”*).

**The Sūrah of Blessings**

Al-Qurṭubī records that some of the early scholars called this sūrah the Sūrah of Blessings, because of this verse and the long catalogue of provision that runs through its opening verses. The name fits the way the chapter works: rain, cattle, crops, the sea, the ships, the stars used for navigation, the child brought out of the womb knowing nothing, the birds held in the air. The catalogue ends where the verse in front of us ends, with the reader out of his depth, and the name is a reminder that the sūrah is not a list to be finished but a habit of noticing to be formed.

**The Two Names at the End**

The verse closes with the statement that God is Forgiving, Merciful, and the pairing is placed here on purpose. A man who has been given more than he can count, and who has thanked God for a fraction of it, is looking at a debt he cannot pay. The two names answer that position. The Book gives the same answer in the promise it repeats to the Children of Israel: if you are grateful, I will surely give you more (14:7 — *“And ˹remember˺ when your Lord proclaimed, ‘If you are grateful, I will certainly give you more. But if you are ungrateful, surely My punishment is severe.’””*). What the verse leaves the reader is not a burden of accounting but a direction of life: the gifts cannot be repaid, so the least a person can do is notice them and live as one who has noticed.
verses.19:
> And Allah knows what you conceal and what you reveal

**The Knowledge That Includes the Secret**

The verse is short and complete: God knows what you conceal and what you reveal. The pair of words covers the whole of a person's life — the thought kept inside, the deed done in private, the word spoken in public, the act done in the open. Al-Ṭabarī read it as the answer to the question of what a human being actually is before God: the claim he makes with his tongue is weighed against what his heart is holding, and both are in view.

**Why the Sentence Sits Here**

The verse stands between the sūrah's long catalogue of blessings and the argument that follows against the idols. The idols, the next verses say, do not create anything, are dead, and do not know when they will be raised (16:20-21 — *“They are dead, not alive—not even knowing when their followers will be resurrected”*). The contrast is between a knower and things that cannot know. A god who is unaware of a secret need cannot be asked to supply it; the Lord who sees both the hidden and the open is the only one worth calling on. The Book uses the same knowledge of hidden and open as evidence for God elsewhere, in the argument with the angels over Adam (2:33 — *“Then when Adam did, Allah said, “Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?””*) and in the statement that God knows what people hide (27:74 — *“And surely your Lord knows what their hearts conceal and what they reveal”*), and the same words come back later in this sūrah (16:23 — *“Without a doubt, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal. He certainly does not like those who are too proud”*).

**The Blessing and the Warning in One Sentence**

The sūrah has just been counting gifts a person cannot number and has just described God as forgiving and merciful. The sentence in front of us is what makes those two facts a test rather than a comfort. Gratitude for the gifts and trust in the mercy can both be performed with the tongue; the verse says the performance does not settle the matter, because the One receiving it already knows the difference between the words and the heart. It also prepares the reader for what the sūrah says a few verses later about the plotters whose plans were made in secret and who were met by the punishment from a direction they had not considered (16:26 — *“Indeed, those before them had plotted, but Allah struck at the ˹very˺ foundation of their structure, so the roof collapsed on top of them, and the torment came upon them from where they did not expect”*).
verses.20:
> But those ˹idols˺ they invoke besides Allah cannot create anything—they themselves are created

**The Idols That Create Nothing**

Wa-al-ladhīna yadʿūna min dūni Allāhi lā yakhluqūna shay'an wa-hum yukhlaqūn — but those they invoke besides Allah do not create anything, and they themselves are created. Yadʿūna means to call upon, invoke, pray to, worship. Min dūni Allāh means besides Allah, apart from Allah, as rivals. Lā yakhluqūna shay'an — they do not create anything, not even a small thing. Shay'an is indefinite, indicating nothing at all, even the smallest. Wa-hum yukhlaqūn — while they themselves are created, made, fashioned. The contrast is absolute: Creator vs created, active vs passive. Al-Ṭabarī explains that idols are made by humans from stone, wood, metal; they are created by hands that themselves were created by Allah. How then can they be gods? The verse continues the argument from verse 17: can One who creates be like those who do not? Now it adds, not only do they not create, they are themselves created, doubly disqualified. A creator cannot be equal to a non-creator who is himself created.

**Why The Verse Emphasizes Creation**

Creation is chosen as criterion because it was acknowledged by Makkans themselves. When asked who created heavens and earth, they said Allah, as 29:61 — *“If you ask them ˹O Prophet˺ who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon ˹for your benefit˺, they will certainly say, “Allah!””* and 31:25 — *“And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will definitely say, “Allah!” Say, “Praise be to Allah!” In fact, most of them do not know”* report. Yet they worshipped idols alongside Allah, giving them a share of devotion. The verse says, if you admit Allah creates and idols are created, then worship should go to Creator alone. This is the Qur'anic definition of tawḥīd al-rubūbiyyah leading to tawḥīd al-ulūhiyyah: acknowledging Allah as Lord, Creator, leads to worshipping Him alone. Al-Rāzī notes that lā yakhluqūna shay'an includes inability to create even a fly, as 22:73 — *“O humanity! A lesson is set forth, so listen to it ˹carefully˺: those ˹idols˺ you invoke besides Allah can never create ˹so much as˺ a fly, even if they ˹all˺ were to come together for that.”* says, or to create themselves. Their being created is visible: idols are carved, erected, broken, repaired. The Makkans saw idols being made in workshops. The verse asks them to reflect on what they saw with their own eyes: you make them, then you worship them.
verses.21:
> They are dead, not alive—not even knowing when their followers will be resurrected

**Dead, Not Living**

Amwātun ghayru aḥyā'in — they are dead, not living. This is the final disqualification of idols after they were described as not creating and themselves created. Now they are described as dead, without life. Amwāt is plural of mayyit, dead. Ghayru aḥyā' stresses negation: not alive at all, not in any sense. Al-Ṭabarī explains that idols are inanimate stones and wood, no life, no hearing, no seeing, no knowledge. Even if they are given forms of living beings, they lack life. The contrast with Allah is stark: Allah is al-Ḥayy, the Living, who does not die, as in 2:255 — *“Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him, the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining.”*: *Allah, there is no god except Him, the Living, the Sustainer* (2:255 — *“Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him, the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining.”*) and 25:58 — *“Put your trust in the Ever-Living, Who never dies, and glorify His praises. Sufficient is He as All-Aware of the sins of His servants”*: *And rely upon the Living who does not die* (25:58 — *“Put your trust in the Ever-Living, Who never dies, and glorify His praises. Sufficient is He as All-Aware of the sins of His servants”*). A living worshipper calling upon dead objects is a reversal of reality. Al-Rāzī notes that describing idols as dead also refutes those who worshipped angels, jinn, or dead humans as intermediaries; even if those beings had life once, their idols do not, and their ability to help after death is nonexistent.

**Not Knowing When They Will Be Resurrected**

Wa-mā yashʿurūna ayyāna yubʿathūn — and they do not perceive when they will be raised. Yashʿurūn from sh-ʿ-r means to perceive, sense, be aware. Ayyāna means when, at what time. Yubʿathūn means they will be resurrected, raised. There are two main interpretations reported. One is that the pronoun refers to idols: idols do not know when they themselves will be resurrected, if Allah gives them life on Day of Judgment to disavow worshippers. The other is that it refers to idolaters: idols do not know when their worshippers will be resurrected. Al-Qurṭubī mentions a report from Ibn ʿAbbās that Allah will give life to idols on Resurrection Day and gather them with devils to enter Fire, so that worshippers see their false gods condemned.

**Why Life And Knowledge Are Required For Divinity**

A god, to be worthy of worship, must be living, knowing, powerful. The Qur'an repeats this criterion: living, not dead; knowing, not ignorant; creating, not created. Idols fail all three. They are dead, not alive; they do not create; they do not know when resurrection will be. Allah succeeds all three: He is Living, Creator, Knower of when Hour will come, as 31:34 — *“Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware”* says: *Indeed Allah alone has knowledge of the Hour* (31:34 — *“Indeed, Allah ˹alone˺ has the knowledge of the Hour.”*). The verse therefore completes the demolition of shirk that began in 16:17 — *“Can the One Who creates be equal to those who do not? Will you not then be mindful”*. Verse 17 asked can Creator be equal to non-creator? Verse 20 said non-creators are themselves created. Verse 21 adds they are dead and ignorant. The progression leaves no room for idols to claim divinity. Al-Zamakhsharī notes the rhetorical force of amwātun ghayru aḥyā' — dead, not living — as a deliberate redundancy to remove any metaphorical interpretation that idols might be alive in some spiritual sense.

**A Verse That Completes The Demolition Of False Gods**

This verse completes the argument that began in 16:17 — *“Can the One Who creates be equal to those who do not? Will you not then be mindful”* and continued through 16:20 — *“But those ˹idols˺ they invoke besides Allah cannot create anything—they themselves are created”*. The idols are non-creating, created, dead, not alive, not knowing when they will be resurrected. Each step adds disqualification. The final step, not knowing when they will be raised, shows they lack knowledge of Hour, which is essential for divinity. Allah alone knows Hour, as 31:34 — *“Indeed, Allah ˹alone˺ has the knowledge of the Hour.”* says. The progression is logical and cumulative, making argument memorable and decisive for anyone who reflects on blessings and seeks truth.
verses.22:
> Your God is ˹only˺ One God. As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are in denial, and they are too proud

**Affirmation After Negation**

Ilāhukum ilāhun wāḥid — your God is One God. After verses 17-21 demolished idols as non-creating, created, dead, ignorant, this verse affirms the positive: your God, the One you already know as Creator and Provider, is One. Ilāh means god, object of worship, one to whom devotion is directed. Wāḥid means one, unique, without partner. The phrase ilāhukum, your God, is possessive and personal: the God who created you from a drop, who gave cattle, rain, crops, sea, mountains, is your God, not a distant deity. The repetition ilāhun wāḥid stresses oneness at bottom, attributes, and right to worship. Al-Ṭabarī explains that this is the core message that angels brought in verse 2: *Warn that there is no god except Me*. Now it is stated directly to the audience. The verse does not say there is one god among many; it says your God is One God, meaning the only true object of worship is One. This is tawḥīd in its simplest form, accessible to all.

**Why Hereafter Is Mentioned Here**
