The sūrah opened with *The command of Allah is at hand* (16:1 — *“The command of Allah is at hand, so do not hasten it. Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate ˹with Him in worship˺”*), referring to Hour. It then listed blessings that prove power to resurrect. Now it says those who do not believe in Hereafter have hearts that deny and are arrogant. The connection is that belief in Hereafter is necessary for gratitude to be complete. If this life is all, then blessings can be seen as mere chance to be enjoyed without thanks. If there is return, then blessings become trust to be accounted for. Al-Qurṭubī notes that Makkan idolaters did believe in Allah as Creator but denied resurrection, as 23:82 — *“They said, “Once we are dead and reduced to dust and bones, will we really be resurrected”* says: *When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we be resurrected?* (23:82 — *“They said, “Once we are dead and reduced to dust and bones, will we really be resurrected”*). Their denial was not of Allah's existence but of return, and that denial allowed them to continue injustice without fear. The verse says their hearts are munkiratun — they find truth strange, unfamiliar, because their hearts are accustomed to denial. The cure, implied, is dhikr and tawāḍuʿ, remembrance and humility.

**The Link Between Tawḥīd And Humility**

Your God is One God — this statement demands humility. If God is One, then no human can claim partnership in divinity, no tribe can claim its idol is equal, no self can claim independence. Arrogance, istikbār, is the opposite of tawḥīd because arrogance is claiming greatness for self that belongs to Allah alone. The Qur'an says *He does not like the arrogant* (16:23 — *“Without a doubt, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal. He certainly does not like those who are too proud”*). The sūrah will later say *So enter gates of Hell to abide in it; evil indeed is abode of arrogant* (16:29 — *“So enter the gates of Hell, to stay there forever. Indeed, what an evil home for the arrogant!””*). The sequence shows that arrogance is not a minor fault but a barrier to accepting oneness. Al-Rāzī explains that mustakbirūn are those who deem themselves too great to worship Allah alone or to follow a messenger who is a human like them. Their pride says, how can we follow a man, how can we abandon what our fathers worshipped? Tawḥīd requires humility to say, I am servant, not partner.

**A Verse That Summarizes The Makkan Conflict**

This verse condenses the whole Makkan conflict into two sentences. The Qur'an often describes disbelief as disease of heart, not defect of mind, as in 2:10 — *“There is sickness in their hearts, and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase. They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies”*: *In their hearts is disease, so Allah increased their disease* (2:10 — *“There is sickness in their hearts, and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase. They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies”*).
verses.23:
> Without a doubt, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal. He certainly does not like those who are too proud

**Certainty Of Divine Knowledge**

Lā jarama anna Allāha yaʿlamu mā yusirrūna wa-mā yuʿlinūn — without doubt, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Lā jarama is an emphatic expression meaning no doubt, certainly, without question. It introduces a statement that is definitive. The phrase repeats verse 19 almost verbatim: *Allah knows what you conceal and reveal*, but now with lā jarama and with third person yusirrūna, what they conceal, referring to those who deny Hereafter and are arrogant in previous verse. Al-Ṭabarī explains that this is to stress that Allah knows their denial and arrogance even when they hide it with polite words or public justifications. What they conceal includes hidden motives: pride, desire to keep status, fear of losing customers for idols. What they reveal includes open mockery: *ancient fables* (16:24 — *“And when it is said to them, “What has your Lord revealed?” They say, “Ancient fables!””*). Both are known. The repetition from verse 19 to 23 shows that knowledge was mentioned first as general principle, now as specific warning to deniers.

**The Connection To Next Verse About Fables**

Verse 24 will say when they are asked what has your Lord revealed, they say ancient fables. That answer is an example of what they reveal openly, but its root is concealed arrogance. They say fables because they deem themselves too great to accept revelation as guidance. The verse 23 therefore prepares for 24 by stating Allah knows both hidden arrogance and open dismissal. Al-Qurṭubī notes that lā yuḥibbu al-mustakbirīn is both statement and threat: if Allah does not love arrogant, then arrogant will not be guided, as 16:37 — *“Even though you ˹O Prophet˺ are keen on their guidance, Allah certainly does not guide those He leaves to stray, and they will have no helpers”* will say *Allah does not guide those He leaves to stray*, and will end in Hell as 16:29 — *“So enter the gates of Hell, to stay there forever. Indeed, what an evil home for the arrogant!””* says *evil abode of arrogant*. The sequence from knowledge to dislike to punishment is consistent.

**The Repetition Of Knowledge Phrase**

The phrase yaʿlamu mā yusirrūna wa-mā yuʿlinūn appears in 16:19 — *“And Allah knows what you conceal and what you reveal”* and again here in 16:23, almost identical. Repetition in Qur'an is never without purpose. First occurrence came after uncountable blessings and forgiveness, to remind that forgiveness requires sincerity. Second comes after describing hearts that deny and are arrogant, to warn that denial and arrogance are known even when hidden. The repetition frames the argument against idols: between two statements of divine knowledge, idols are shown to be ignorant and dead. The contrast is intentional: Allah knows hidden and open; idols know nothing, not even when they will be raised. Which deserves worship? The repetition also stresses that knowledge is central to divinity. A god who does not know cannot guide, cannot judge, cannot forgive. Allah's knowledge is what makes His forgiveness meaningful and His dislike just.
verses.24:
> And when it is said to them, “What has your Lord revealed?” They say, “Ancient fables!”

**A Question That Exposes Attitude**

Wa-idhā qīla lahum mādhā anzala rabbukum qālū asāṭīru al-awwalīn — and when it is said to them, what has your Lord revealed, they say, ancient fables. The question mādhā anzala rabbukum, what has your Lord revealed, is asked to test response to revelation. Rabbukum, your Lord, is personal, the One who created, sustains, knows. The expected answer from a grateful heart would be to acknowledge blessing. Instead, they say asāṭīru al-awwalīn — fables of ancients, tales of old peoples, myths. Asāṭīr is plural of usṭūrah, story, fable, often with connotation of fabricated tales that entertain but have no truth. Al-awwalīn means ancients, earlier peoples. Al-Ṭabarī explains that Makkan deniers called Qur'an asāṭīr because it contains stories of previous nations like Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, and they claimed these were merely old tales copied, not revelation. The same accusation appears in 6:25 — *“The disbelievers would ˹even˺ come to argue with you, saying, “This ˹Quran˺ is nothing but ancient fables!””*, 8:31 — *“This ˹Quran˺ is nothing but ancient fables!””*, 23:83 — *“We have already been promised this, as well as our forefathers earlier. This is nothing but ancient fables!””*, 25:5 — *“And they say, “˹These revelations are only˺ ancient fables which he has had written down, and they are rehearsed to him morning and evening.””*, 27:68 — *“We have already been promised this, as well as our forefathers earlier. This is nothing but ancient fables!””*, 68:15 — *“whenever Our revelations are recited to him, he says, “Ancient fables!””*, 83:13 — *“Whenever Our revelations are recited to them, they say, “Ancient fables!””*. It is a way to dismiss without engaging: label it as old stories, not relevant, not divine.

**Why They Call Revelation Fables**

Calling revelation fables serves two purposes for deniers. First, it avoids having to argue against its content. If Qur'an is from Allah, then its warnings about Hereafter and its calls to abandon idols must be taken seriously. If it is merely fables, it can be ignored as entertainment. Second, it protects social status. To admit that what Muhammad ﷺ recites is from your Lord would require changing worship, economy, and tribal customs. To call it fables allows continuation of existing ways while appearing to have a reason. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that asāṭīru al-awwalīn implies that these stories are not only old but also false, invented by ancients and now retold. The accusation is therefore that Prophet ﷺ is not a messenger but a storyteller who learned old tales from others, as 25:5 — *“And they say, “˹These revelations are only˺ ancient fables which he has had written down, and they are rehearsed to him morning and evening.””* says: *And they say, fables of ancients which he has written down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening* (25:5 — *“And they say, “˹These revelations are only˺ ancient fables which he has had written down, and they are rehearsed to him morning and evening.””*). The sūrah will answer this accusation later by pointing to linguistic inimitability and by noting that the Prophet ﷺ was unlettered and had no human teacher for such stories.

**Fables Accusation And The Theme Of Knowledge**

The accusation asāṭīru al-awwalīn is ironic because the stories in Qur'an are presented as true accounts with lessons, not fables for amusement. The Qur'an says *In their stories is a lesson for those of understanding; it is not a fabricated tale* (12:111 — *“In their stories there is truly a lesson for people of reason.”*). By calling them fables, deniers show they do not reflect on purpose of stories. The stories of destroyed peoples are warnings, not entertainment. The sūrah opened with command at hand and said do not hasten it, then listed blessings as signs, then argued idols are dead. Stories of ancients who denied and were destroyed fit this pattern: they are evidence that command does come. To call them fables is to refuse to be mindful, yadhakkarūn, and to refuse to understand, yaʿqilūn. The accusation therefore is not literary criticism but moral evasion.

**How Believers Should Respond To Such Dismissal**

The Qur'an teaches believers not to respond to fables accusation with anger alone but with clarity and patience. The sūrah later says *Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good urging* (16:125 — *“Surely your Lord ˹alone˺ knows best who has strayed from His Way and who is ˹rightly˺ guided”*). When someone says revelation is fables, the believer is to show that it is not: it contains guidance, law, mercy, knowledge of unseen, linguistic miracle, and consistent message of tawḥīd that fables do not contain. The believer also recognizes that label fables often comes from lack of reflection on blessings. A heart that has not reflected on cattle, rain, and stars as signs will also not reflect on stories of past peoples as lessons. The remedy is same: reflection, remembrance, humility. The verse therefore invites believers to be patient with deniers while remaining firm that revelation is from their Lord, not fables.
verses.25:
> Let them bear their burdens in full on the Day of Judgment as well as some of the burdens of those they mislead without knowledge. Evil indeed is what they will bear

**The Load Carried by the Misleaders**

The verse explains why the men who called the revelation old stories are not finished with the matter: they will carry their own burden in full on the Day of Judgement, and with it a share of the burden of the people they led astray without knowledge. The picture is a load on the back. The Book uses the same word of the leaders who lead others away, saying that they will bear their own burdens and other burdens along with them (29:13 — *“Yet they will certainly ˹be made to˺ carry their own burdens, as well as other burdens along with their own.”*). The Prophet put the rule in a plain sentence: whoever calls people to guidance has a reward like the rewards of those who follow him, and whoever calls to misguidance carries a sin like theirs, without anything being taken from the followers' own records (Muslim 2674). The follower is not excused by having been led; he answers for his own choice, and the man who opened the road answers for the road.

**"Without Knowledge"**

The words without knowledge fall on both sides of the scene. The misleaders did not study the matter and then deny it; they asserted with no evidence, and they dressed their ignorance in confidence, which is how one respected man's remark becomes the settled view of a whole town. The people who followed followed in the same blindness, taking their elders' word on a question the signs in the sky, the provision in their hands and the messengers among them had all addressed. Al-Rāzī noted that the phrase excuses neither party, since knowledge was within reach, and the Book is hardest on the man who sells his guess as certainty. The sūrah forbids the other version of that speech in the same passage, where men invent a rule and call it God's: do not say, of what your tongues falsely describe, that this is lawful and that is forbidden, inventing lies about God (16:116 — *“Do not falsely declare with your tongues, “This is lawful, and that is unlawful,””*).

**Speech That Carries Other People**

The verse stands right after the sentence in which they called the revelation ancient fables (16:24 — *“And when it is said to them, “What has your Lord revealed?” They say, “Ancient fables!””*), and the order is the point. Dismissing the Book was not a private opinion. Spoken by a man the town trusted, it became the reason other men never looked at it. The Book keeps every word on the record — not a word does a person utter without a watcher by him ready (50:18 — *“not a word does a person utter without having a ˹vigilant˺ observer ready ˹to write it down˺”*) — and it uses the same image of beasts carrying loads for the weight a person feels later (16:7 — *“And they carry your loads to ˹distant˺ lands which you could not otherwise reach without great hardship. Surely your Lord is Ever Gracious, Most Merciful”*). The warning is about the weight of what people say about God: a light sentence about old stories is written down as a burden, and it is carried together with the loads of everyone it turned away from the door.
verses.26:
> Indeed, those before them had plotted, but Allah struck at the ˹very˺ foundation of their structure, so the roof collapsed on top of them, and the torment came upon them from where they did not expect

**Plotting That Seems Secure**

Qad makara al-ladhīna min qablihim — indeed those before them had plotted. Makara means to plot, scheme, plan secretly with cunning, often to deceive or harm. Al-ladhīna min qablihim refers to previous nations who plotted against their messengers, like people of Nūḥ, ʿĀd, Thamūd, Pharaoh. Their plotting included mocking messengers, calling revelation fables, building structures of power to oppose truth. Al-Ṭabarī explains that makr here includes both ideological plotting, like saying revelation is fables, and physical plotting, like building strongholds to resist. The verse says qad, indeed, emphasizing that this is not hypothetical; it happened. Those before them plotted, just as Makkans plot now. The past is precedent. The sūrah uses past to warn present: you are not first to plot, and you will not be first to escape consequence.

**A Warning To Makkans And All Plotters**

The verse is addressed to Makkans who plotted against Prophet ﷺ, who met in Dār al-Nadwah to decide to imprison, kill, or expel him, as 8:30 — *“And ˹remember, O Prophet,˺ when the disbelievers conspired to capture, kill, or exile you. They planned, but Allah also planned. And Allah is the best of planners”* says: *And when those who disbelieved plotted against you to restrain you or kill you or expel you* (8:30 — *“And ˹remember, O Prophet,˺ when the disbelievers conspired to capture, kill, or exile you. They planned, but Allah also planned. And Allah is the best of planners”*). Their plotting was secret, but Allah knew, as verse 19 and 23 said He knows what they conceal. The verse says those before you plotted and their building collapsed; yours can too. Al-Qurṭubī notes that this is both warning and consolation: warning to plotters that their foundations are vulnerable, consolation to believers that plotting against truth ultimately fails. The verse's placement after discussion of bearing burdens of those misled shows that plotters not only bear own burdens but also cause collapse of those who follow them. Their bunyān includes followers who trusted their roof.
verses.27:
> Then on the Day of Judgment He will humiliate them and say, “Where are My ˹so-called˺ associate-gods for whose sake you used to oppose ˹the believers˺?” Those gifted with knowledge will say, “Surely disgrace and misery today are upon the disbelievers.”

**Humiliation After Plotting**

Thumma yawma al-qiyāmati yukhzīhim — then on Day of Resurrection He will humiliate them, disgrace them. Yukhzīhim from kh-z-y means to humiliate, disgrace, expose shame. After describing worldly collapse of their building in verse 26, this verse moves to otherworldly humiliation. Thumma indicates sequence: first worldly punishment from unexpected direction, then Resurrection Day humiliation. Al-Ṭabarī explains yukhzīhim as exposing their falsehood and making their disgrace visible to all. In world, plotters may appear powerful, respected; on Day, their plotting is exposed and they are humiliated. The verse shows that divine justice has two stages: immediate and ultimate. Worldly collapse may be seen by some, but Resurrection humiliation will be seen by all. This is both warning and consolation: oppressors may seem to escape in world, but they will not escape humiliation on Day.

**The Connection To Arrogance**

Verse 27 mentions humiliation, khizy, which is opposite of arrogance, istikbār, mentioned in verses 22-23, 29. Arrogant sought greatness in world by opposing believers for sake of idols; on Day they are humiliated. The Qur'an often pairs arrogance in world with humiliation in Hereafter, as in 40:76 — *“Enter the gates of Hell, to stay there forever. What an evil home for the arrogant!””*: *Enter gates of Hell to abide in it; evil indeed is abode of arrogant* (40:76 — *“Enter the gates of Hell, to stay there forever. What an evil home for the arrogant!””*). The question *Where are My partners?* also humiliates because it exposes that what they were arrogant for is nothing. They were proud of idols, proud of opposing believers, proud of their plotting. Now idols absent, opposition failed, plotting collapsed.

Those given knowledge in world become witnesses in Hereafter because knowledge entails responsibility to convey. The Qur'an says *so We have made you a middle community that you may be witnesses over people* (2:143 — *“And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community so that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you.”*).
verses.28:
> Those whose souls the angels seize while they wrong themselves will then offer ˹full˺ submission ˹and say falsely,˺ “We did not do any evil.” ˹The angels will say,˺ “No! Surely Allah fully knows what you used to do

**Souls Seized While Wronging Themselves**

Al-ladhīna tatawaffāhum al-malā'ikatu ẓālimī anfusihim — those whom angels take in death while they are wronging themselves. Tatawaffā from w-f-y means to take fully, to cause to die, to take soul. Al-malā'ikah, angels, are agents of death, as in 32:11 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Your soul will be taken by the Angel of Death, who is in charge of you. Then to your Lord you will ˹all˺ be returned.””*: *Say, the angel of death who is entrusted with you will take you* (32:11 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Your soul will be taken by the Angel of Death, who is in charge of you. Then to your Lord you will ˹all˺ be returned.””*). Ẓālimī anfusihim means wronging themselves, wrongdoers to themselves, because sin harms self first. Al-Ṭabarī explains that wronging self here means persisting in shirk, denial, and opposition to messengers, by this harming own souls that will face punishment. The phrase indicates that at moment of death, they are still in state of wrongdoing, not having repented. Angels come to take souls while they are in that state, making death itself a moment of exposure. The same phrase appears in 4:97 — *“When the angels seize the souls of those who have wronged themselves—scolding them, “What do you think you were doing?” they will reply, “We were oppressed in the land.””* for those who wronged themselves by staying among disbelievers without emigrating when able. Fa-alqaw al-salama — then they will offer submission, peace, surrender. The Qur'an describes similar deathbed claims in 6:23 — *“Their only argument will be: “By Allah, our Lord! We were never polytheists.””*: *By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists* (6:23 — *“Their only argument will be: “By Allah, our Lord! We were never polytheists.””*), and in 63:10 — *“And donate from what We have provided for you before death comes to one of you, and you cry, “My Lord!”*: *My Lord, if only You would delay me for brief term so I would give charity* (63:10 — *“If only You delayed me for a short while, I would give in charity and be one of the righteous.””*). All are too late.

**Why This Scene Is Placed Here**

After describing worldly collapse of plotters and Resurrection humiliation, the sūrah now describes death scene, which is intermediate between world and Resurrection. It shows that humiliation begins at death, not only on Day. Those who plotted and called revelation fables will at death try to surrender and deny, but angels will reject denial. This prepares for verse 29: *Enter gates of Hell to abide in it*. The sequence is: plotting in world, building collapse, death with false submission, angels' rebuttal, entry to Hell, then contrast with righteous. The scene also teaches that submission must be in world before death, not at death when seen. The Qur'an says *But repentance is not for those who do evil until when death comes to one of them, he says, indeed I have repented now* (4:18 — *“However, repentance is not accepted from those who knowingly persist in sin until they start dying, and then cry, “Now I repent!” nor those who die as disbelievers. For them We have prepared a painful punishment”*). True submission is before seeing angels.

**Why False Claim Of No Evil Fails**

Claiming *we did not do any evil* fails for three reasons. First, Allah knows, as verse says. Second, angels have recorded deeds, as 82:10-12 — *“honourable angels, recording ˹everything˺”* says *Indeed over you are keepers, noble writers who know what you do* (82:10-12 — *“honourable angels, recording ˹everything˺”*). Third, limbs will testify, as 36:65 — *“On this Day We will seal their mouths, their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will testify to what they used to commit”* says *Today We seal their mouths and their hands speak to Us and their feet bear witness to what they used to earn* (36:65 — *“On this Day We will seal their mouths, their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will testify to what they used to commit”*). The false claim therefore is futile. It also reveals self-deception: they truly believed their deeds were not evil because their hearts were in denial and arrogant, as verse 22 said. Their denial at death is continuation of denial in life. The angels' response *No, Allah knows* breaks self-deception and establishes truth before punishment.

**A Lesson On Sincerity Before Death**

The verse teaches that sincerity must be before death. Once angels arrive, claims of innocence are not accepted. True repentance is in world, when unseen, not at death when seen. The Qur'an says *Until when death comes to one of them, he says My Lord send me back, that I might do righteousness in what I left behind. No, it is a word he speaks* (23:99-100 — *“When death approaches any of them, they cry, “My Lord! Let me go back”*). The time for doing good is now, while soul is still in body and choice remains. The verse therefore urges listener not to delay repentance, not to be among those who wrong themselves and then offer false submission at last moment. The door of repentance is open now, as verse 18 said Allah is Forgiving, Merciful, but it closes at death.
verses.29:
> So enter the gates of Hell, to stay there forever. Indeed, what an evil home for the arrogant!”

**Command To Enter Hell**

Fa-udkhulū abwāba jahannama khālidīna fīhā — so enter gates of Hell to abide in it forever. The command udkhulū, enter, is said to those whose souls were taken while wronging themselves and who falsely claimed innocence. Abwāba jahannama, gates of Hell, indicates Hell has gates, doors, levels, as in 15:44 — *“It has seven gates, to each a group of them is designated.””*: *It has seven gates, for each gate is a portion assigned* (15:44 — *“It has seven gates, to each a group of them is designated.””*). Entering gates implies being ushered into punishment, not merely seeing it. Khālidīna fīhā means abiding in it forever, remaining permanently. Al-Ṭabarī explains khālidīna as remaining without end for those who died in shirk and denial. The command is given by angels after rebutting false claim of innocence. It shows that after death, there is no chance to argue; judgment is executed. The phrase fa-udkhulū, so enter, indicates consequence: because you wronged yourselves, denied, claimed no evil, and Allah knows what you did, therefore enter.

**What An Evil Home For The Arrogant**

Fa-la-bi'sa mathwā al-mutakabbirīn — indeed what an evil abode, dwelling, home for the arrogant. Bi'sa is exclamation of dispraise: how evil, how wretched. Mathwā from th-w-y means abode, dwelling, place where one stays, from same root as thāwī, resident. Al-mutakabbirīn, arrogant, those who sought greatness, refused truth. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that mathwā indicates place of residence, home, implying that Hell will be their home, where they stay, not temporary visit. The phrase la-bi'sa mathwā al-mutakabbirīn is used elsewhere: *So enter gates of Hell to abide in it; evil indeed is abode of arrogant* (16:29; 39:72 — *“It will be said to them, “Enter the gates of Hell, to stay there forever.” What an evil home for the arrogant”*; 40:76 — *“Enter the gates of Hell, to stay there forever. What an evil home for the arrogant!””*). Repetition shows that arrogance is specifically linked to Hell as its home. Why? Because arrogant refused to be servants in world, claimed greatness, so their fitting home is abode of humiliation.

**Why Arrogance Leads To Hell**

Arrogance, istikbār and takabbur, is repeatedly linked to Hell because it prevents acceptance of truth. Now consequence: evil home for arrogant. The Qur'an says *But those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell humiliated* (40:60 — *“Your Lord has proclaimed, “Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Surely those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, fully humbled.””*).

**The Contrast With Righteous Home**

Verse 30-31 will contrast this evil home with excellent home of righteous: *How excellent indeed is home of righteous, Gardens of Eternity* (16:30-31 — *“How excellent indeed is the home of the righteous”*). The pairing of evil home vs excellent home is deliberate: two homes, two groups, two answers to question what has your Lord revealed. Those who said ancient fables get evil home; those who said all best get excellent home. The sūrah uses mathwā for arrogant and dār for righteous? Actually verse 30 says *excellent is abode of righteous*, using mathwā? Let's check: verse 30 says *How excellent indeed is home of righteous* — same word mathwā? In Arabic, verse 30 says *wa-la-niʿma dāru al-muttaqīn*, excellent is abode of righteous, using dār, while verse 29 uses mathwā. Both mean home, but dār is more honorable. The contrast is clear: arrogant get wretched mathwā, righteous get excellent dār.

**Why Gates Are Mentioned**

Gates suggest that Hell is enclosed, with entry points that are controlled. No one enters without permission, and no one exits without permission. The image of gates also suggests that Hell has already been prepared, its gates exist now, waiting. The Qur'an says *Indeed Hell has been lying in wait* (78:21 — *“Indeed, Hell is lying in ambush”*). The command to enter gates therefore is not creation of new punishment but ushering into already prepared abode. Al-Rāzī notes that mentioning gates also indicates that Hell has different levels of punishment appropriate to different sins, and each gate leads to different level. The arrogant who opposed believers for sake of idols will enter through gate appropriate to arrogance and shirk. The mention of gates also contrasts with gates of Paradise that will be opened for righteous, as 39:73 — *“When they arrive at its ˹already˺ open gates, its keepers will say, “Peace be upon you!”* says *Until when they reach it, its gates are opened and its keepers say Peace be upon you* (39:73 — *“When they arrive at its ˹already˺ open gates, its keepers will say, “Peace be upon you!”*). Two sets of gates, two greetings, two homes.

The Qur'an says *And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups until when they reach it, its gates are opened* (39:71 — *“Those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in ˹successive˺ groups.”*).
verses.30:
> And ˹when˺ it is said to those mindful ˹of Allah˺, “What has your Lord revealed?” They say, “All the best!” For those who do good in this world, there is goodness. But far better is the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter. How excellent indeed is the home of the righteous

**A Contrasting Answer To Same Question**

Wa-idhā qīla li-l-ladhīna ittaqaw mādhā anzala rabbukum qālū khayran — and when it is said to those who are mindful of Allah, what has your Lord revealed, they say, all the best, goodness. This mirrors verse 24 where same question was asked to deniers and they said ancient fables. Now question asked to muttaqīn, those mindful, reverent, God-conscious, and they say khayran, goodness, best. Khayr means good, best, beneficial. Al-Ṭabarī explains that muttaqīn answer with khayran because they see revelation as good, containing guidance, mercy, law, stories that teach, promises that encourage. Their answer is short but comprehensive: all the best. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that khayran is indefinite, indicating great goodness, all kinds of goodness, not limited. The contrast between fables and goodness reveals hearts: deniers see revelation as old tales to dismiss, mindful see it as best to follow. Same revelation, opposite perceptions, due to difference in taqwa.

**Far Better Is Home Of Hereafter**

Wa-la-dāru al-ākhirati khayrun — but home of Hereafter is better. Lā here is emphatic, surely, indeed. Dāru al-ākhirah, home of Hereafter, is better than goodness in world. Al-Qurṭubī explains that even if worldly goodness is given to righteous, Hereafter is better in quality, quantity, and duration. Worldly goodness is mixed with hardship, temporary, limited; Hereafter goodness is pure, eternal, unlimited.

**Why The Home Is Called Excellent**

Niʿma dāru al-muttaqīn — how excellent is home of righteous — is praise that invites desire. The Qur'an often uses niʿma to praise Paradise, as in 3:136 — *“Their reward is forgiveness from their Lord and Gardens under which rivers flow, staying there forever. How excellent is the reward for those who work ˹righteousness˺”* and 29:58 — *“˹As for˺ those who believe and do good, We will certainly house them in ˹elevated˺ mansions in Paradise, under which rivers flow, to stay there forever. How excellent is the reward for those who work ˹righteousness!˺”*. The home is excellent because it is free from hardship, pure, eternal, and contains whatever righteous desire, as next verse says: *they will have whatever they desire* (16:31 — *“the Gardens of Eternity which they will enter, under which rivers flow. In it they will have whatever they desire. This is how Allah rewards the righteous”*). Al-Qurṭubī explains that dār here is excellent because its Builder is Allah, its inhabitants are righteous, its duration is forever, and its contents are beyond imagination. The colon at end of translation indicates that description follows, linking this verse to next. The listener who hears excellent home will naturally ask, what is that home? Next verse answers: Gardens of Eternity under which rivers flow.

The comparison wa-la-dāru al-ākhirati khayrun is similar to 87:17 — *“even though the Hereafter is far better and more lasting”*: *But Hereafter is better and more lasting* (87:17 — *“even though the Hereafter is far better and more lasting”*).
verses.31:
> the Gardens of Eternity which they will enter, under which rivers flow. In it they will have whatever they desire. This is how Allah rewards the righteous—

**Whatever They Desire**

Lahum fīhā mā yashā'ūn — in it they will have whatever they desire, whatever they wish. Mā yashā'ūn means whatever they will, desire, want. This is a comprehensive promise: in Paradise, desires are fulfilled without restriction, unlike world where desires often exceed ability or are prohibited. Al-Qurṭubī notes that this includes both what they desired in world and what they will desire in Paradise, and that their desires themselves will be purified, so they will not desire anything harmful. The phrase appears in several descriptions of Paradise, as in 41:31 — *“We are your supporters in this worldly life and in the Hereafter. There you will have whatever your souls desire, and there you will have whatever you ask for”*: *You will have in it whatever your souls desire* (41:31 — *“We are your supporters in this worldly life and in the Hereafter. There you will have whatever your souls desire, and there you will have whatever you ask for”*). Al-Rāzī explains that having whatever one desires is the ultimate freedom, because in world humans are constrained by need, law, and inability, while in Paradise constraints are removed for righteous, yet their will is aligned with good, so they desire only good.

**Why Eternity Matters**

ʿAdn, eternity, is stressed because worldly gardens are temporary: they wither, need maintenance, can be lost. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that ʿadn also implies residence that is settled, not traveling, so inhabitants feel at home, not as visitors. This contrasts with worldly life which is travel, as Prophet ﷺ said *Be in world as stranger or traveler* (Bukhārī 6416). In world, even excellent home is temporary; in Hereafter, excellent home is eternal.

**The Connection To Earlier Blessings**

Gardens with rivers flowing recall earlier blessings: rain from sky, rivers on earth, crops, fruits. In world, those blessings are signs and temporary provision. In Paradise, they become permanent reward, perfected. Rivers in world can flood or dry; rivers in Paradise flow continuously without harm. Fruits in world are seasonal; fruits in Paradise are always available, as 13:35 — *“The description of the Paradise promised to the righteous is that under it rivers flow; eternal is its fruit as well as its shade.”* says *Its fruit is permanent and its shade* (13:35 — *“The description of the Paradise promised to the righteous is that under it rivers flow; eternal is its fruit as well as its shade.”*). Whatever they desire in Paradise includes best of what they had in world, purified and increased. The sūrah so moves from worldly blessings that are uncountable but temporary to otherworldly blessings that are eternal, showing that gratitude for worldly blessings leads to eternal reward.

**Why Rivers Flowing Is Repeated**

The phrase under which rivers flow appears dozens of times in Qur'an as anchor of imagination. Water in desert is life, coolness, beauty, and its flow indicates continuity. A garden with river that stops would disappoint; a garden where rivers flow continuously is secure. Al-Rāzī notes that rivers flowing beneath indicates inhabitants are above rivers, in elevated position, looking down at flowing water, a scene of honor. The rivers are of different types: water, milk, honey, wine that does not intoxicate, as 47:15 — *“The description of the Paradise promised to the righteous is that in it are rivers of fresh water, rivers of milk that never changes in taste, rivers of wine delicious to drink, and rivers of pure honey.”* says. The diversity matches diversity of desires. Repetition is not filler but reminder that Paradise provision is flowing, not stagnant, always fresh.

**Desire Fulfilled As Ultimate Freedom**

Having whatever they desire is ultimate freedom because in world desires are constrained by inability, prohibition, and consequence. In Paradise, constraints are removed for righteous whose desires have been purified by taqwa. Al-Qurṭubī explains that they will not desire harmful because hearts purified, as 15:47 — *“We will remove whatever bitterness they had in their hearts. In a friendly manner, they will be on thrones, facing one another”* says. So fulfillment does not lead to excess; it leads to contentment. The phrase mā yashā'ūn indicates desires granted as they arise, without delay, without work. This is opposite of world where desire requires effort and may not be fulfilled. The promise is both about provision and will: your will, frustrated in world, will be fulfilled in Paradise as reward for aligning will with Allah's will through taqwa.
verses.32:
> those whose souls the angels take while they are virtuous, saying ˹to them˺, “Peace be upon you! Enter Paradise for what you used to do.”

**Souls Taken While Virtuous**

Al-ladhīna tatawaffāhum al-malā'ikatu ṭayyibīn — those whose souls angels take while they are virtuous, good, pure. Tatawaffāhum al-malā'ikatu, angels take them, same verb as in verse 28 for wrongdoers, but state differs: ẓālimī anfusihim vs ṭayyibīn. Ṭayyibīn means good, pure, virtuous, from ṭ-y-b, to be good, pure, pleasant. Al-Ṭabarī explains ṭayyibīn as those who are pure from shirk, sincere in faith, good in deeds, or those whose souls are taken in easy, gentle manner, without hardship. The contrast with verse 28 is deliberate: same angels, same act of taking souls, but different states and different greetings.

**Peace Be Upon You**

Yaqūlūna salāmun ʿalaykum — saying, peace be upon you. Angels say salām, peace, security, greeting. Salāmun ʿalaykum is greeting of Paradise, also greeting among believers in world, and greeting from Allah, as 36:58 — *“And “Peace!” will be ˹their˺ greeting from the Merciful Lord”* says *Peace, a word from a Merciful Lord* (36:58 — *“And “Peace!” will be ˹their˺ greeting from the Merciful Lord”*). Al-Qurṭubī says angels greet righteous at death with peace to calm fear, give glad tidings, and convey that they are safe from punishment. The greeting is in present tense, indicating ongoing peace, not temporary. It also indicates that angels are not harsh to righteous; they are gentle, welcoming. The same greeting will be heard in Paradise from angels and inhabitants, as 13:24 — *““Peace be upon you for your perseverance. How excellent is the ultimate abode!””* says *Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured* (13:24 — *““Peace be upon you for your perseverance. How excellent is the ultimate abode!””*). The death greeting is foretaste of Paradise greeting.

**Enter Paradise For What You Used To Do**

Udkhulū al-jannata bi-mā kuntum taʿmalūn — enter Paradise for what you used to do, because of what you used to do. Bi-mā kuntum taʿmalūn indicates cause: because of your deeds, your faith, your patience, your good works. Al-Ṭabarī explains that entry to Paradise is by Allah's mercy, but deeds are cause and evidence of sincerity, and reward is according to deeds. The phrase does not mean Paradise is earned solely by deeds without mercy; it means deeds are sign of faith that Allah rewards. Al-Rāzī notes that bi-mā kuntum taʿmalūn includes both inward and outward deeds: belief, gratitude, patience, trust, as verses 41-42 will mention for emigrants. The same phrase appears in other descriptions of Paradise entry, as in 16:32 and 52:19 — *“˹They will be told,˺ “Eat and drink happily for what you used to do.””*. It shows that Paradise is not arbitrary; it is for those who did what was required.

**The Meaning Of Ṭayyibīn**

Ṭayyibīn can mean pure from shirk, pure in speech and action, or those whose death is easy, without hardship. Al-Ṭabarī reports both interpretations and says they are compatible: those who are pure in faith have easy death. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that ṭayyib is opposite of khabīth, foul, impure, used for shirk and evil deeds. The righteous are ṭayyib because they avoided khabīth of shirk and ingratitude. Their souls are ṭayyibah, good, so angels take them in ṭayyib manner, with peace. The word also suggests that their lives were ṭayyibah, good life, as 16:97 — *“Whoever does good, whether male or female, and is a believer, We will surely bless them with a good life, and We will certainly reward them according to the best of their deeds”* says *We will surely give them good life* (16:97 — *“Whoever does good, whether male or female, and is a believer, We will surely bless them with a good life, and We will certainly reward them according to the best of their deeds”*). Good life leads to good death leads to good home.
verses.33:
> Are they only awaiting the coming of the angels or the command of your Lord ˹O Prophet˺? So were those before them. And Allah never wronged them, but it was they who wronged themselves

**What Are They Waiting For?**

Hal yanẓurūna illā a ta'tiyahum al-malā'ikatu aw ya'tiya amru rabbika — are they only waiting for angels to come or command of your Lord to come? Hal is interrogative, are they, do they? Yanẓurūna from n-ẓ-r means to wait, await, expect. Illā a ta'tiyahum al-malā'ikatu, except that angels come to them, meaning angels of death to take souls, or angels of punishment, or angels for reckoning. Aw ya'tiya amru rabbika, or command of your Lord comes, meaning punishment in world or Hour in Hereafter. The question is rhetorical, criticizing delay in believing until undeniable signs come. Al-Ṭabarī explains that Makkan deniers were waiting for angels to come with punishment or for Allah's command of destruction or Resurrection to come before believing, but by then belief will not benefit. The same question appears in 6:158 — *“Are they awaiting the coming of the angels, or your Lord ˹Himself˺, or some of your Lord’s ˹major˺ signs?”*: *Do they await except that angels should come to them or your Lord should come or some signs of your Lord should come?* (6:158 — *“Are they awaiting the coming of the angels, or your Lord ˹Himself˺, or some of your Lord’s ˹major˺ signs?”*). The answer is that waiting until then is foolish, because then it is too late.

**Allah Did Not Wrong Them, They Wronged Themselves**

Wa-mā ẓalamahum Allāhu wa-lākin kānū anfusahum yaẓlimūn — and Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. Ẓalama means to wrong, to oppress, to put thing in wrong place. Allah did not wrong them by punishing without reason or by not giving signs; He gave blessings, sent messengers, showed straight way, gave time. They wronged themselves by choosing denial, arrogance, calling revelation fables, plotting, opposing believers. Al-Qurṭubī explains that self-wronging includes harming own souls by committing deeds that lead to punishment, and also includes putting worship in wrong place by giving it to idols. The phrase appears many times in Qur'an, as in 16:118 — *“To the Jews, We have forbidden what We related to you before. We did not wrong them, but it was they who wronged themselves”* and 29:40 — *“Allah would not have wronged them, but it was they who wronged themselves”*, to emphasize divine justice and human responsibility. It answers hidden objection: if Allah could have guided all, as verse 9 said, why does He punish those not guided? Answer: He did not wrong them; they wronged themselves by refusing guidance shown.
verses.34:
> Then the evil ˹consequences˺ of their deeds overtook them, and they were overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule

**Evil Consequences Overtaking**

Fa-aṣābahum sayyi'ātu mā ʿamilū — then evil consequences of what they did overtook them, befell them. Aṣābahum from ṣ-w-b means to hit, befall, overtake. Sayyi'āt means evil deeds and their evil consequences, plural of sayyi'ah, evil, bad. Mā ʿamilū, what they did, what they used to do. Al-Ṭabarī explains that sayyi'āt here means punishment for evil deeds, evil outcome that results from deeds. Their deeds were shirk, denial, calling revelation fables, plotting, opposing believers. The evil consequences are punishment in world and Hereafter that results. Fa- indicates consequence: because they wronged themselves and waited for angels or command, then evil consequences overtook them. The verb aṣābahum suggests that consequences are not random but targeted, hitting them as arrow hits target. Their deeds created consequences that then caught up with them, as 30:36 — *“If We give people a taste of mercy, they become prideful ˹because˺ of it. But if they are afflicted with an evil for what their hands have done, they instantly fall into despair”* says *If evil befalls them for what their hands sent forth, they despair* (30:36 — *“But if they are afflicted with an evil for what their hands have done, they instantly fall into despair”*). Wa-ḥāqa bihim mā kānū bihi yastahzi'ūn — and they were overwhelmed, surrounded, encompassed by what they used to ridicule. Then punishment they ridiculed surrounded them, as flood surrounded mockers of Nūḥ, wind surrounded mockers of Hūd, etc. What they ridiculed becomes what overwhelms them, a fitting recompense: you mocked punishment, now punishment mocks you by surrounding you from where you did not expect, as verse 26 said torment came from where they did not perceive.

**The Pattern Of Ridicule And Overwhelming**

The Qur'an often pairs ridicule of punishment with being overwhelmed by it, as in 6:10 — *“˹Other˺ messengers had already been ridiculed before you ˹O Prophet˺, but those who mocked them were overtaken by what they used to ridicule”*: *And indeed messengers before you were ridiculed, but those who mocked them were overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule* (6:10 — *“˹Other˺ messengers had already been ridiculed before you ˹O Prophet˺, but those who mocked them were overtaken by what they used to ridicule”*) and 21:41 — *“˹Other˺ messengers had already been ridiculed before you ˹O Prophet˺, but those who mocked them were overtaken by what they used to ridicule”* and 46:26 — *“And ˹so˺ they were overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule”*. The pattern is consistent: deniers ridicule warning, warning becomes reality that surrounds them. In al-Naḥl, ridicule took form of calling revelation ancient fables (16:24 — *“And when it is said to them, “What has your Lord revealed?” They say, “Ancient fables!””*) and demanding hastening of command (16:1 — *“The command of Allah is at hand, so do not hasten it. Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate ˹with Him in worship˺”*). The verse says that very thing ridiculed — command, punishment, Hour — will surround them. The ridicule does not prevent reality; it ensures that when reality comes, it comes as overwhelming, not as gentle reminder. Al-Rāzī explains that ḥāqa bihim indicates that punishment they thought would never come actually encompasses them from all sides, leaving no escape, as 29:54 — *“They urge you to hasten the punishment. And Hell will certainly encompass the disbelievers”* says *Indeed Hell will encompass disbelievers* (29:54 — *“They urge you to hasten the punishment. And Hell will certainly encompass the disbelievers”*).

**A Lesson On Speech And Consequence**

The verse highlights that ridicule, yastahzi'ūn, is not harmless speech. It is deed with consequence. To ridicule revelation, messengers, or punishment is to put oneself in position where what is ridiculed will overwhelm. The Qur'an warns against mocking: *O you who believe, let not a people ridicule another people, perhaps they may be better* (49:11 — *“O believers! Do not let some ˹men˺ ridicule others, they may be better than them, nor let ˹some˺ women ridicule other women, they may be better than them.”*). If mocking people is prohibited, mocking Allah's signs is worse. The verse teaches that speech should be guarded, because what is said in mockery may become reality that surrounds speaker. The Makkans who said *bring punishment if truthful* were in fact calling punishment upon themselves, as 8:32 — *“And ˹remember˺ when they prayed, “O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky or overcome us with a painful punishment.””* shows.

**How Consequences Catch Up**

Consequences catching up is law of moral world as gravity is law of physical world. A person may do evil and feel nothing immediate, thinking he escaped. But deeds create consequences that travel, like arrow shot, and eventually hit. The Qur'an says *And whatever affliction befalls you is for what your hands earned* (42:30 — *“Whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your own hands have committed. And He pardons much”*). Each has consequence: shirk leads to Hell, denial leads to humiliation, calling fables leads to bearing burdens of misled, plotting leads to building collapse, opposing believers leads to disgrace. The verse says these consequences overtook them, meaning they could not outrun them. The Makkans who plotted in Dār al-Nadwah thought they were securing future; their plotting's evil consequences overtook them at Badr and beyond.
verses.35:
> The polytheists argue, “Had Allah willed, neither we nor our forefathers would have worshipped anything other than Him, nor prohibited anything without His command.” So did those before them. Is not the messengers’ duty only to deliver ˹the message˺ clearly

**Using Divine Will As Excuse For Shirk**

Wa-qāla al-ladhīna ashrakū law shā'a Allāhu mā ʿabadnā min dūnihi min shay'in naḥnu wa-lā ābā'unā wa-lā ḥarramnā min dūnihi min shay' — and those who associate partners said, had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything besides Him. This is argument of polytheists who claim that since Allah allowed them to worship idols and prohibit certain animals as ḥarām, therefore Allah wills and approves their shirk and prohibitions. Al-Ṭabarī explains that they argued: if Allah did not like our worship of idols and our prohibiting cattle, He would have prevented us, so since He did not prevent, He approves. This is misuse of divine will to justify disobedience. Al-Rāzī notes that they confused divine will that allows human choice with divine approval. Allah wills to allow humans to choose, but does not approve shirk. The same argument appears in 6:148 — *“The polytheists will argue, “Had it been Allah’s Will, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated others with Him ˹in worship˺ or made anything unlawful.””*: *Those who associate will say, had Allah willed, we would not have associated nor would our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything* (6:148 — *“The polytheists will argue, “Had it been Allah’s Will, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated others with Him ˹in worship˺ or made anything unlawful.””*). The Qur'an answers that this argument was used by those before them and is invalid.

**Our Forefathers And Prohibitions**

Naḥnu wa-lā ābā'unā, we nor our forefathers, indicates that they appealed to tradition: our fathers did shirk, so it must be acceptable, and if Allah willed otherwise, He would have stopped our fathers. Wa-lā ḥarramnā min dūnihi min shay', nor would we have prohibited anything besides Him, refers to their practice of prohibiting certain cattle as ḥarām for idols, as 6:139-144 — *“Some cattle are fit for labour, others are too small. Eat of what Allah has provided for you and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. Certainly, he is your sworn enemy”* describes: they prohibited certain camels, cattle, saying this is for idols. They claimed that since Allah allowed them to prohibit, He approves prohibition. Al-Qurṭubī explains that they made unlawful what Allah made lawful, like certain cattle. Claimed it was by Allah's command, when in fact it was by their own invention, as 16:116 — *“Do not falsely declare with your tongues, “This is lawful, and that is unlawful,””* will say *Do not say what your tongues falsely describe, this is lawful and this is forbidden, inventing lie against Allah* (16:116 — *“Do not falsely declare with your tongues, “This is lawful, and that is unlawful,””*). Their argument uses divine will to justify both shirk in worship and shirk in legislation.

**Why This Argument Is Invalid**

The argument *had Allah willed we would not have worshipped others* is invalid for several reasons. Allah allows humans to choose disbelief, but does not approve it, as 39:7 — *“If you disbelieve, then ˹know that˺ Allah is truly not in need of you, nor does He approve of disbelief from His servants.”* says *If you disbelieve, indeed Allah is free from need of you, and He does not approve disbelief for His servants* (39:7 — *“If you disbelieve, then ˹know that˺ Allah is truly not in need of you, nor does He approve of disbelief from His servants.”*). Second, if argument were valid, it would justify all sins: had Allah willed, we would not have stolen, killed, etc., which would eliminate moral responsibility. Third, Allah has willed to show straight way and to send messengers to clarify, so excuse that He did not will guidance is false: He did will to show way, as verse 9 said *upon Allah is to show straight way*.
verses.36:
> We surely sent a messenger to every community, saying, “Worship Allah and shun false gods.” But some of them were guided by Allah, while others were destined to stray. So travel throughout the land and see the fate of the deniers

**One Message for Every Community**

The verse states the rule that runs through the sūrah: God has sent a messenger to every community with one command — worship God and keep away from false gods, the *ṭāghūt*. The word carries the sense of everything that has gone past its limit and been raised to the place of God: idols, devils, and the powers that demand a person's obedience as though they were his Lord. Al-Ṭabarī explained the community here as a people or a generation sharing the same time and place; al-Rāzī noted that the two halves of the command belong together, since a man cannot truly serve God while also serving what is set up beside Him. The message never changed: the Sūrah of the Prophets has God say that every messenger before Muḥammad was sent with the same revelation, that there is no god but Him (21:25 — *“We never sent a messenger before you ˹O Prophet˺ without revealing to him: “There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Me, so worship Me ˹alone˺.””*), and the rule of a warner in every community is stated again in the Sūrah of the Creator (35:24 — *“We have surely sent you with the truth as a deliverer of good news and a warner. There is no community that has not had a warner”*).

**Some Guided, Some Deserving to Stray**

Not every community answered alike. Some of them God guided, because they accepted the message, humbled themselves and looked at what they had been shown; others fell into straying, and the verse says the straying was deserved. Al-Ṭabarī read the sentence as: the road was shown to all of them through the messengers, and the men who refused, were arrogant and called the revelation old stories settled their own case. Al-Rāzī made the same point against the idea that God forces anyone away from Himself: the guidance was offered, and the refusal was theirs. The Sūrah of the Cow gives the rule in its own words, that God misguides many by the same things by which He guides many, and misguides none but those who have already set themselves outside (2:26 — *“Through this ˹test˺, He leaves many to stray, and guides many.”*).

**Travel and Look at the End of Things**

The verse closes with a command that is also a way of learning: travel the land and see how the deniers ended. Al-Ṭabarī read it as a call to look at the ruins of the peoples the Book has named — ʿĀd, Thamūd and the house of Pharaoh; al-Qurṭubī added that the journey may be made with the body or with the mind, reading the history. The sūrah gives the same instruction elsewhere (30:42 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Travel throughout the land and see what was the end of those ˹destroyed˺ before ˹you˺—most of them were polytheists.””*), and it has already run through the fate of the communities of the past (16:26-34 — *“Indeed, those before them had plotted, but Allah struck at the ˹very˺ foundation of their structure, so the roof collapsed on top of them, and the torment came upon them from where they did not expect”*). The point is aimed at the reader as much as at the first hearers: a nation can be certain of itself and end in a ruin that travellers walk past. The messengers were men from the towns, not angels (12:109 — *“Have the deniers not travelled through the land to see what was the end of those ˹destroyed˺ before them?”*), and the account of what happened to those who denied them is written on the ground for anyone willing to look.
verses.37:
> Even though you ˹O Prophet˺ are keen on their guidance, Allah certainly does not guide those He leaves to stray, and they will have no helpers

**The Prophet's Keenness for His People**

The verse opens by acknowledging what the Prophet wanted. He was eager for the guidance of his people, grieved when they refused, and the Book describes his state in two other places with a picture that has never needed improving: perhaps you would kill yourself with grief because they do not believe (26:3; and 18:6, where the same grief is shown over their turning away). Al-Ṭabarī explained the keenness as mercy: he wanted them saved from the punishment, and the sūrah has already called him a mercy to the believers (9:128 — *“There certainly has come to you a messenger from among yourselves. He is concerned by your suffering, anxious for your well-being, and gracious and merciful to the believers”*). The verse does not correct the wish. It puts it inside the larger fact that follows.

**Guidance Is Not a Matter of the Prophet's Effort**

What follows is the sentence the verse exists for: God does not guide the people He leaves to stray, and they will have no helpers. The commentators were careful about the wording. The people who are left to stray are those who chose the refusal, were arrogant, and called the revelation old stories; the abandonment came after the choice, not before it. Al-Rāzī made the point that the verse does not describe a God who blocks a willing man from the truth — it describes men who turned away first, and the same sūrah has already said of them that they preferred the life of this world, and God does not guide a people who deny (16:107 — *“This is because they prefer the life of this world over the Hereafter. Surely Allah never guides those who ˹choose to˺ disbelieve”*). A prophet's task is the delivery of the message; the opening of the heart is not in his hands, and the verse releases him from a burden he was never asked to carry.

**Nobody to Help Them at the End**

The verse ends with the statement that they will have no helpers. The idols they called on for protection will not appear for them, and their wealth, their numbers and their plans will be of no use on the Day the account is opened. The Book uses the same phrase for those who deny elsewhere (2:270 — *“Whatever charities you give or vows you make are surely known to Allah. And the wrongdoers will have no helpers”*; 3:192 — *“Our Lord! Indeed, those You commit to the Fire will be ˹completely˺ disgraced! And the wrongdoers will have no helpers”*), and the sūrah's earlier verses have already shown the partners being asked where they are (16:27 — *“Then on the Day of Judgment He will humiliate them and say, “Where are My ˹so-called˺ associate-gods for whose sake you used to oppose ˹the believers˺?””*). The verse's last word is a comfort to the man who was grieving over them: he was told the truth, and the outcome of the refusers was never his to carry.
verses.38:
> They swear by Allah their most solemn oaths that Allah will never raise the dead to life. Yes ˹He will˺! It is a true promise binding on Him, but most people do not know

**The Oath They Swore Against the Resurrection**

The verse reports what the men of Makkah were saying with the greatest force they could put behind a sentence: they swore by God, with their strongest oaths, that God would never raise the dead to life. The Book records the same kind of oath being used for other promises the deniers made and did not keep, when they swore that they would believe if a sign came down (6:109 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Signs are only with Allah.””*; 35:42 — *“They swore by Allah their most solemn oaths that if a warner were to come to them, they would certainly be better guided than any other community.”*). Here the oath is used against the most basic claim of the message, and the verse answers it with one word: yes, He will.

**"Yes — a Promise Binding on Him"**

The answer takes the form of an oath met by a stronger statement. The Book says the resurrection is a promise God has made binding on Himself, and it says the same thing elsewhere: the promise of God is true (10:55 — *“Surely to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Surely Allah’s promise is ˹always˺ true, but most of them do not know”*). The reason the Book can answer a human oath so briefly is that the two things being weighed are not equal. On one side stands a man swearing by God's name; on the other stands God's own word about what He will do.

**The Contradiction Inside the Oath**

There is an irony in the sentence the verse preserves, and the commentators point it out: the men swear by God while denying God's power. To swear by someone is to admit that he is great enough to be invoked; the same greatness they were conceding in the oath is the greatness that makes the raising of the dead a small matter. Al-Zamakhsharī noted that the oath's very earnestness made the error heavier, since a man does not swear so hard about a thing he has examined and understood. The Book also records the argument they were leaning on, the old question about bones turning to dust: shall we be raised as a new creation? (17:49 — *“And they say ˹mockingly˺, “When we are reduced to bones and ashes, will we really be raised as a new creation?””*). The sūrah has spent its earlier verses answering that with the things they looked at every day — the sky, the rain, the cattle, the child — and it closes the matter here by naming the resurrection as something God has promised rather than something they must approve.
verses.39:
> ˹He will do that˺ to make clear to them what they disagreed on, and for the disbelievers to know that they were liars

**Why the Dead Are Raised: To Settle the Dispute**

The verse gives the purpose of the resurrection in two halves. The first is that God will make clear to them the matters they differed about. The disputes in view are the ones the sūrah has been addressing all along: whether there is one God or many, whether the Book is revelation or old stories, whether the dead are raised, and what is lawful and what is not. In this world the arguments stay open because the people who argue refuse the evidence; on the Day the question is not argued, because the truth stands in front of everyone at once. The Book states the same purpose for revelation itself, sent down to make clear to people what they differed about (16:64 — *“We have revealed to you the Book only to clarify for them what they differed about, and as a guide and mercy for those who believe”*), so that the world's message and the world to come are doing the same work: the first settles the dispute for the person willing to listen, and the second settles it for everyone.

**"And the Disbelievers Will Know They Were Liars"**

The second half names what the deniers will learn: that they were liars. The Book does not say merely that they were wrong. Their claim had been that the Book was fables, that there was no raising, that their idols had a share in the rule; the Day shows the shape of what they had said. Al-Rāzī noted that the knowledge on that Day will not be an opinion they can weigh; it will be the knowledge of men looking at the thing itself, which is the state the Book describes elsewhere when it says that if you could only see the wrongdoers bowing their heads before their Lord and saying: our Lord, we have seen and heard (32:12 — *“If only you could see the wicked hanging their heads ˹in shame˺ before their Lord, ˹crying:˺ “Our Lord!”*). The verse thus leaves the reader with a sober picture of the end of argument: the people who spent their lives talking their way past the truth will not be answered with an argument, but with the sight of what they denied.
verses.40:
> If We ever will something ˹to exist˺, all We say is: “Be!” And it is

**The Command Be And It Is**

Innamā qawlunā li-shay'in idhā aradnāhu a naqūla lahu kun fa-yakūn — our word for a thing when We will it is only to say to it Be and it is. Qawlunā, Our word, speech. Li-shay'in, for a thing, for something. Idhā aradnāhu, when We will it, wish it, intend it. An naqūla lahu kun, that We say to it Be. Fa-yakūn, and it is, becomes. Al-Ṭabarī explains that when Allah wills something to exist, whether resurrection, creation, provision, punishment, He only says to it kun, Be, and it is, without effort, without delay, without intermediary. The phrase innamā, only, stresses ease: Our word is only Be. This is same amr, command, that opened sūrah: command at hand, angels descend with spirit from command, stars subjected by command. Now command is explained: command is kun, Be. Al-Rāzī notes that kun fa-yakūn shows that Allah's will is executed by His word alone, without need for tools, time, or assistance, unlike human creation which requires effort and time.

Verses 38-39 said they swear Allah will not raise dead, but it is true promise to make clear what they differed and for disbelievers to know they were liars. Verse 40 says if We will something, We say Be and it is. The connection is that resurrection, which they think impossible, is easy for Allah: He only says Be and it is. If He could create heavens and earth, create humans from drop, create cattle, rain, crops, sea, mountains, all with kun, then resurrecting dead is even easier, as 30:27 — *“And He is the One Who originates the creation then will resurrect it—which is even easier for Him.”* says *It is He who originates creation then repeats it, and that is easier for Him* (30:27 — *“And He is the One Who originates the creation then will resurrect it—which is even easier for Him.”*). The verse therefore answers denial of resurrection with ease of divine command.

**The Power Of Kun**

Kun, Be, is imperative of kāna, to be, exist. Some commentators discuss whether kun is literal speech or metaphor for immediate execution. Majority say it is literal speech that Allah speaks, but its nature is beyond human comprehension, as 42:51 — *“It is not ˹possible˺ for a human being to have Allah communicate with them, except through inspiration, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger-angel to reveal whatever He wills by His permission.”* says *It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation or from behind veil or by sending messenger* (42:51 — *“It is not ˹possible˺ for a human being to have Allah communicate with them, except through inspiration, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger-angel to reveal whatever He wills by His permission.”*).
verses.41:
> As for those who emigrated in ˹the cause of˺ Allah after being persecuted, We will surely bless them with a good home in this world. But the reward of the Hereafter is far better, if only they knew

**Emigration After Persecution**

Wa-al-ladhīna hājarū fī Allāhi min baʿdi mā ẓulimū — as for those who emigrated in cause of Allah after being persecuted, wronged. Hājarū from h-j-r means to emigrate, to leave home, to abandon. Fī Allāhi means in cause of Allah, for sake of Allah, because of faith. Some say verse 41 refers specifically to Abyssinian emigrants, while verse 110 refers to Madinan emigrants. Others say it is general for all who emigrate after being wronged for faith. The persecution included torture, boycott, and social pressure, as experienced by Bilāl, ʿAmmār, and others. The verse acknowledges their wronging and promises recompense.

**A Lesson For All Who Are Wronged**

Though verse refers to specific historical emigration, its principle is general: those who are wronged for sake of Allah and who leave wrongdoing environment for Allah will be blessed with good home in world and greater in Hereafter. Al-Qurṭubī extends it to anyone who leaves sinful environment, abandons bad company, or migrates from place where he cannot practice faith. The promise of good home in world is not necessarily physical house but good life, as 16:97 — *“Whoever does good, whether male or female, and is a believer, We will surely bless them with a good life, and We will certainly reward them according to the best of their deeds”* says We will give them good life. The verse therefore offers hope to anyone feeling persecuted for faith: your sacrifice will be rewarded with good now and far better later, if you knew how great reward is, you would not hesitate. The sūrah gives the reason for the promise in the verse that follows, where it names the two qualities of the men who were given the good home: patience, and reliance on their Lord (16:42 states both — *“˹It is˺ they who have patiently endured, and in their Lord they put their trust”*). The Book says in another sūrah that the man who leaves his home for God's sake will find plenty of places of refuge and room in the earth (4:100 states the promise — *“Whoever emigrates in the cause of Allah will find many safe havens and bountiful resources throughout the earth.”*), and it names the men and women who migrate as the ones whose reward is guaranteed.
verses.42:
> ˹It is˺ they who have patiently endured, and in their Lord they put their trust

**The Two Qualities of the People Described**

The verse describes the people praised just before it: those who endured patiently, and who put their trust in their Lord. The patience covers more ground than the endurance of persecution. Al-Ṭabarī listed the kinds of patience the word holds here: patience under hardship, patience in leaving home for the faith, patience in carrying out what God asks, and patience in holding back from what He forbids. The second quality is what makes the first possible. Trust in God is what a person falls back on when his own strength has run out, and the Book pairs the two qualities for that reason, describing elsewhere the men who are patient and rely on their Lord (29:59 — *“those who patiently endure, and put their trust in their Lord”*).

**Why Patience Comes First**

The order of the two words is deliberate. Patience is what a person needs while the situation is still in front of him; trust is what he needs when he looks past it. Put the other way round, a person who trusts God but will not endure has nothing to stand on while he waits, and a person who tries to endure without trust carries the load alone. The verse gives the two together, which is what the previous verse's people are remembered for: they were forced out of their homes and they went on, and their confidence was not in the plan they had made but in the Lord they had.

**What the Two Qualities Produce**

The sūrah says later that whoever does good work, man or woman, and believes, God will give him a good life (16:97 — *“Whoever does good, whether male or female, and is a believer, We will surely bless them with a good life, and We will certainly reward them according to the best of their deeds”*). The men described in this verse have already found the first shape of that promise: a life that is not eaten away by resentment, because the wrongs they suffered were left with God rather than carried around. The good life in the Book is not only provision and safety; it is a settled heart, and the two qualities named here are how the Book describes the settled heart in action.
verses.43:
> We did not send ˹messengers˺ before you ˹O Prophet˺ except mere men inspired by Us. If you ˹polytheists˺ do not know ˹this already˺, then ask those who have knowledge ˹of the Scriptures˺

**Messengers Were Mere Men Inspired**

Wa-mā arsalnā min qablika illā rijālan nūḥī ilayhim — We did not send before you except men We inspired. Mā arsalnā, We did not send, negates that messengers were angels or gods. Min qablika, before you, O Prophet, indicating continuity of messengership. Illā rijālan, except men, human males, not angels, not supernatural beings. Nūḥī ilayhim, We inspired them, revealed to them, from w-ḥ-y, to inspire, reveal secretly. Al-Ṭabarī explains that Makkan polytheists found it strange that messenger is human like them, eating food, walking in markets, as 25:7 — *“And they say ˹mockingly˺, “What kind of messenger is this who eats food and goes about in market-places ˹for a living˺?”* says *What is this messenger who eats food and walks in markets?* (25:7 — *“And they say ˹mockingly˺, “What kind of messenger is this who eats food and goes about in market-places ˹for a living˺?”*). The verse answers that all messengers before you were men, not angels, inspired by Us. This is to make message relatable: a human messenger understands human needs, speaks human language, lives human life. Al-Rāzī notes that being men is wisdom: if messengers were angels, people would say we cannot follow angels because we are not angels; since they are men, following is possible.

**The Human Messenger**

The verse answers the objection that had been raised against every messenger: he is only a man (16:43-44). The Book does not deny it. It says that God sent men with inspiration and with the clear proofs and the Books, and it tells the doubters to ask the people who had studied the earlier scriptures if they did not know. The same answer is given in the Sūrah of the Prophets, in almost the same words (21:7 — *“If you ˹polytheists˺ do not know ˹this already˺, then ask those who have knowledge ˹of the Scriptures˺”*), and the Sūrah of the Cave states the reason a human messenger is the point: a person can only follow what he can approach, and if angels had walked the earth as messengers they would still have been sent as men (17:94-95 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Had there been angels walking the earth, well settled, We would have surely sent down for them an angel from heaven as a messenger.””*; 25:7 — *“If only an angel had been sent down with him to be his co-warner”*). The Book's answer to the demand for an angel is that the messenger was sent to be followed, and that requires someone a person can stand next to.
verses.44:
> ˹We sent them˺ with clear proofs and divine Books. And We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Reminder, so that you may explain to people what has been revealed for them, and perhaps they will reflect

**What the Earlier Messengers Brought**

The verse states what the messengers before the Prophet were sent with: clear proofs and the Books. The proofs are the signs that made the message unmistakable — the staff of Moses, the healings of Jesus — and the Books are the writings that carried the guidance into the hands of the people. The point is that a human messenger was never left without evidence. The verse just before this one has said that the messengers were men, inspired and given a message; this verse adds that they came with what their people could check and read, so that nobody could say that the message had arrived without proof and then blame God for the darkness.

**The Task Given to the Prophet Here**

The second half of the verse names the Prophet's own task with the Reminder sent down to him: that he may make clear to the people what was sent down for them, so that they may reflect. The Book's verses are often brief and general, and the stories and rulings inside them need a teacher; without explanation, people disagree about what a verse means, which is exactly what the Book says has happened to earlier communities, and what it says the sending of the Book is meant to end (16:39 — *“˹He will do that˺ to make clear to them what they disagreed on, and for the disbelievers to know that they were liars”*; 16:64 — *“We have revealed to you the Book only to clarify for them what they differed about, and as a guide and mercy for those who believe”*). The verse therefore establishes the Prophet's teaching role as part of the revelation itself, not as an addition to it.

**How the Explanation Works**

The sūrah says in its own closing instruction that the call is to be made with wisdom and a good word (16:125 — *“Invite ˹all˺ to the Way of your Lord with wisdom and kind advice, and only debate with them in the best manner. Surely your Lord ˹alone˺ knows best who has strayed from His Way and who is ˹rightly˺ guided”*), and the Prophet's explanation followed that rule: he taught by speech, by action and by the way he lived, turning statements about honesty, prayer and dealing with people into things the community could watch. The last words of the verse point the same way. The Book is not sent down to be memorised and left; it is sent down so that a person reflects on it, and the reading that produces reflection is the object of the exercise.
verses.45:
> Do those who devise evil plots feel secure that Allah will not cause the earth to swallow them? Or that the torment will not come upon them in ways they cannot comprehend

**The Plotters Who Feel Safe**

The verse puts a question to the men who spend their nights arranging harm against the Prophet and the believers: do they feel safe that God will not open the earth and let it take them down, or that His punishment will not reach them from a direction they never watch? Al-Ṭabarī connected the opening with the men of Makkah who gathered in the council house to plot against the Prophet, and the Book has already recorded the end of one man who felt safe in his wealth: the earth swallowed Qārūn and his house (28:81 — *“Then We caused the earth to swallow him up, along with his home. There was no one to help him against Allah, nor could he even help himself”*). The question expects the answer no. The plotters were not free from the law that swallowed a richer man than any of them.

**The Delusion of Safety**

The feeling of security is the real disease in the verse. Trust in God is praised everywhere in the Book; the assumption that punishment will not come, while a man keeps on committing the crime, is the opposite of trust, and the Book names it directly: do they feel safe from the plan of God?
