No one feels safe from God's plan except a people who are the losers (7:99 — *“Did they feel secure against Allah’s planning? None would feel secure from Allah’s planning except the losers”*). Al-Qurṭubī counted the point among the deadly sins: to keep sinning and to be certain that nothing will follow is to treat the mercy of God as a licence rather than a gift.

**The Punishment From Where They Are Not Looking**

The second half of the question adds the other way a reckoning arrives: not through the ground opening, but through the ordinary turning of events that no planner can watch. A man can guard the door he knows about and never see the one that opens behind him. The verse leaves the plotters with no safe line to stand on. The Book has already told them, in the same sūrah, that God's command comes and they cannot outrun it (16:1 — *“The command of Allah is at hand, so do not hasten it. Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate ˹with Him in worship˺”*), and the following verses continue with the same warning, so that the passage reads as one long answer to the confidence of men who thought their cleverness put them out of reach.
verses.46:
> Or that He will not seize them while they go about ˹their day˺, for then they will have no escape

**No Escape When Seized**

Fa-mā hum bi-muʿjizīn — for then they will have no escape, will not be able to escape, frustrate, evade. Muʿjizīn from ʿ-j-z means to be unable, to escape, to make helpless, from same root as iʿjāz, inimitability. Al-Ṭabarī says fa-mā hum bi-muʿjizīn means they will not be able to escape Allah's punishment, to frustrate His plan, to make Him unable. When Allah seizes, there is no escape. The phrase appears in other warnings, as in 29:22 — *“And you cannot escape Him on earth or in heaven. Nor have you any protector or helper besides Allah.””*: *You will not be able to escape on earth nor in heaven* (29:22 — *“And you cannot escape Him on earth or in heaven. Nor have you any protector or helper besides Allah.””*). The verse stresses that feeling secure while going about is delusion because when seizure comes, escape is impossible. The time to seek security is before seizure, by abandoning evil plotting and turning to gratitude and tawḥīd.

**The Connection To Security And Gratitude**

Sūrat al-Niʿam stresses that security is from Allah, not from plotting or wealth. Mountains prevent earth from shaking with you as mercy, but if you plot evil, that security can be removed. The verse asks do they feel secure that He will not seize them while going about, implying that true security is only for those who are grateful and mindful, not for plotters. The righteous who emigrated after being wronged and were patient and trusted Lord were given good home in world as security, but that security came after patience and trust, not while plotting evil. The contrast is clear: plotters feel false security while plotting, righteous receive true security after patience and trust.
verses.47:
> Or that He will not destroy them gradually? But your Lord is truly Ever Gracious, Most Merciful

**Gradual Destruction**

Aw ya'khudhahum ʿalā takhawwufin — or that He will not seize them gradually, with fear, by diminishing. Takhawwuf from kh-w-f means fear, but also gradual reduction, taking away little by little, causing fear through erosion. Al-Ṭabarī explains that ʿalā takhawwufin means Allah seizes them gradually, reducing their wealth, strength, numbers, little by little, so they fear and anticipate total destruction, or that He seizes some and leaves others to fear. Al-Rāzī says takhawwuf can mean that punishment comes with fear, causing them to be in fear while being seized, or that it comes by diminishing their sides, reducing their territory, as 13:41 — *“Do they not see that We gradually reduce their land from its borders? Allah decides—none can reverse His decision. And He is swift in reckoning”* says *Do they not see that We come to land reducing it from its borders?* (13:41 — *“Do they not see that We gradually reduce their land from its borders? Allah decides—none can reverse His decision. And He is swift in reckoning”*). The question is continuation: do plotters feel secure that He will not destroy them gradually? They should not, because gradual destruction is also possible and is happening.

**Graciousness And Mercy As Reason For Delay**

The seal la-ra'ūfun raḥīm explains why punishment is delayed despite plotting. Allah is gracious, preventing immediate destruction, and merciful, granting time and provision even to plotters, as 10:11 — *“If Allah were to hasten evil for people as they wish to hasten good, they would have certainly been doomed. But We leave those who do not expect to meet Us to wander blindly in their defiance”* says *If Allah were to hasten evil for people as they hasten good, their term would have ended* (10:11 — *“If Allah were to hasten evil for people as they wish to hasten good, they would have certainly been doomed.”*). Delay is mercy that allows repentance. Al-Zamakhsharī notes that ra'ūf is more intense than raḥīm in preventing harm, so mention of both indicates Allah both prevents immediate harm and grants time for good. The verse therefore balances warning with hope: warning that punishment can come in many ways, hope that delay is due to mercy that invites return. The sūrah's blessings catalogue also showed graciousness and mercy: cattle bearing loads without hardship because Lord is gracious, merciful. Now same names explain delay in punishment: Lord is gracious, merciful, so He delays. The two uses show that graciousness and mercy appear both in provision and in forbearance.
verses.48:
> Have they not considered how the shadows of everything Allah has created incline to the right and the left ˹as the sun moves˺, totally submitting to Allah in all humility

**A Question About Shadows**

The verse asks its readers to look at something they have seen every day of their lives: the shadows of everything God has created, leaning to the right and to the left as the sun moves, and how they fall low in submission to God. Every created thing that casts a shadow is included — the tree, the mountain, the animal, the person walking. The Book puts the same picture in another sūrah, where everything in the heavens and the earth submits to God willingly or unwillingly, and their shadows do it in the mornings and the evenings (13:15 — *“To Allah ˹alone˺ bow down ˹in submission˺ all those in the heavens and the earth—willingly or unwillingly—as do their shadows, morning and evening”*).

**What the Shadow Says About Its Owner**

The shadow is the Book's teacher of humility in this verse because it depends on two things it does not control: the light and the object that casts it. Without either, it does not exist. Al-Ṭabarī read the prostration of the shadows as this kind of submission — not the prayer of a creature that chose, but the obedience built into the created order. A man who watches his own shadow stretch and shorten and knows that he is as dependent as it is has been given a lesson in the exact quality that ruin comes from lacking; the Book has said elsewhere that the arrogant will find no entry to the garden, and the sūrah of Thunder describes the garden's shade as lasting (13:35 — *“The description of the Paradise promised to the righteous is that under it rivers flow; eternal is its fruit as well as its shade. That is the ˹ultimate˺ outcome for the righteous. But the outcome for the disbelievers is the Fire”*), while the proud who refused the command have no shade left to them.

**Why the Question Is Addressed to the Doubters**

The verse's question is aimed at the men who kept demanding proofs. The proof is lying on the ground in front of them, moving the whole day long. The Book's way with such readers is not to invent a new sign for them but to insist that they look at the one they walk through every afternoon.
verses.49:
> And to Allah ˹alone˺ bows down ˹in submission˺ whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of living creatures, as do the angels—who are not too proud ˹to do so˺

**Everything Bows**

The verse says that everything in the heavens and everything on the earth bows down to God — the living creatures that move on the ground, and the angels, who are not too proud to do it. The bowing of the creatures is the submission built into their making: they follow the law God placed in them, they live and die under His command, and they cannot step outside it. The Sūrah of Thunder states the same thing plainly: everything in the heavens and the earth bows to God, some willingly and some unwillingly (13:15 — *“To Allah ˹alone˺ bow down ˹in submission˺ all those in the heavens and the earth—willingly or unwillingly—as do their shadows, morning and evening”*).

**The Angels Who Are Not Too Proud**

The angels are named separately, though they are already among the inhabitants of the heavens, because their bowing is the willing kind: they serve without weariness and never count themselves above the command. Every creature on the earth has its provision resting on God (11:6 — *“There is no moving creature on earth whose provision is not guaranteed by Allah.”*), and the angels who stand nearest to Him are the first to lower themselves before Him (21:19 — *“To Him belong all those in the heavens and the earth. And those nearest to Him are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they tire”*). Al-Qurṭubī drew out the lesson the verse intends: if those who were created pure and never disobeyed are not too proud to bow, what excuse has a man who has disobeyed and still holds his head up?

**Why the Living Creatures Are Named**

The mention of the creatures that crawl and walk makes the bowing visible on the ground the reader stands on — the bee building in the hills, the bird in the air, the ant on its path. Their service is not the prayer of a man, but it is obedience to the One who made them, and the verse leaves the human reader with the uncomfortable position that he is the one creature who can refuse.
verses.50:
> They fear their Lord above them, and do whatever they are commanded

**The Fear of the Angels**

The verse carries on the description of the angels: they fear their Lord above them, and they do whatever they are commanded. Their fear is not the alarm of a creature caught in a fault; it is the reverence of those who know the greatness of the One they serve. The Book says of God that He holds authority over His servants (6:18 — *“He reigns supreme over His creation. And He is the All-Wise, All-Aware”*), and the angels who stand closest to Him, and who never disobeyed, are described as the ones who feel that authority most. Al-Ṭabarī read the words about their Lord being above them as the plain truth that God is high over His creation, which the earliest Muslims accepted without trying to picture how.

**Obedience Without Argument**

Their second quality is simpler and harder than the first: they do whatever they are commanded. The Book describes them the same way elsewhere, saying that they do not disobey God in what He commands them and they do exactly what they are told (66:6 — *“O believers! Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones, overseen by formidable and severe angels, who never disobey whatever Allah orders—always doing as commanded”*). There is no bargaining in that sentence, no delay, no asking what the command is for. The sūrah is drawing the comparison with human beings, who are given the same kind of obligation and find reasons to put it off. Al-Qurṭubī noted what the verse's position implies: if the angels, who have no sin to regret, fear their Lord and obey Him completely, what is the excuse of a man who has sinned and still stands up straight?
verses.51:
> And Allah has said, “Do not take two gods. There is only One God. So be in awe of Me ˹alone˺.”

**Connection To Universal Prostration**

Verses 48-50 described shadows prostrating, living creatures and angels bowing, fearing Lord above, doing what commanded. Verse 51 says Allah said do not take two gods, there is only One, so be in awe of Me alone. The connection is that universal prostration to One God shows that taking two gods contradicts what all creation does. All creation bows to One; why do you take two? The command to be in awe of Me alone is supported by universal submission: if everything bows to One, you should too. The verse also prepares for next: to Him belongs whatever in heavens and earth and to Him alone is everlasting devotion, will you fear other than Allah? If you fear Me alone, you will give everlasting devotion to Me alone.

**A Verse That Summarizes Tawḥīd**

This verse summarizes tawḥīd in three parts: prohibition, affirmation, consequence. Prohibition: do not take two gods. Affirmation: indeed He is One God. Consequence: so be in awe of Me alone. This mirrors lā ilāha illā Allāh: no god except Allah, so fear Him alone. Al-Qurṭubī says this verse is one of clearest statements of tawḥīd in Qur'an, comparable to 112:1-4 — *“And there is none comparable to Him.””*. It is direct speech from Allah, not reported, to emphasize authority: Allah Himself says do not take two gods. The direct speech makes it more powerful than if messenger said it. The listener hears Allah speaking, commanding oneness and awe.
verses.52:
> To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him ˹alone˺ is the everlasting devotion. Will you then fear any other than Allah

**Everything Is His, So the Devotion Is His**

The verse gives the reason for the command just delivered in the verse before it — do not take two gods, and be in awe of Me alone — by naming what God owns: whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Al-Ṭabarī read the sentence as a statement of creation and possession at once: the angels in the sky and the people, animals, mountains and seas below all belong to Him, and nothing owns itself. The Book uses the same phrase to establish the same point in other sūrahs (2:284 — *“To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.”*; 10:68 — *“To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.”*).

**A Devotion That Does Not Move**

The second clause names the religion that belongs to Him with a word that means steadfast, unmoving: the devotion that lasts. The verse is telling the reader where loyalty properly rests — not on the power of the moment, not on an idol that can be carried away, but on the One to whom everything returns. To Him belongs everything, and to Him belongs the lasting devotion; the two clauses are one argument, and the verse ends with the question that closes it.

**"Will You Then Fear Other Than God?"**

The question is put in the form of an amazement. If everything belongs to Him, then nobody else can harm or benefit without His leave, so what is there to be afraid of in anything beside Him? Al-Rāzī made the point that fear is part of worship: the man who fears a creature the way he should fear God has given that creature a share of his religion. Al-Qurṭubī put the reasoning in the simplest terms: an owner can give, withhold, help and hurt, so the only one whose harm and help are real is the owner of everything. The sūrah of Jonah says the same thing directly: do not call on what can neither help nor hurt you (10:106 — *“and ‘Do not invoke, instead of Allah, what can neither benefit nor harm you—for if you do, then you will certainly be one of the wrongdoers,’”*), and if God touches you with harm, there is none to remove it but Him (10:107 — *“and ‘If Allah touches you with harm, none can undo it except Him.”*). The verse's question is therefore not a puzzle but a correction — the fear of the idols is fear spent on property.
verses.53:
> Whatever blessings you have are from Allah. Then whenever hardship touches you, to Him ˹alone˺ you cry ˹for help˺

**Every Good Thing Comes From Him**

The verse states plainly what the sūrah has been building toward through its long list of blessings: whatever good you have is from God. The word for blessing here is wide enough to hold all of them — the rain and the crops, the cattle and the sea, the family, the health, and the guidance itself. Al-Ṭabarī read the sentence as the answer to every misattribution the sūrah has been exposing: not the idols, not a man's own cleverness, and not luck. Al-Rāzī pointed at the way the second half is worded, because the same people who thank their idols in the good times are the ones who cry out to God alone when hardship lands on them.

**The Cry in the Storm**

The verse turns on that difference. When harm touches you, it says, it is to Him that you call aloud. The Book uses the same scene more than once: when harm comes to you at sea, the ones you call upon besides Him disappear from your mind, and only He is left (17:67 — *“When you are touched with hardship at sea, you ˹totally˺ forget all ˹the gods˺ you ˹normally˺ invoke, except Him.”*). That reaction is not hypocrisy of the ordinary kind; it is human nature telling the truth in the moment that matters, when everyone discovers who actually holds the ropes. The verse does not praise the cry of distress as a virtue; it uses it as evidence. The One who hears that cry in the storm is the One who should have been asked in the calm, and the verses before this one have been showing the blessing and its Giver in the same hand all along.
verses.54:
> Then as soon as He removes the hardship from you, a group of you associates ˹others˺ with their Lord ˹in worship˺

**Saved, Then Forgetting Who Saved Him**

The verse names a pattern that runs through the sūrah like a crack in a wall: when hardship lands, they call on God alone, and the moment He lifts it, a group of them goes back to giving partners to their Lord. The Book traces the same man elsewhere — the one who called on God when harm touched him, and who passed on as though he had never called when the harm was removed (10:12 — *“But when We relieve their hardship, they return to their old ways as if they had never cried to Us to remove any hardship!”*), and the travellers saved at sea who turn away the moment they reach dry land (17:67 — *“When you are touched with hardship at sea, you ˹totally˺ forget all ˹the gods˺ you ˹normally˺ invoke, except Him.”*). The verse's wording makes the speed of the reversal its subject: no sooner is the trouble gone than the partnership is back.

**What the Relief Actually Proves**

A man who has been carried through an illness, a debt or a storm knows exactly whose hand held him. The verse treats that knowledge as a witness he will have to answer for, since the hand that took away the trouble is the hand he set aside once he was comfortable. The sūrah has spent several verses counting out blessings, and this verse is the mirror image of them: the gifts are received, and the credit is given somewhere else.

**"Enjoy Yourselves — You Will Soon Know"**

The sentence that follows arrives as a permission and lands as a threat: enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know. The Book uses the same sentence when it weighs the pleasure of this world against what comes after it, calling the world's comfort a brief enjoyment that is followed by a painful punishment (16:117 — *“˹It is only˺ a brief enjoyment, then they will suffer a painful punishment”*). The word "soon" is doing deliberate work. The day the account is opened is nearer to any man than the length of his comfort suggests, and the verse ends with that word left hanging over the pattern, waiting for it.
verses.55:
> only returning Our favours with ingratitude. So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know

**The Human Pattern Of Forgetting After Relief And Its Warning**

Thumma idhā kashafa al-ḍurra ʿankum idhā farīqun minkum bi-rabbihim yushrikūn — then when He removes hardship from you, behold, a group of you associates others with their Lord. This verse describes a pattern that appears throughout Qur'an and human experience: in hardship you turn to Allah alone, in ease you forget. Al-Ṭabarī explains that when Allah removes hardship that made them cry to Him alone, a group returns to associating idols, forgetting that Allah alone removed hardship. The pattern is described in 10:12 — *“But when We relieve their hardship, they return to their old ways as if they had never cried to Us to remove any hardship!”* where after harm removed he passes on as if he never called Us, and in 17:67 — *“When you are touched with hardship at sea, you ˹totally˺ forget all ˹the gods˺ you ˹normally˺ invoke, except Him.”* where after being saved at sea they turn away on land. The verse uses idhā twice to show suddenness: when He removes, behold, a group associates. The suddenness indicates ingratitude and heedlessness. The sūrah's theme of gratitude vs ingratitude appears here: to associate after being saved is to return favour with ingratitude, as next verse says only returning Our favours with ingratitude. The verse exposes human inconsistency: in hardship tawḥīd, in ease shirk, and calls to consistency in all states. The lesson is that true faith remains after relief, not only during distress.
verses.56:
> And they ˹even˺ assign to those ˹idols˺—who know nothing—a share of what We have provided for them. By Allah! You will certainly be questioned about whatever ˹lies˺ you used to fabricate ˹against Allah˺

**A Share of the Provision Given to the Powerless**

The verse names one of the Makkans' inventions: they set aside a portion of what God has provided and hand it to idols who know nothing. The practice is described in the Sūrah of the Cattle, where they divided their crops and their herds and said that one part belonged to God and another to their idols (6:136 — *“The pagans set aside for Allah a share of the crops and cattle He created, saying, “This ˹portion˺ is for Allah,” so they claim, “and this ˹one˺ for our associate-gods.””*). The claim they built on it fell apart at once. They themselves admitted that the harvest, the rain, the cattle and the children came from God; then they gave a share of His own gift to beings who had no hand in it. The verse's word for those beings is that they know nothing, which is the sharpest possible contrast with the One who provides, who knows all things.

**The Question They Will Be Asked**

The verse closes with an oath: by God, you will be questioned about what you used to invent. The Book does not treat the practice as a harmless piece of local custom. The verses that follow press the same charge home — the men who assign daughters to God and sons to themselves (16:57 — *“And they attribute ˹angels as˺ daughters to Allah—glory be to Him!—the opposite of what they desire for themselves”*), and the man who goes dark in the face when a daughter is born to him (16:58 — *“Whenever one of them is given the good news of a baby girl, his face grows gloomy, as he suppresses his rage”*). The whole series is about people who decided for themselves what should be given to God and what to their idols, and the verse in front of us puts every such arrangement on the record, with a question waiting for it at the end.
verses.57:
> And they attribute ˹angels as˺ daughters to Allah—glory be to Him!—the opposite of what they desire for themselves

**Daughters for God and Sons for Themselves**

The verse reports one of the Makkan claims about God: they made the angels His daughters, and they said it while they themselves wished for sons and thought little of daughters. The Book answers the claim in a phrase — glory be to Him — which is not decoration but the immediate rejection of the claim just made. God has neither children nor partners; the Book says plainly that He begets not and is not begotten (112:3 — *“He has never had offspring, nor was He born”*), and the sūrah's own opening declares Him above everything they associate with Him (16:1 — *“The command of Allah is at hand, so do not hasten it. Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate ˹with Him in worship˺”*; 16:3 — *“He created the heavens and the earth for a purpose. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him ˹in worship˺”*).

**An Insult Wrapped in Worship**

The men who made the claim were worshipping the angels they described, and looking for their intercession. The Book names that too: those who do not believe in the Hereafter give the angels female names (53:27 — *“Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter label angels as female”*). What the verse exposes is the contradiction inside the worship. They took the daughters they themselves disliked and assigned them to God, while reserving sons for their own houses; and then, when a daughter was born to one of them, his face went dark and he kept out of people's sight (16:58-59 — *“Whenever one of them is given the good news of a baby girl, his face grows gloomy, as he suppresses his rage”*). The verse before this one has already told them they will be questioned about what they invented (16:56 — *“And they ˹even˺ assign to those ˹idols˺—who know nothing—a share of what We have provided for them. By Allah! You will certainly be questioned about whatever ˹lies˺ you used to fabricate ˹against Allah˺”*).

**What the Verse Is Really Correcting**

The Book's objection is not to daughters. It is to the low estimate by which the men measured them, and to the way they then built a religion on their own prejudice. The practice that grew out of that estimate was the burying alive of infant girls, which the Book answers on the Day of Judgement with the question put to the buried child about what sin she was killed for (81:8-9 — *“and when baby girls, buried alive, are asked”*), and which it condemns in the next verses as an evil judgment (16:59 — *“He hides himself from the people because of the bad news he has received. Should he keep her in disgrace, or bury her ˹alive˺ in the ground? Evil indeed is their judgment”*). What the passage says to its first hearers, and to any reader who inherits the same bias, is that a person has no right to decide the value of a human being, and no right to hand his own contempt for a thing over to God.
verses.58:
> Whenever one of them is given the good news of a baby girl, his face grows gloomy, as he suppresses his rage

**Why Daughters Were Disliked**

Pre-Islamic Arabs disliked daughters for several reasons: fear of poverty, as daughters considered economic burden; fear of shame, as daughters might be captured in war and bring dishonor; desire for sons who would be warriors and carry name. The Qur'an critiques this bias as evil judgment, as verse 59 says. Al-Qurṭubī notes that dislike of daughters was not universal among Arabs; some tribes honored daughters, but among those who worshipped angels as daughters of Allah, dislike was pronounced, making attribution to Allah even more contradictory: you attribute to Allah what you consider bad news for yourself. The verse exposes contradiction: you consider daughter as bad news for you, yet you say angels, whom you consider daughters of Allah, are worthy of worship and intercession.

**How This Verse Critiques Gender Bias**

The verse critiques gender bias by describing its outward and inward signs: face gloomy, rage suppressed, hiding from people, deciding whether to keep in disgrace or bury alive. It does not endorse bias but exposes as evil judgment. The Qur'an elsewhere honors daughters: *Wealth and children are adornment of worldly life* (18:46 — *“Wealth and children are the adornment of this worldly life, but the everlasting good deeds are far better with your Lord in reward and in hope”*) includes daughters as adornment, and Prophet ﷺ said *Whoever has three daughters and is patient with them and clothes them from his wealth, they will be shield for him from Fire* (Ibn Mājah 3669). The verse therefore calls to value daughters as good news, not bad, and to not attribute to Allah what you hate for yourself, but to attribute to Allah finest attributes as verse 60 says.

**A Lesson On Receiving News**

The verse teaches how to receive news: birth of child, male or female, is good news, blessing from Allah, as verse 72 will say Allah gave you children and grandchildren as provision. To receive good news of daughter with gloomy face and suppressed rage is to be ungrateful for blessing, as verse 53 said blessings from Allah. The verse therefore calls to gratitude for daughters as well as sons.

The believer should receive news of daughter with joy, gratitude, recognizing it as blessing from Allah who gives whatever He wills, as 42:49 — *“He creates whatever He wills.”* says *To Allah belongs dominion of heavens and earth, He creates what He wills, He gives to whom He wills females and gives to whom He wills males* (42:49 — *“He creates whatever He wills.”*).
verses.59:
> He hides himself from the people because of the bad news he has received. Should he keep her in disgrace, or bury her ˹alive˺ in the ground? Evil indeed is their judgment

**The Man Who Hides**

The verse pictures the father who has been told that his child is a daughter. He keeps out of people's sight, and his mind turns over two options: keep her, but in disgrace, or put her into the ground. The verse reports the debate inside him and then passes its verdict in a single line — how evil is the judgement they make.

**What the Two Options Mean**

The first option keeps the child alive but in humiliation, treated as a mark against the household; the second was the practice of burying infant daughters alive, which the Book names as a crime in its own right, and which it answers on the Day of Judgement when the buried girl is asked for what sin she was killed (81:8-9 — *“and when baby girls, buried alive, are asked”*). The same Book forbids the killing of children for fear of poverty (17:31 — *“Do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you. Surely killing them is a heinous sin”*), and it gives the verdict of evil to what such men carry as well as to what they decide (16:25 — *“Let them bear their burdens in full on the Day of Judgment as well as some of the burdens of those they mislead without knowledge. Evil indeed is what they will bear”*). Al-Ṭabarī noted that the man is not choosing between a good thing and a bad thing but between two kinds of shame, and al-Rāzī said the verse's sentence covers both choices, because whichever one he picks, the picking itself is the wrong he is being judged for.

**The Judgement That Is Condemned**

The verses around this one complete the contradiction. The same men who claimed that the angels were God's daughters, and thought they were honouring Him with the claim, went dark in the face when a daughter was born to them (16:57-58 — *“And they attribute ˹angels as˺ daughters to Allah—glory be to Him!—the opposite of what they desire for themselves”*). So the sūrah does not only forbid the burying; it condemns the whole way of weighing that treats a girl as bad news. The Prophet's teaching in the reports goes the other way — that a man who raises his daughters with patience will find them a shield for him from the Fire — and the Book lists daughters among the good gifts of God. What the verse condemns, then, is a judgement about value; the practices it names were only what that judgement grew into when the door was left open.
verses.60:
> To those who disbelieve in the Hereafter belong all evil qualities, whereas to Allah belong the finest attributes. And He is the Almighty, All-Wise

**Finest Attributes Belong To Allah**

Wa-li-Allāhi al-mathalu al-aʿlā — and to Allah belongs highest, finest example, attributes. Mathalu al-aʿlā means highest description, finest attributes, most sublime example. Al-Ṭabarī says to Allah belongs finest attributes: oneness, power, knowledge, mercy, etc., as 59:24 — *“He is Allah: the Creator, the Inventor, the Shaper. He ˹alone˺ has the Most Beautiful Names. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth ˹constantly˺ glorifies Him. And He is the Almighty, All-Wise”* says *To Him belong finest names* (59:24 — *“He is Allah: the Creator, the Inventor, the Shaper. He ˹alone˺ has the Most Beautiful Names. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth ˹constantly˺ glorifies Him. And He is the Almighty, All-Wise”*). Al-Zamakhsharī explains that al-mathalu al-aʿlā means Allah has attributes that are highest, beyond comparison, perfect, while disbelievers have lowest, evil. The contrast li-l-ladhīna lā yu'minūna mathalu al-saw' wa-li-Allāhi al-mathalu al-aʿlā creates sharp dichotomy: evil for disbelievers, finest for Allah. This is to show that attributing daughters to Allah while keeping sons for self is opposite of what should be: to Allah belongs finest, not what you hate.

**How This Verse Teaches To Attribute Finest To Allah**

The verse teaches to attribute to Allah finest attributes, not what you hate for yourself. Al-Rāzī says al-mathalu al-aʿlā includes all perfect attributes: knowledge, power, mercy, etc., and excludes all defects: having children, having partners, etc. To attribute daughters to Allah while hating daughters is to attribute to Allah what is not finest in your own view, which is injustice. True tawḥīd is to attribute to Allah finest, as 59:24 — *“He is Allah: the Creator, the Inventor, the Shaper. He ˹alone˺ has the Most Beautiful Names. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth ˹constantly˺ glorifies Him. And He is the Almighty, All-Wise”* says finest names belong to Him, and to believe that disbelievers in Hereafter have evil qualities, not Allah. The believer should therefore describe Allah with what He described Himself, with finest attributes, and should avoid evil qualities like arrogance, denial, and gender bias that belong to disbelievers in Hereafter.
verses.61:
> If Allah were to punish people ˹immediately˺ for their wrongdoing, He would not have left a single living being on earth. But He delays them for an appointed term. And when their time arrives, they cannot delay it for a moment, nor could they advance it

The verse opens the passage on the delay of punishment with a conditional that no city could survive: if God took people to task for what they do as it happens, nothing living would be left on the earth. The Book states the same in Sūrah Fāṭir, where the withholding of punishment is named as a term God has set, and it repeats here that the delay runs to an appointed time, and that when the term arrives it cannot be moved by an hour either way (16:61). The verse's function in the sūrah is to explain the mockers' survival: their continuance is not evidence that their position is sound, but part of the respite in which repentance is still possible. The sūrah names that mercy explicitly elsewhere: proof follows proof, so that people may return (30:41 — *“Corruption has spread on land and sea as a result of what people’s hands have done, so that Allah may cause them to taste ˹the consequences of˺ some of their deeds and perhaps they might return ˹to the Right Path˺”*).

---

The Book states the same fact elsewhere in nearly the same words: if God were to take people to account for what they have earned, He would not leave a living creature on the face of the earth (35:45 — *“If Allah were to punish people ˹immediately˺ for what they have committed, He would not have left a single living being on earth.”*), and He is the one who defers them to an appointed term (16:61). The commentators read the verse as the answer to the demand for the punishment to be hurried, a demand the sūrah records on the lips of the Makkans elsewhere (13:6 — *“Surely your Lord is full of forgiveness for people, despite their wrongdoing, and your Lord is truly severe in punishment”*). The reason for the delay is stated in the same breath: God is Forgiving and Merciful, and the respite is part of the invitation rather than a slackening of the account.

**What the Conditional States**

The verse says that if God were to take people to task for what they have earned, He would not leave a creature on the earth, and it then gives the other side: He gives them respite until a term appointed, and when their term comes they cannot delay it or advance it by an hour. The sentence is one of the Book's clearest statements about the delay of punishment, and it comes in the passage that answers the men who asked why the punishment had not arrived.
**What the Commentators Explained**

The older commentators read the first clause as a description of what justice alone would produce, and the second as a description of what mercy and decree actually produce. They noted that the Book uses the same structure in the Sūrah of the Originator, where people are called to the earth and told to be mindful (35:45 — *“If Allah were to punish people ˹immediately˺ for what they have committed, He would not have left a single living being on earth.”*), and in the Sūrah of the Spoils, where the community is told that God would not punish them while the Prophet was among them (8:33 — *“But Allah would never punish them while you ˹O Prophet˺ were in their midst. Nor would He ever punish them if they prayed for forgiveness”*). The two passages and the verse in front of us give the community the same doctrine in three forms.
**Where the Passage Sits**

The verse before it answers the idolaters' claim about daughters, and the verse after it gives the rule about the term and the reckoning. The sūrah is dealing with a community that had been given years of warning, and the verse states both halves of the arrangement: what the world deserved, and what God gave it instead. The community's preachers used the sentence about the term in their warnings, and the Book returns to it in several places because the delay was the hardest part of the message for the men who mocked.
verses.62:
> They attribute to Allah what they hate ˹for themselves˺, and their tongues utter the lie that they will have the finest reward. Without a doubt, for them is the Fire, where they will be abandoned

The verse exposes a contradiction the sūrah has already named. The idolaters reserved daughters — a thing they hated for themselves — and assigned them to God, and they were asked how they could judge so unfairly (16:57–59 — *“And they attribute ˹angels as˺ daughters to Allah—glory be to Him!—the opposite of what they desire for themselves”*); now they go further and say out loud that the best outcome is theirs. The Book calls the claim *qawl al-zūr*, the speech of falsehood, and answers it in the same verse: their share is the Fire, and they are the ones being sent ahead to it. Al-Ṭabarī reads the passage as a description of what lies behind the words: a person will assert a comfortable future in order to keep the life he has. The sūrah follows the logic the way it has followed every false claim in the passage — not with a denial of the claim's logic, but with the destination the claimant has chosen.

**The Shape of the Charge**

The verse is the sūrah's answer to a claim that had already been exposed as absurd. The idolaters hated the idea of having daughters and yet assigned daughters to God (16:57-59 — *“And they attribute ˹angels as˺ daughters to Allah—glory be to Him!—the opposite of what they desire for themselves Whenever one of them is given the good news of a baby girl, his face grows gloomy, as he suppresses his rage He hides himself from the people because of the bad news he has received. Should he keep her in disgrace, or bury her ˹alive˺ in the ground? Evil indeed is their judgment”*), and the Book repeats the same argument elsewhere in a sharp question: has God taken daughters for Himself and given you sons? (43:16 — *“Has He taken ˹angels as His˺ daughters from what He created, and favoured you ˹O pagans˺ with sons”*; 52:39 — *“Or does He have daughters ˹as you claim˺, while you ˹prefer to˺ have sons”*). Here the claim grows bolder. They say the best share is theirs, and the Book names the words for what they are: *qawl al-zūr*, the speech of falsehood. The verse then states the destination, and the next verse moves on to earlier nations who said the same thing and had their deeds made to look fair to them by Satan (16:63 — *“By Allah! We have surely sent messengers to communities before you ˹O Prophet˺, but Satan made their misdeeds appealing to them.”*). The passage is not an argument about who has daughters; it is about men who wrote themselves a comfortable future and went on living in it.
verses.63:
> By Allah! We have surely sent messengers to communities before you ˹O Prophet˺, but Satan made their misdeeds appealing to them. So he is their patron today, and they will suffer a painful punishment

The verse states the history of the charge and names its author. Messengers were sent to communities before, and when they came the same accusations arrived with them — the Book lists them elsewhere: a poet, a madman, a man taught by others, a soothsayer (52:29–30 — *“So ˹continue to˺ remind ˹all, O Prophet˺. For you, by the grace of your Lord, are not a fortune-teller or a madman Or do they say, “˹He is˺ a poet, for whom we ˹eagerly˺ await an ill-fate!””*; 44:14 — *“then they turned away from him, saying, “A madman, taught by others!””*; 69:41–42 — *“It is not the prose of a poet ˹as you claim˺, ˹yet˺ you hardly have any faith Nor is it the mumbling of a fortune-teller, ˹yet˺ you are hardly mindful”*). The verse answers with the one thing that can follow the ordinary resistance of people: they are shown what they do not turn away from, and their turning away is credited to their own hearts. The Book's answer to the whole charge is in 16:103 — *“And We surely know that they say, “No one is teaching him except a human.” But the man they refer to speaks a foreign tongue, whereas this ˹Quran˺ is ˹in˺ eloquent Arabic”*, where it notes that the man they point to speaks a foreign tongue while the revelation is in clear Arabic.

---

The author named here is the same one the sūrah has spoken of in describing the enemies of every prophet: the Book says that God has made for every prophet an enemy among the devils of humankind and the jinn, who inspire one another with fine talk to deceive (6:112 — *“And so We have made for every prophet enemies—devilish humans and jinn—whispering to one another with elegant words of deception.”*). The promise attached to the verse — that God will guide whom He wills, and He knows best who is rightly guided — answers the prophet's grief rather than the accusers' charge. The sūrah of Ṭā Hā records the same counsel when it tells the Prophet that God knows best who has strayed and who is guided (20:135 — *“Say ˹to them, O Prophet˺, “Each ˹of us˺ is waiting, so keep waiting! You will soon know who is on the Straight Path and is ˹rightly˺ guided.””*).
verses.64:
> We have revealed to you the Book only to clarify for them what they differed about, and as a guide and mercy for those who believe

The verse states why the Book was sent down, and it gives the reason in two parts: to make clear what people differ about, and to be a guide and a mercy for those who believe. Most of this sūrah has been doing the first part, arguing about God, the idols, the resurrection and what is lawful to eat. This verse says why the argument is being made at all.

The Book makes the same claim in the sūrah of the Ant, where it judges between the Children of Israel about most of what they differed over and is a guide and a mercy to the believers (27:76 gives the claim — *“Indeed, this Quran clarifies for the Children of Israel most of what they differ over”*). Notice where the mercy is placed: with belief, not with the explanation alone. Many people in Makkah heard the explanation and went away unchanged.

**What the Sūrah Has Been Doing**

By this point the reader has watched the first purpose being carried out for many verses. Every dispute in the sūrah has been answered: what the idolaters claimed about daughters, the mockers' demand for a sign, the accusation that a foreigner was teaching the Prophet, and the arguments about lawful food. The Book came to settle these matters, and the sūrah settles them by returning to the same two facts about God. He made the world, and He will judge it.

**The Same Words Elsewhere**

The sūrah of the Ant states the same description in almost the same words, adding that the Book will judge between the Children of Israel about most of what they differed over (27:76 and 27:77 give it), and the sūrah of the Cow says the Book was sent so that God could judge between people in their disagreements (2:213 states it — *“Then Allah raised prophets as deliverers of good news and as warners, and revealed to them the Scriptures in truth to judge among people regarding their disputes.”*).

The Book never claims to end every argument. It claims that it states the truth about the matters that count, and that those who believe it find mercy in it. The verse after this one lifts the reader's eyes from the Book back to the sky and the earth, with rain that brings dead land to life.
verses.65:
> And Allah sends down rain from the sky, giving life to the earth after its death. Surely in this is a sign for those who listen

Rain is the sūrah's evidence of resurrection carried in a picture anyone can see. The Book says the earth is revived after its death. It does the same in Sūrah al-Rūm, where the sight of the revived land is given as proof of the One who brings out the dead (30:19 — *“He brings forth the living from the dead and the dead from the living. And He gives life to the earth after its death. And so will you be brought forth ˹from the grave˺”*), and in Sūrah al-Ḥajj, where the earth swells and grows after the shower is sent down (22:5 — *“And you see the earth lifeless, but as soon as We send down rain upon it, it begins to stir ˹to life˺ and swell, producing every type of pleasant plant”*). The verse's ending gives the condition for the sign's value: it is a sign for those who listen, and sūrah 22 repeats that it is a sign for people who understand. The pattern is the sūrah's way of measuring the audience rather than the evidence.

**The Rain They Themselves Ascribed to God**

The verse's argument had already been won in the mouths of those who heard it. The Book reports the exchange more than once: if you asked them who sends down water from the sky and revives the earth by it, they would say God (29:63 — *“And if you ask them who sends down rain from the sky, giving life to the earth after its death, they will surely say, “Allah!””*), and if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would answer that the Almighty, the All-Knowing did (43:9 — *“If you ask them ˹O Prophet˺ who created the heavens and the earth, they will certainly say, “The Almighty, All-Knowing did.””*; 43:87 — *“If you ask them ˹O Prophet˺ who created them, they will certainly say, “Allah!” How can they then be deluded ˹from the truth˺”*). The Makkans admitted the sender of the rain and still denied the raising of the dead, and the Book takes their admission and puts it to work: the One who brings a dead land to life can raise the dead who lie in it (36:33 — *“There is a sign for them in the dead earth: We give it life, producing grain from it for them to eat”*; 50:9-11 — *“And We send down blessed rain from the sky, bringing forth gardens and grains for harvest”*). The verse's closing words, that this is a sign for those who listen, name the gap exactly — the evidence was never the obstacle, and the listeners were.

**The Prayer for Rain and the Word of Thanks**

The community's practice kept the verse's lesson in the calendar. The Prophet led the prayer for rain when the land was dry and asked God to send water down on the people and the land, and the reports describe him going out into it and letting it fall on him, saying that it had just come from its Lord (Abū Dāwūd). When the rain came he named the two possible sentences about it: we have been given rain by the bounty and mercy of God, which is faith in the Giver, and the rain has come by the favour of such-and-such a star, which is a denial of Him (al-Bukhārī). So a plain statement about water and dead ground ends where the sūrah's verses on nature always end, with the hearer rather than the weather: the sign is free, and the thankfulness or the ignoring of it is the human act.
verses.66:
> And there is certainly a lesson for you in cattle: We give you to drink of what is in their bellies, from between digested food and blood: pure milk, pleasant to drink

Milch cattle are offered as a lesson rather than an ornament, and the verse describes the process with an accuracy that the hearers could verify in their own tents: milk comes from between the digested food and the blood, and it arrives pure for the drinkers. The Book repeats the account in Sūrah al-Muʾminūn, attached to the same list of blessings, and adds the detail that the animals also provide meat and hides (23:21–22 — *“And there is certainly a lesson for you in cattle, from whose bellies We give you ˹milk˺ to drink, and in them are many other benefits for you, and from them you may eat”*). The scholars read the pair "food and blood" as a description of where milk forms in the animal, which is why the verse's word for it, *khalisan sāʾighan*, pure and easy to swallow, is agreed by anyone who has drunk it. The sign is placed among the blessings the sūrah is counting, not in a chapter of biology.

---

The same lesson is drawn from the cattle in the sūrah of the Believers, where they are named among the signs and the drink is described as coming out of what is in their bellies (23:21 — *“And there is certainly a lesson for you in cattle, from whose bellies We give you ˹milk˺ to drink, and in them are many other benefits for you, and from them you may eat”*), and in the sūrah of the Troops, where the milk is called pure and pleasant to those who drink it (16:66; 39:6 — *“He created you ˹all˺ from a single soul, then from it He made its mate. And He produced for you four pairs of cattle. He creates you in the wombs of your mothers ˹in stages˺, one development after another, in three layers of darkness. That is Allah—your Lord! All authority belongs to Him. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. How can you then be turned away”*). The verse's detail about the route the milk takes — from between what is digested and the blood — is the Qur'an's way of making the sign concrete for people who knew the process from their herds. The Book elsewhere names the cattle the bearers of loads and the source of food (6:142 — *“Some cattle are fit for labour, others are too small. Eat of what Allah has provided for you and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. Certainly, he is your sworn enemy”*), so the lesson is one entry in the sūrah's running account of provisions.
verses.67:
> And from the fruits of palm trees and grapevines you derive intoxicants as well as wholesome provision. Surely in this is a sign for those who understand

The verse names both sides of the same fruit: the intoxicant the people made of dates and grapes, and the wholesome provision God made of them. Al-Ṭabarī and the later commentators note the sequence: the Book calls wine *sakar* here, and it treats its use as a thing people chose while provision is what God gave. The same sūrah later forbids what intoxicates through the command to eat what is lawful and good (16:114–115 — *“So eat from the good, lawful things which Allah has provided for you, and be grateful for Allah’s favours, if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺”*), and the full prohibition of wine came in Madinah with the verse that calls it an abomination of Satan's handiwork (5:90–91 — *“O believers! Intoxicants, gambling, idols, and drawing lots for decisions are all evil of Satan’s handiwork. So shun them so you may be successful”*). The verse is therefore read as a reminder that the mercy in a fruit is not the same thing as the use people make of it, and the sign is for those who understand.

**The Fruit and the Drink**

The verse puts the two uses of the same harvest side by side: the crop the people turned into *sakar*, and the provision God placed in it — good food for those who understand. The word *sakar* covers what clouds the mind, and the sūrah leaves it at that, because the chapter was given in Makkah and this is how the Book works: it first names an evil, then draws the hearers away from it, and only later closes the door. The Sūrah of the Cow states the earlier stage with its balance sheet: some benefit for people, and a sin greater than the benefit (2:219 — *“Say, “There is great evil in both, as well as some benefit for people—but the evil outweighs the benefit.””*). By the time the community had a state and a law, the ruling came in full: intoxicants are the work of Satan, so avoid them (5:90-91 — *“O believers! Intoxicants, gambling, idols, and drawing lots for decisions are all evil of Satan’s handiwork. So shun them so you may be successful”*). The verse in front of us is the moment when the question was planted, and the sign it points to is the crop itself — a gift that is a gift in the eating and a trap in the drinking.
verses.68:
> And your Lord inspired the bees: “Make ˹your˺ homes in the mountains, the trees, and in what people construct

The bee's instruction is one of the sūrah's clearest examples of revelation reaching a creature that cannot speak: *awḥā rabbuka ilā al-naḥl* — your Lord inspired the bee. The Book uses the same verb for the inspiration given to the mother of Moses (28:7 — *“We inspired the mother of Moses: “Nurse him, but when you fear for him, put him then into the river, and do not fear or grieve.”*) and for the instinct of the heavens and the earth (41:12 — *“So He formed the heaven into seven heavens in two Days, assigning to each its mandate. And We adorned the lowest heaven with ˹stars like˺ lamps ˹for beauty˺ and for protection. That is the design of the Almighty, All-Knowing.””*), so what the verse reports is guidance built into a creature rather than a message delivered by a messenger. The bee is told where to build — mountains, trees, and what people construct — and the verse names the three kinds of home in the order of their security, ending with the one built by human hands, which is the one the honey the reader eats was most likely made in. The sūrah's sequence of blessings then continues with what comes out of the bee, in the next verse.
verses.69:
> and feed from ˹the flower of˺ any fruit ˹you please˺ and follow the ways your Lord has made easy for you.” From their bellies comes forth liquid of varying colours, in which there is healing for people. Surely in this is a sign for those who reflect

The bee's product is the sūrah's third food, and it arrives with the same structure as the milk and the fruit: the animal does what God inspired it to do, and what comes out of it is useful to human beings. The Book gives the syrup a description — a liquid of varying colours — and names what it is for: healing for people. The commentators note that the Book says *shifāʾ li-al-nās*, healing for people, without limiting the illness or claiming that honey replaces every remedy. The bee is also presented as a teacher of organisation: nations and houses have taken from its building and its order. The verse closes the section of blessings with a sign, as the previous ones did, and it is a sign for people who think.

---

The drink the bee produces is named as a healing in the same sentence, and the Prophet ﷺ is reported in the Ṣaḥīḥ collections to have named honey among the means of healing God has provided for people, and to have treated a stomach complaint with it. The bee's industry is also used as a pattern of the community's work: the sūrah of Muhammad describes the rivers of the Garden as including one of purified honey (47:15 — *“The description of the Paradise promised to the righteous is that in it are rivers of fresh water, rivers of milk that never changes in taste, rivers of wine delicious to drink, and rivers of pure honey.”*), which puts the bee's product in the world's provision and the world to come. The verse's phrase about following the ways the Lord has made easy for it describes an instinct that is itself an instruction, so that the creature's orderliness is part of the sign.

**What the Verse Names**

The verse gives the bee its work and the product that comes out of it, a drink of different colours in which there is healing for people, and it closes with the sentence that in this is a sign for people who reflect. The Book's account of the bee is the third of the sūrah's product passages, after the milk of the cattle and the fruits of the palms and the vines (16:66-67 — *“And from the fruits of palm trees and grapevines you derive intoxicants as well as wholesome provision. Surely in this is a sign for those who understand”*), and the three are arranged in the same shape: what the creature does, what comes out of it, and what it means.
**What the Commentators Wrote**

The older commentators noted the detail about the bee's work, which the verses before this one describe, where the insect is given its instinct to build its house in the mountains and the trees and to eat from every kind of fruit. The Book calls what comes out of it a drink rather than a food, and the scholars wrote about the healing in the honey through the reports and the medicine that was known in their time; the general reading is that the verse names the healing without limiting it to one use. The Prophet's word about the two remedies, honey and the Recitation, is in the collections, and the community's physicians read it with this verse.
**Where the Passage Stands**

The sūrah has been listing the signs since its fifth verse, and the passage on the bee is followed by the account of God's favour in the institution of marriage and the family (16:72 — *“And Allah has made for you spouses of your own kind, and given you through your spouses children and grandchildren. And He has granted you good, lawful provisions. Are they then faithful to falsehood and ungrateful for Allah’s favours”*). The Book's arrangement keeps the natural world and the human world side by side, and the verse in front of us is the last of the animal passages before the sūrah turns to the community's own life. The sentence about reflection is repeated at the end of several of the sūrah's passages, and it is the response the whole catalogue is looking for.
verses.70:
> Allah has created you, and then causes you to die. And some of you are left to reach the most feeble stage of life so that they may know nothing after having known much. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, Most Capable

**The Two Ends of a Life Put Side by Side**

The verse sets out three stages and names God as the one who runs all three. He created you, then He causes you to die, and among you there is the one who is brought back to the weakest age of life, so that after knowing a great deal he knows nothing.

Old age enters the sūrah as part of the answer to the idolaters' reasoning. The point is that the One who made a person and the One who causes his death is the One who has power over both ends of the life between them. If He can start a person from nothing and turn him back into a state like the beginning, nothing about the return after death is difficult for Him.

**The Same Three Stages Elsewhere**

The Book repeats this sequence in the sūrah of the Pilgrimage, where creation, death and the return to the feeblest age are used together as proof of the raising (22:5 gives all three — *“O humanity! If you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then ˹know that˺ We did create you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then ˹developed you into˺ a clinging clot ˹of blood˺, then a lump of flesh—fully formed or unformed—in order to demonstrate ˹Our power˺ to you.”*). The sūrah of Yāsīn states the reversal in its own words, saying that whoever is given a long life is turned back in creation (36:68 states it — *“And whoever We grant a long life, We reverse them in development. Will they not then understand”*).

The repetition is the teaching. The Book uses the shape of a human life as one of its clearest arguments for the life to come, because everyone watching a family knows what it looks like. A child grows into strength, and strength fades back into the helplessness of the beginning, and the person who lived through both stages had no power over either.

**What the Verse Says to the Idolaters**

The Makkans argued that their ancestors had lived and died and that there was nothing beyond. This verse answers the argument with a fact they could see in their own homes and streets. The same hand that brought a person into the world takes him out of it, and the same hand that lets a man build up knowledge and strength takes them back.

So the answer to the reasoning about the forefathers is that the One who spans both ends of every life has knowledge of every course. Nothing about a person's beginning or his end is outside the arrangement, and the closing word of the verse names the accounting that follows for everyone who was given the whole span of years to use. The sūrah then continues with the signs of provision and mercy, since the argument has been built on what people use every day rather than on what they cannot see.
verses.71:
> And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision. But those who have been much favoured would not share their wealth with those ˹bondspeople˺ in their possession, making them their equals. Do they then deny Allah’s favours

The sūrah turns from the gifts to the human order built on them. Provision is distributed unequally under God's arrangement, and the verse points out that the men who hold the surplus would not hand it over to those whom their right hands possess so that they might become equal in it. The verse does not condemn the mark of difference; it uses their own behaviour as an argument about God. If a man will not share the wealth he was given with his own servants, how can he set up equals with the One who gave it to both? The Companion ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have read the verse the same way, as an argument against assigning partners in worship to the source of all provision.

**Where the Argument Goes Next**

The verse is the first of a set, and the ones that follow complete the reasoning. The Book presses the same point twice more in the passage: the comparison between the man's attitude to his own servants and his willingness to assign partners to God, and then the warning against drawing conclusions from outward provision — *and God has favoured some of you over others in provision* (16:71 continues into the next verses on marriage and the law of the household). The sūrah then asks the question that settles the matter for the reader: is the one who does right and the one who does not equal? Do they remember? (16:76-77 in the same sequence — *“Can such a person be equal to the one who commands justice and is on the Straight Path”*). The argument is built so that a man who would never surrender a share in his own wealth to a servant finds himself explaining why he should surrender a share in God's authority to a stone.
verses.72:
> And Allah has made for you spouses of your own kind, and given you through your spouses children and grandchildren. And He has granted you good, lawful provisions. Are they then faithful to falsehood and ungrateful for Allah’s favours

The list of gifts continues and moves to the family. Spouses are said to be "of your own kind" — *min anfusikum* — which the commentators take as a statement about the design of companionship as well as about species, and the sūrah of the Romans adds the purpose: tranquillity, affection and mercy placed between husband and wife (30:21 — *“And He has placed between you compassion and mercy.”*). The children and grandchildren named here are given in the same sentence as good provision, and the next verse turns to the absurdity that follows: after all this, people worship what cannot give anything. The verse works in the sūrah's order of argument — a gift, the failure to be grateful, and then the question of who deserves the worship.

---

**From Your Own Kind**

The verse's phrase *min anfusikum* is the first thing the commentators weigh. Spouses are given from the same kind, and the phrase covers two mercies at once: a companion who can understand what a human being goes through, and a bond that is not a crossing of species. The sūrah of the Romans names the fruit of this arrangement — tranquillity, affection and mercy settled between the two (30:21 — *“And one of His signs is that He created for you spouses from among yourselves so that you may find comfort in them. And He has placed between you compassion and mercy. Surely in this are signs for people who reflect”*) — and the sūrah of the Discrimination describes the same act from a wider angle, the One who made from water a human being and gave him lineage and marriage (25:54 — *“And He is the One Who creates human beings from a ˹humble˺ liquid, then establishes for them bonds of kinship and marriage. For your Lord is Most Capable”*).
**Sons and Grandsons**

The verse names *banīn wa-ḥafadah*, sons and grandchildren. Some commentators read *ḥafadah* as the grandchildren, some as the sons-in-law and the helpers a large family brings; either way, the word covers the generation the parents did not raise alone and cannot repay, the ones who carry the household's name and burden both. That is the physical side of the gift, and the verse sets it beside the provision of good things as one package.
**The Question the Verse Turns On**

The verse ends on a question that the reader is meant to feel in his own chest: *do they then believe in falsehood and deny the favour of God?* (16:72). The charge is not simply that the idolaters are mistaken but that they are ungrateful — they accept gifts from one hand every day and thank another. The whole passage runs that way: gift, gratitude, and then the absurdity of where the gratitude went.
verses.73:
> Yet they worship besides Allah those ˹idols˺ who do not afford them any provision from the heavens and the earth, nor do they have the power to

**Idols That Cannot Provide**

The verse states the charge against the idolaters with exact words: they worship, besides God, beings that cannot give them any provision out of the heavens or the earth, and have no power to do it. The passage has been listing what God alone does: He sends down rain from the sky and brings the earth to life with it, He gives the date palm and the grape and every fruit (16:11 names them — *“With it He produces for you ˹various˺ crops, olives, palm trees, grapevines, and every type of fruit. Surely in this is a sign for those who reflect”*), and He alone knows what every female carries. The verse in front of the reader takes the objects of worship and measures them against that list, and they come out at nothing.

**What Idols Can and Cannot Do**

The Book makes the same argument in several places. It says of the objects of worship that they did not create anything and were themselves created, that they cannot help their worshippers and cannot even help themselves (the sūrah of the Criterion states it at 25:3 — *“Yet they have taken besides Him gods who cannot create anything but are themselves created.”*), and it challenges the idolaters in the sūrah of Sabaʾ to ask those gods of theirs for rain, or to name a share of the earth they created. The most the idolaters claimed for their gods was that they could carry a request to God, since everyone could see that wood and stone do not feed anybody. The Book answers that a being which holds no property and gives no provision has no say in what belongs to God (the sūrah of Jonah reports their claim at 10:18 — *“Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Are you informing Allah of something He does not know in the heavens or the earth?”*, and the sūrah of the Throngs gives the answer at 39:43 — *“Or have they taken others besides Allah as intercessors? Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “˹Would they do so,˺ even though those ˹idols˺ have neither authority nor intelligence?””* and 39:44 — *“Say, “All intercession belongs to Allah ˹alone˺. To Him belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. Then to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned.””*). The argument in the verse is therefore aimed at the claim that was actually being made, and it leaves nothing of it standing.

**What the Passage Has Set Beside It**

The sūrah has been travelling through the signs in the world and in the human being, and the verses before this one name what God gives and what He withholds. It told the community about the honey bee and the shade and the roads, and it named the towns that were destroyed for the same wrong the verse in front of the reader is describing (16:112 gives the example of a town that was given provision and then denied it). The chapter keeps the same method as the sūrah of Abraham, where the argument is put plainly: the things people worship cannot hear them and cannot harm them, and God knows what they say (19:42 records Abraham's words to his father, and the argument runs on through the same sūrah).

**What the Verse Asks of the Reader**

The verse invites the reader to look at what he actually depends on each day: bread, water, weather, children, health. None of it comes from wood or stone, and the verse states the fact so plainly that the reader can test it in his own kitchen. The same sūrah says a few verses later that if anyone were to try to count the blessings of God he would not manage it (16:18 states it — *“If you tried to count Allah’s blessings, you would never be able to number them. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*), and the road from the blessings to the One who gives them is the road the verse is asking the reader to walk. The sūrah of the Criterion states the same about the objects of worship when it says that they did not create anything and cannot help even themselves (25:3 — *“Yet they have taken besides Him gods who cannot create anything but are themselves created.”*).
verses.74:
> So do not set up equals to Allah, for Allah certainly knows and you do not know

The command not to set up equals to God is followed by a reason in the same verse: God knows and the people do not know. The contrast is the sūrah's way of stating that idolatry is a mistake in knowledge before it is a mistake in worship, and that the One who sees the reality of things has forbidden the thing itself. The Book gives the same argument in Sūrah al-Najm with its strongest form: do not set up any other god with Allah, for He knows everything and no one shares His knowledge. The instruction is repeated in the sūrah's own voice, and the next verses switch to parables that show the difference between a partner who owns nothing and a master who owns everything.

**Why the Ban Is Stated This Way**

The verse does not argue the case for God's oneness in long form. It gives the ban and then gives the reason: He knows and you do not know. That is the sūrah's method whenever it deals with idolatry, and the reason is a statement about knowledge. Anyone who measures the Creator by created things has already chosen a scale that cannot weigh what is being discussed, and the Sūrah of Consultation states the result plainly: there is nothing like Him (42:11 — *“There is nothing like Him, for He ˹alone˺ is the All-Hearing, All-Seeing”*). The Book also warns in another place that eyes cannot take Him in while He takes in all eyes (6:103 — *“No vision can encompass Him, but He encompasses all vision. For He is the Most Subtle, All-Aware”*). The next verses carry the point into pictures: a servant who owns nothing set beside one whom God has provided generously, and a man who cannot speak and can do nothing set beside a man who commands justice (16:75-76 — *“Can such a person be equal to the one who commands justice and is on the Straight Path”*). The command not to set up equals therefore ends in the place it began: the One being compared is not known the way the compared are known.
verses.75:
> Allah sets forth a parable: a slave who lacks all means, compared to a ˹free˺ man to whom We granted a good provision, of which he donates ˹freely,˺ openly and secretly. Are they equal? Praise be to Allah. In fact, most of them do not know

The parable sets two men side by side: one who is owned and has no power over anything, and one whom God has given a good provision which he spends openly and in secret. The Book asks whether they can be equal, and its expected answer is the same one the hearer already gives for people. That is the argument. If two servants of yours — one with nothing of his own and one with property — are not equal in your eyes, then the idol you keep as a partner of God is not equal to its Lord. The verse is followed by a second parable that compares a man who can do nothing with a man who commands justice and follows a straight path, so that the two stories together cover both the powerless partner and the useless one.

---

The commentators read the two men in two ways that point the same way: the slave is the idol that owns nothing and can do nothing, set against God the Provider who spends as He wills, or the two are the disbeliever and the believer, one bound by his own falsehood and the other enriched and free with what he has been given. The parable belongs to the sūrah's argument about the associate-gods: a being that possesses nothing of itself cannot be the source of anything for another, and the whole chapter is built at this point to separate what God does from what the creatures do (16:72–74 — *“And Allah has made for you spouses of your own kind, and given you through your spouses children and grandchildren. And He has granted you good, lawful provisions. Are they then faithful to falsehood and ungrateful for Allah’s favours”*). The question that closes the verse is the audience's own verdict, put to them before the conclusion is drawn.

**The Second Parable and the Man Who Cannot Speak**

The verse after this one completes the argument with a second pair of men: a man who is owned, who has no power over anything, who is a burden on his master wherever he is sent because he cannot make himself understood, set beside a man who commands justice and stands on a straight path (16:76 — *“He is a burden on his master.”*). Read together, the two parables make one point from two angles. The first names the idol as a servant who owns nothing; the second names it as a servant who cannot do anything. The commentators applied the pair both to the idols and to the contrast between the man of faith and the man without it, and both readings serve the sūrah, since the argument is that a being which owns nothing of itself cannot be the source of anything for anyone. The section is framed by two statements that make the comparison safe to read: the verse before it warns the reader not to invent comparisons with God (16:74 — *“So do not set up equals to Allah, for Allah certainly knows and you do not know”*), and the verse after it says that God's command, when He wills a thing, is a single word (16:77 — *“To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs ˹the knowledge of˺ the unseen in the heavens and the earth. Bringing about the Hour would only take the blink of an eye, or even less. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”*). The Book gives the parables, and then it removes the distance between the parables and their Lord.
verses.76:
> And Allah sets forth a parable of two men: one of them is dumb, incapable of anything. He is a burden on his master. Wherever he is sent, he brings no good. Can such a person be equal to the one who commands justice and is on the Straight Path

The second parable draws a man who is dumb and incapable of anything, a burden on his master wherever he is sent. The Book then sets beside him the man who commands justice and stands on a straight path. The first figure is read by the commentators as a description of the idols — useless in themselves, unable to speak or to bless — and the second as a description of God, whose rule is justice and whose way is straight. The verse does not name either figure, which is how parables in this sūrah work: the hearer assigns the parts himself, and the assignment is the argument. The sūrah's own conclusion follows in the next verses, where the unseen and the Hour are declared to be God's alone.

---

The second figure is read as the idol itself or as the person who follows it: speechless, unable to act for anyone, a burden to whoever owns it. The man who commands justice and stands on a straight path is the opposite in every clause, and the Book uses the same imagery of walking a straight road for the believer's life elsewhere (6:153 — *“Indeed, that is My Path—perfectly straight.”*; 1:6 — *“Guide us along the Straight Path”*). The pair of parables in this passage works by contrast: one presents the difference of power, and this one presents the difference of benefit, and the two together establish what the sūrah has been saying about the worthlessness of the gods the audience served.

**What the Parable Is Doing in This Sūrah**

The two men in this verse are the fourth picture the sūrah has used to make the same point. The Book has already set the servant who owns nothing beside the master provided for generously (16:75 — *“Allah sets forth a parable: a slave who lacks all means, compared to a ˹free˺ man to whom We granted a good provision, of which he donates ˹freely,˺ openly and secretly. Are they equal? Praise be to Allah. In fact, most of them do not know”*), and it has asked whether the one who does right and the one who does not can be equal. The verse in front of us takes the argument to its end: a man who cannot speak, who has to be carried by his master wherever he is sent and brings no good from the errand, set beside a man who commands justice and stands on a straight path. The question that follows is whether the two are equal, and the Book leaves it as a question because the answer is obvious to anyone who heard it.
**Who the Two Were Taken To Be**

The commentators read the mute figure as the idol, which cannot speak and can do nothing, and the man who commands justice as God, or as the believer who acts on God's command. Both readings were recorded, and both work with the sūrah's argument, since the idols of the town were literally silent objects and the men who served them were the ones being addressed. The Sūrah of the Heights makes the same case in plain words, saying that the false gods are created and cannot create (7:191 — *“Do they associate ˹with Allah˺ those ˹idols˺ which cannot create anything, but are in fact created”*), and the Sūrah of the Cattle asks whether the blind man and the seeing man can be the same (6:50 — *“Say, “Are those blind ˹to the truth˺ equal to those who can see?”*).
**The Word for Justice**

The verse says the free man *yaʾmuru bi-al-ʿadl* — he commands justice — and the phrase is one the Book uses for the highest form of human authority, since it is the command God gives to rulers and to the community itself (16:90 — *“Indeed, Allah commands justice, grace, as well as courtesy to close relatives.”*; 4:58 — *“Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners; and when you judge between people, judge with fairness. What a noble commandment from Allah to you! Surely Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing”*). Setting a man whose whole life is the command of justice against an object that cannot utter a word is the sūrah's way of stating the difference between the creator and the made.
