The next verse gives the conclusion, naming the fact that belongs to God alone and asking whether the people will remember it.
verses.77:
> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs ˹the knowledge of˺ the unseen in the heavens and the earth. Bringing about the Hour would only take the blink of an eye, or even less. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything

The verse states both halves of the argument for the Hour: its knowledge belongs to God alone, and its coming is closer to the blink of an eye than the hearer imagines. The Book uses the same comparison in Sūrah al-Qamar, where God's command is described as a single act like the twinkling of an eye (54:50 — *“Our command is but a single word, done in the blink of an eye”*), and in Sūrah al-Rūm, where the Hour arrives in an instant (30:55 — *“And on the Day the Hour will arrive, the wicked will swear that they did not stay ˹in this world˺ more than an hour. In this way they were always deluded ˹in the world˺”*). The word the translators render as "blink" — *lamḥ al-baṣar* — is a glimpse so fast that sight cannot hold it, and the verse's closing comparison, "or nearer," is left unqualified. The claim answers the demand of the mockers that the punishment be hurried, and it reduces the whole wait to something the eye cannot measure.

---

The image of the blink of an eye — and the verse adds that God's command is simply to say "Be" — is the Qur'an's standard statement of the ease with which the Hour arrives: the sūrah of the Moon says the command is but a single blast, like the twinkling of an eye (54:50 — *“Our command is but a single word, done in the blink of an eye”*), and the sūrah of al-Shūrā says the day is near and there is no doubt of it (42:17 — *“It is Allah Who has revealed the Book with the truth and the balance ˹of justice˺. You never know, perhaps the Hour is near”*). The verse's first half states the limit of knowledge: the unseen in the heavens and the earth belongs to God alone, which answers the Makkan question about the timing of the promise, recorded earlier in the sūrah of Jonah (10:48 — *“They ask ˹the believers˺, “When will this threat come to pass if what you say is true?””*).
verses.78:
> And Allah brought you out of the wombs of your mothers while you knew nothing, and gave you hearing, sight, and intellect so perhaps you would be thankful

The verse's list of gifts is the sūrah's argument for gratitude in a single line: the child is brought out of the womb knowing nothing, and then given hearing, sight and intellect. The Book uses the same trio in Sūrah al-Muʾminūn and Sūrah al-Sajdah, where the faculties are named in order and gratitude is expected for them (23:78 — *“He is the One Who created for you hearing, sight, and intellect. ˹Yet˺ you hardly give any thanks”*; 32:9 — *“then He fashioned them and had a spirit of His Own ˹creation˺ breathed into them. And He gave you hearing, sight, and intellect. ˹Yet˺ you hardly give any thanks”*), and it warns in the same sūrahs against making little use of what the organs are for — the eye, the ear, and the heart are the things a person will be asked about. The word *afʾidah*, hearts and minds, carries both the seat of understanding and of feeling, which is why the Book treats it as the organ of judgement.

**Hearing Before Sight**

The order in the verse is not casual. Hearing is named first, then sight, then the hearts, and the same order stands in the Sūrah of the Believers, the Sūrah of the Prostration, and the Sūrah of the Bee's other listing of the organs (23:78 — *“He is the One Who created for you hearing, sight, and intellect. ˹Yet˺ you hardly give any thanks”*; 32:9 — *“then He fashioned them and had a spirit of His Own ˹creation˺ breathed into them. And He gave you hearing, sight, and intellect. ˹Yet˺ you hardly give any thanks”*; 76:2 — *“˹For˺ indeed, We ˹alone˺ created humans from a drop of mixed fluids, ˹in order˺ to test them, so We made them hear and see”*; 67:23 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “He is the One Who brought you into being and gave you hearing, sight, and intellect. ˹Yet˺ you hardly give any thanks.””*). The commentators noted the reason: a child takes in the world through his ears before his eyes can weigh it, and the message that saves is heard before it is understood. The Book also states the account that comes with the organs: the hearing, the sight and the heart are all going to be asked about how they were used (17:36 — *“Do not follow what you have no ˹sure˺ knowledge of. Indeed, all will be called to account for ˹their˺ hearing, sight, and intellect”*), and the men who had the faculties and made no use of them are described as worse than cattle, since the cattle at least do not misuse what they were given (7:179 — *“They have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with, and ears they do not hear with.”*).

**The Gifts Handed Over**

The verse begins from the child's arrival with nothing: brought out of the womb knowing nothing, then given hearing, sight and the inner hearts. The Prophet's words about the new-born stand beside it: every child is born on the fiṭrah, and it is his parents who set him on the road he walks (al-Bukhārī; Muslim). The two statements fit together — a person starts with nothing, receives the organs, then receives the teaching that shows him what the organs are for — and the response the verse asks is gratitude. What that gratitude is, the sūrah goes on to say: not a warm feeling but the use of the gift for the purpose it was given. The man who hears the words of God and does not act on them still has ears. The verse's own last word is not a threat but an invitation: so that you may be thankful.
verses.79:
> Have they not seen the birds glide in the open sky? None holds them up except Allah. Surely in this are signs for those who believe

The birds are the sūrah's standing sign of the created order, and the verse asks a question the hearers could test by looking up: who holds them up in the open sky? The Book repeats the picture in Sūrah al-Mulk, where the birds spread their wings above and close them, and the question is asked who holds them back except the Most Compassionate (67:19 — *“Have they not seen the birds above them, spreading and folding their wings? None holds them up except the Most Compassionate. Indeed, He is All-Seeing of everything”*), and in Sūrah al-Nūr, where the birds are described in ranks, each knowing its prayer and its praise (24:41 — *“Each ˹instinctively˺ knows their manner of prayer and glorification.”*). The point in this sūrah is placed among the blessings: a bird's flight is a provision of air and balance that no human made, and the verse's sign is addressed to people who believe.

**The Question Put to the Eyes**

The verse opens with a question — have they not looked at the birds above them? — and it is a rebuke aimed at people who use their eyes without using their minds. The Book gives the birds their own place in the story of the prophets: the hills and the birds joined David in praise (21:79 — *“We subjected the mountains as well as the birds to hymn ˹Our praises˺ along with David. It is We Who did ˹it all˺”*; 34:10 — *“Indeed, We granted David a ˹great˺ privilege from Us, ˹commanding:˺ “O mountains! Echo his hymns! And the birds as well.” We made iron mouldable for him”*), Solomon was taught the speech of the birds and marched with them in his ranks (27:16 — *“And David was succeeded by Solomon, who said, “O people!”*), and a bird carried his letter to Sheba (27:28 — *“Go with this letter of mine and deliver it to them, then stand aside and see how they will respond.””*). The point is never that flight is strange; it is that flight is normal, ordered and held by someone. The same question is put in the Sūrah of the Kingdom, where the birds hold their wings out and fold them in and the reader is asked who keeps them aloft but the Most Merciful (67:19 — *“Have they not seen the birds above them, spreading and folding their wings? None holds them up except the Most Compassionate. Indeed, He is All-Seeing of everything”*). A thing that happens every morning is still the work of a hand.

**Birds as a Community**

The Book narrows the sign in another place to a sentence with a wide meaning: there is no creature on the earth, and no bird flying on its wings, that does not form communities like the human community, and all of them will be gathered to their Lord (6:38 — *“Then to their Lord they will be gathered all together”*). Their praise is real in the Book's account, each of them knowing its prayer and its praise (24:41 — *“Each ˹instinctively˺ knows their manner of prayer and glorification.”*), and the law that carries a swallow through the open air is the same law that holds a person upright on the ground. The verse's ending, that here are signs for people who believe, gives the believer a habit of noticing: the rooftops, the trees and the open sky are full of evidence for anyone willing to look at the One who holds them up.
verses.80:
> And Allah has made your homes a place to rest, and has given you tents from the hide of animals, light to handle when you travel and when you camp. And out of their wool, fur, and hair He has given you furnishings and goods for a while

The verse moves from the sky to the household, and it names the simplest goods first: the house as a place of rest, and tents from hides that are light enough to carry on the day a family travels and to pitch when they settle. The Book lists the hides alongside other materials of shelter — wool, hair and fur, and furnishings used for a time (16:80). The description is practical rather than poetic, and that is the sūrah's method in the blessing section: food, drink, children, animals, homes, clothing and armour are counted one after another so that the reader reaches the question at the end of the list — whose are they, and who gave them?

---

The list moves through the whole range of shelter: houses for rest, tents of hide that a family carries and pitches, and then the furnishings made from wool, fur and hair that the sūrah names next (16:80). The Book uses the same order in describing creation's provisions for humans in the sūrah of the Cessation: skins of the livestock for tents and furnishings (16:80; 5:95 — *“O believers! Do not kill game while on pilgrimage. Whoever kills game intentionally must compensate by offering its equivalence—as judged by two just men among you—to be offered at the Sacred House, or by feeding the needy, or by fasting so that they may taste the consequences of their violations. Allah has forgiven what has been done. But those who persist will be punished by Allah. And Allah is Almighty, capable of punishment”*). What the verse draws out is that the simplest and most portable goods — a tent, a mat, a basket — are as much signs of provision as the sky and the cattle, and the chapter returns to the same language at 16:81 — *“And Allah has provided you shade out of what He created, and has given you shelter in the mountains. He has also provided you with clothes protecting you from the heat ˹and cold˺, and armour shielding you in battle. This is how He perfects His favour upon you, so perhaps you will ˹fully˺ submit ˹to Him˺”* before it names the purpose of the enumeration.

**What the Verse Counts**

The sūrah has been listing the gifts of the created world since its beginning, and the verse turns from the animals and the sky to the house. It names the fixed dwelling as a place of rest, the tents made of skins that a family carries on a journey, the wool and fur and hair used for furnishings and for a while, and the shade of what God has made and the refuge in the mountains, and it closes with garments against the heat and armour against violence. The Book gives the reader a list of ordinary things and then states what they are for, and the completeness of the inventory is the point: there is no comfort in a house that the Book has not named as a gift.
**The Word for Rest**

The word used for the fixed house is the one the Book also uses elsewhere for the deliverance from hardship, so that a home is described as the place where a person is freed from the heat and the road. The Book uses the same idea for the rest that follows the labour of this life, when the people of the Garden say that all sorrow has been taken from them (35:34-35 — *“˹He is the One˺ Who—out of His grace—has settled us in the Home of Everlasting Stay, where we will be touched by neither fatigue nor weariness.””*), and for the safety of a traveller who reaches his own home. The verse in front of us uses the word for a roof over a person's head, which is where the Book puts the first taste of it.
**What the Sūrah Says About the Sky's Shade and the Mountain's Shelter**

The middle of the verse names the shade God made and the mountains He made as places of refuge, and the commentators read the two halves as the protections of a journey: the shade of a tree, and the cave in a mountain. It then lists the clothing that protects from heat and the armour that protects from blows, and the Book's arrangement keeps the peaceful protection and the violent one in the same sentence. The verse after these closes the passage on the blessing of God and the response it asks for, which the sūrah states as gratitude.
verses.81:
> And Allah has provided you shade out of what He created, and has given you shelter in the mountains. He has also provided you with clothes protecting you from the heat ˹and cold˺, and armour shielding you in battle. This is how He perfects His favour upon you, so perhaps you will ˹fully˺ submit ˹to Him˺

The list closes with shade, shelter in the mountains, clothing that protects against heat, and armour that protects in battle. The verse's ending names the purpose of the enumeration: this is how God perfects His favour on the people, so that they may submit to Him, and the submission is the response the whole section has been building toward. The Book uses the same verb — to perfect and complete the favour — in Sūrah al-Māʾidah, in the verse of the religion perfected at ʿArafah (5:3 — *“Today I have perfected your faith for you, completed My favour upon you, and chosen Islam as your way.”*), so the sūrah treats the ordinary blessings of shelter and clothing as the floor of the same completion. The choice left to the hearer is stated in the same breath as the gift.

---

The shade and the mountain hideaways are followed by clothing that covers the heat and by armour that protects in battle, and the verse closes by naming the point: this is how God completes His favour on the community, so that they may submit. The Book mentions the gift of the garment in the same tone in the sūrah of the Heights: clothing to cover and to adorn, and the garment of mindfulness as the better of the two (7:26 — *“O children of Adam! We have provided for you clothing to cover your nakedness and as an adornment.”*). The mention of armour recalls the gift of the same craft to David (21:80 — *“We taught him the art of making body armour to protect you in battle. Will you then be grateful”*), which makes the verse's list run from the shade of a tree to the industry of nations under one sentence of thanksgiving.

**The Two Kinds of Covering**

The verse names the garments made to protect the body from heat and the coats made to protect a fighter from violence, and the Book uses the same word for a covering that is not made of cloth. The Sūrah of the Heights states the pairing directly, saying that God has given the children of Adam clothing to cover them and an adornment for them, and that the garment of awareness of God is the best of the two (7:26 — *“O children of Adam! We have provided for you clothing to cover your nakedness and as an adornment.”*). The verse in front of us therefore lists the visible clothing of the world and leaves the reader with the other kind in view. The sūrah has been counting blessings since verse five, and this verse closes the catalogue with the roof over a person's head.
**The Blessings the Sūrah Had Already Counted**

The same passage has named the cattle and their warmth and their food (16:5 — *“And He created the cattle for you as a source of warmth, food, and ˹many other˺ benefits”*), the horses and mules and donkeys for riding and display (16:8 — *“˹He also created˺ horses, mules, and donkeys for your transportation and adornment. And He creates what you do not know”*), the homes made of skins and wool and the furnishings taken on a journey (16:80 — *“And out of their wool, fur, and hair He has given you furnishings and goods for a while”*), and the shade that anything God created gives. The verse in front of us gathers the last of these, and the arrangement is worth noticing: the Book lists the tent and the coat before it says what the list is for. The reader is being invited to see a household's ordinary comfort as a set of specific gifts.
**The Purpose in the Last Clause**

The verse ends by naming what the enumeration is meant to produce: that the favour may be completed and the people may submit. The Book uses the same word for the favour completed in the verse of the religion at ʿArafah (5:3 — *“Today I have perfected your faith for you, completed My favour upon you, and chosen Islam as your way.”*), and it uses the word for submission as the response the whole sūrah has been asking for from its first page. The instruction the Prophet was given at the head of the sūrah — to call to the way of his Lord with wisdom and good argument (16:125 — *“Invite ˹all˺ to the Way of your Lord with wisdom and kind advice, and only debate with them in the best manner.”*) — is the human side of that submission, and the verse in front of us is the ground it stands on.
verses.82:
> But if they turn away, then your duty ˹O Prophet˺ is only to deliver ˹the message˺ clearly

The verse answers the possibility that the audience will refuse everything the sūrah has said: if they turn away, the Messenger's duty is only to deliver the message clearly. The Book states the same limit in Sūrah al-Māʾidah, where the Messenger is told that his duty is conveyance while judgement belongs to God (5:99 — *“The Messenger’s duty is only to deliver ˹the message˺. And Allah ˹fully˺ knows what you reveal and what you conceal”*), and in Sūrah al-Raʿd, where the Prophet is told he is only a warner (13:40 — *“Whether We show you ˹O Prophet˺ some of what We threaten them with, or cause you to die ˹before that˺, your duty is only to deliver ˹the message˺. Judgment is for Us”*). The line is not resignation but a boundary: the responsibility for belief was never placed on the messenger, and the sūrah's next verse turns to the account the people will face for knowing the favours and denying them.

---

The limit on the messenger's duty is stated again in the sūrah of the Table, where the Prophet is told that his charge is conveyance and that God is the keeper of what they do (5:99 — *“The Messenger’s duty is only to deliver ˹the message˺. And Allah ˹fully˺ knows what you reveal and what you conceal”*), and in the sūrah of the Thunder, where he is told he is only a warner and that every people has a guide (13:7 — *“The disbelievers say, “If only a sign could be sent down to him from his Lord.” You ˹O Prophet˺ are only a warner. And every people had a guide”*). The Book's rule is that the messenger is not responsible for belief, and the same limit is applied to the Prophet personally at the sūrah of the Heifer with the words that he is not over them as a guardian (6:107 — *“Had Allah willed, they would not have been polytheists. We have not appointed you as their keeper, nor are you their maintainer”*). The sūrah's next verse turns from the messenger's limit to the account that the audience will face for what they were shown.
verses.83:
> They are aware of Allah’s favours, but still deny them. And most of them are ˹truly˺ ungrateful

The verse names the exact fault the sūrah has been describing: they know God's favour and then deny it, and most of them are ungrateful. The Arabic for gratitude here is *shukr*, and its absence is worded as *kufr*, the same word used for denial, because the sūrah treats ingratitude as a form of disbelieving rather than a lapse of manners. The Book states the same recognition at 29:67 — *“How can they then believe in falsehood and deny Allah’s favours”*, where the disbelievers are said to see the safety God gave them and still worship other than Him, and it makes the point again in the list of blessings when it asks where the provision came from. The verse is the sūrah's summary of a people who knew enough to trust the gifts but not enough to thank the Giver.
verses.84:
> ˹Consider, O Prophet,˺ the Day We will call ˹a prophet as˺ a witness from every faith-community. Then the disbelievers will neither be allowed to plead nor appease ˹their Lord˺

The scene moves to the Day when a witness is called from every community, and the verse notes what happens to the disbelievers in the same setting: they are not permitted to speak, and they are given no opportunity to plead. The Book gives the same picture in Sūrah al-Rūm, where no excuse will be of use on the day the Hour arrives, and in Sūrah al-Jāthiyah, where the record is read and the day is told that they will not be asked to make amends (45:27–29 — *“Every community will be summoned to its record ˹of deeds˺.”*). The witnesses are drawn from the communities themselves, so that the case is closed on the community's own ground, and the Prophet stands as a witness over his people in the verse that follows (16:89 — *“And We will call you to be a witness against these ˹people of yours˺.”*).

---

The witness is the prophet of each community, as the sūrah of the Women states explicitly: God will bring a witness from every community and call the Prophet himself as a witness over them (4:41 — *“So how will it be when We bring a witness from every faith-community and bring you ˹O Prophet˺ as a witness against yours”*), and the sūrah of the Troops adds that the witnesses will be brought to the account (39:69 — *“The earth will shine with the light of its Lord, the record ˹of deeds˺ will be laid ˹open˺, the prophets and the witnesses will be brought forward—and judgment will be passed on all with fairness. None will be wronged”*). The scene's next detail, that the disbelievers are not permitted to speak and given no time to plead, matches the sūrah of the Cave, where the guilty speak and their excuse is not accepted (18:52 — *“And ˹beware of˺ the Day He will say, “Call upon those you claimed were My associate-gods.””*). The passage is one of the Qur'an's clearest statements that revelation has reached every people, and that the reckoning of each is tied to the messenger sent among them.
verses.85:
> And when the wrongdoers face the punishment, it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be delayed ˹from it˺

**No Lightening and No Delay**

The verse says that when the men who did wrong see the punishment, it will not be made lighter for them and they will not be given time. The sentence is short and it closes two doors at once: the door of a reduced penalty and the door of a postponement.

**What the Verse Answers**

The people the sūrah has been arguing with had asked for the punishment to be brought on them as a way of testing the messenger, and the Book answered them in the sūrah of the Spoils by telling them what would happen if it came (8:32 reports their demand and the answer — *“And ˹remember˺ when they prayed, “O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky or overcome us with a painful punishment.””*). The verse in front of the reader tells them what the arrival of the punishment will be like for anybody who sees it: nothing will be taken off the sentence and no extra time will be granted. The Book states the same rule in other places, where it says that nothing will be accepted on the day the punishment comes and that the men who rejected the message will not be given a delay (38:15 speaks of the men who wait for the day and 2:162 says that the punishment is not lightened for them).

**Why the Sūrah Has Put It Here**

The verse sits in a run of verses about the last day, and the verse after it shows the men who worshipped other beings looking at the objects of their worship and admitting where they had gone (16:86 describes the scene — *“And when the polytheists see their associate-gods, they will say, “Our Lord! These are our associate-gods that we used to invoke besides You.” Their gods will throw a rebuttal at them, ˹saying,˺ “You are definitely liars.””*). The Book places the two together so that the reader sees the whole picture: the worshippers will face both the loss of their supposed intercessors and the sentence that nobody can postpone. The sūrah had already described the day in its own words when it said that every soul will be paid in full for what it did and that nobody will be wronged (16:111 states it — *“˹Consider˺ the Day ˹when˺ every soul will come pleading for itself, and each will be paid in full for what it did, and none will be wronged”*), and this verse tells the reader what the men who spent their lives putting off the thought of that day will find when it arrives.

**What the Verse Asks of the Reader**

The verse is a warning, and its value is in the time it assumes. A person reading it still has time to change the direction he is going, and the Book uses the same argument in the sūrah of the Crowd when it tells the servant who has wronged himself not to give up on God's mercy (39:53 states the invitation — *“Say, ˹O Prophet, that Allah says,˺ “O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah’s mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins. He is indeed the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*). The sūrah of the Bee has been telling its readers all the way through what God has given them, and it also tells them that guidance and warning are part of the giving. The verse in front of the reader tells the reader that the day will not wait for him, and the verses after it show him the scene that no amount of delay will change. The sūrah of the Cow states the same rule for the men who will not be let off, where no trade and no friendship will help them on the day (2:254 states it — *“O believers! Donate from what We have provided for you before the arrival of a Day when there will be no bargaining, friendship, or intercession.”*).
verses.86:
> And when the polytheists see their associate-gods, they will say, “Our Lord! These are our associate-gods that we used to invoke besides You.” Their gods will throw a rebuttal at them, ˹saying,˺ “You are definitely liars.”

The scene continues the Day of Judgement from the previous verse and gives it one of its sharpest exchanges. The idolaters, facing the punishment, point to the gods they served and introduce them: these are the partners we used to call on besides You. The gods answer in the same scene by throwing the accusation back: you are the liars. The Book stages the same denial elsewhere — the partners disown their worshippers and say they were not aware of their worship (10:28–30 — *“We will separate them from each other, and their associate-gods will say, “It was not us that you worshipped”*), and the idols are told to bring their proof and learn that the truth belongs to God (28:75 — *“And We will bring forth a witness from every faith-community and ask ˹the polytheists˺, “Show ˹Us˺ your proof.” Then they will ˹come to˺ know that the truth is with Allah ˹alone˺. And whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them”*). So the account of intercession the idolaters had based their hope on is answered by the partners themselves, and their speech becomes the evidence against them.

---

The gods are asked to deny the association, and the sūrah of the Stories records their answer in full: those against whom the word has come due say, "It was you who came to us with the promises of God", and the others say, "No, it was you who used to come to us as deceivers" (28:63). The same exchange appears in the sūrah of the Cattle, where the associates say it was not they who were worshipped (6:22–23 — *“˹Consider˺ the Day We will gather them all together then ask those who associated others ˹with Allah in worship˺, “Where are those gods you used to claim?””*), and in the sūrah of Jonah, where the partners are removed from the scene altogether (10:28–30 — *“We will separate them from each other, and their associate-gods will say, “It was not us that you worshipped”*). The verse's point is that the partnership the idolaters asserted in this life is a claim no one will be willing to own at the reckoning.
verses.87:
> They will offer ˹full˺ submission to Allah on that Day, and whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them

The verse records what the idolaters do when the Day comes: they offer submission to God, and whatever they invented as gods fails them. The Book gives the same confession elsewhere — the idols will disown the worship and deny the claim of the worshippers, as in Sūrah Yūnus, where the partners will be asked whether they called the people to worship them and will deny it (10:28–30 — *“And whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them”*). In Sūrah al-Qaṣaṣ, where they call and are not answered (28:64 — *“It will be said ˹to the disbelievers˺, “Call upon your associate-gods ˹for help˺.””*). The submission of this verse is the same surrender the sūrah named earlier in connection with the Day, since all will be submissive before the One whose claim was refused in the life they were given.
verses.88:
> For those who disbelieve and hinder ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah, We will add more punishment to their punishment for all the corruption they spread

The verse names the addition to the punishment and gives the reason for it: they disbelieved and they hindered others from the way of God, and so they are punished for the corruption they made. The Book's doctrine of doubled guilt for those who mislead is stated in several places — the leaders whose burden includes a share of those who followed (29:13 — *“Yet they will certainly ˹be made to˺ carry their own burdens, as well as other burdens along with their own.”*). The verse in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf where the followed and the followers each receive the punishment and the followers are told they have no superiority over their leaders (7:38–39 — *“Then the leaders will say to their followers, “You were no better than us! So taste the torment for what you used to commit.””*). The verse therefore treats the act of blocking the road as a separate offence from disbelief, with its own measure, and this sūrah is unusually explicit that the punishment is added rather than replaced.

**The Burden Carried by the Misleaders**

The verse says the punishment is increased, and the rest of the Book explains where the increase comes from. The men who block the road carry their own wrong and a share of the wrong of those they turned aside: the same sūrah states that they will carry their own burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection and other burdens along with them, for the people they misled without knowledge (16:25 — *“Let them bear their burdens in full on the Day of Judgment as well as some of the burdens of those they mislead without knowledge. Evil indeed is what they will bear”*). The followers are not excused because they were led. In the Sūrah of the Heights each group enters the Fire cursing the one before it, and the followers are told that their leaders have no superiority over them (7:38-39 — *“Allah will say, “Enter the Fire along with the ˹evil˺ groups of jinn and humans that preceded you.””*), and in the Fire the men who were misled ask God to give the leaders who brought them there a double punishment (33:68 — *“Our Lord! Give them double ˹our˺ punishment, and condemn them tremendously.””*; 38:61 — *“Adding, “Our Lord! Whoever brought this upon us, double their punishment in the Fire.””*). The verse in front of us makes the same division: disbelief is one offence, and closing the road to others is another with its own weight.

**The One Who Sets the Road**

The Prophet's words make the teaching plain: whoever begins a good way in Islam has its reward and the reward of everyone who follows it, and whoever begins an evil way carries its sin and the sin of everyone who follows it, without anything being taken from the followers' own record (Muslim). That sentence explains the verse's language of addition — the sum grows with every person the misleader turns aside. The sūrah calls the act corruption, the Book's widest word for damage done to the common life, and it has already shown the motive earlier in the same chapter: a cheap price taken for God's covenant, and men who lead others away so that they themselves may carry the load (16:95 — *“And do not trade Allah’s covenant for a fleeting gain. What is with Allah is certainly far better for you, if only you knew”*; 16:25 — *“Let them bear their burdens in full on the Day of Judgment as well as some of the burdens of those they mislead without knowledge. Evil indeed is what they will bear”*). A man may keep his own heart in order and still have ruined the road for everyone else, and the verse gives that ruin its own line in the record.
verses.89:
> ˹Consider, O Prophet,˺ the Day We will call against every faith-community a witness of their own. And We will call you to be a witness against these ˹people of yours˺. We have revealed to you the Book as an explanation of all things, a guide, a mercy, and good news for those who ˹fully˺ submit

The verse states the day when a witness from each community is called and the Prophet is called as a witness over these people, and then it states what the Book is in the same breath: an explanation of everything, a guidance, a mercy, and good tidings for those who submit. The Book claims the same completeness elsewhere, in the verse that says nothing has been omitted from it (6:38 — *“All living beings roaming the earth and winged birds soaring in the sky are communities like yourselves. We have left nothing out of the Record. Then to their Lord they will be gathered all together”*) and in the one that calls it a clarification of all things (12:111 — *“This message cannot be a fabrication, rather ˹it is˺ a confirmation of previous revelation, a detailed explanation of all things, a guide, and a mercy for people of faith”*). The Prophet's role as witness over the community that received him is part of the Book's pattern for every messenger, and the sūrah has just shown the witnesses of the earlier communities being brought forward (16:84 — *“˹Consider, O Prophet,˺ the Day We will call ˹a prophet as˺ a witness from every faith-community.”*).

---

**The Day the Witness Stands**

*Wa-yawma nabʿathu fī kulli ummatin shahīdan ʿalayhim min anfusihim* — the day We raise in every community a witness from among themselves. The witness is one of their own, a man they knew, which is what closes the mouth of every excuse: no community can claim it never heard. The verse then gives the Prophet his place in that scene: *and We bring you as a witness over these* — over the community he was sent to. The Book names the same arrangement for the believers as a body: the Messenger is a witness over you and you are witnesses over the people (2:143 — *“And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community so that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you.”*), so the testimony on that day is not a formality but the completion of the office the community was given.
**A Book That Explains Everything**

The second half of the verse states what the Book is: *tibyānan li-kulli shayʾ* — an explanation of everything, and a guidance and a mercy and good tidings for those who submit. The claim is not that the Book contains every fact a person might want, but that nothing needed for finding the way has been left out of the revelation given to the Prophet; the Book points to its completeness in the same terms elsewhere, where it says nothing has been omitted from the Book (6:38 — *“We have left nothing out of the Record.”*) and where it calls the message a clarification of all things (12:111 — *“This message cannot be a fabrication, rather ˹it is˺ a confirmation of previous revelation, a detailed explanation of all things, a guide, and a mercy for people of faith”*). The verse places that claim on the Day of the witnesses, which is where the claim will be tested.
verses.90:
> Indeed, Allah commands justice, grace, as well as courtesy to close relatives. He forbids indecency, wickedness, and aggression. He instructs you so perhaps you will be mindful

The verse is one of the most recited in the Book, and its subject is the whole of social morality in three commands and three prohibitions. *ʿAdl* is justice that gives each person his due; *iḥsān* is the generosity that goes beyond what is due; and *ītāʾ dhī al-qurbā* is the kindness owed to relatives. Against them stand *faḥshāʾ*, acts of gross indecency; *munkar*, what sound minds reject; and *baghy*, aggression that oversteps the rights of others. The Book's order runs from the widest obligation to the narrowest, which is how the sūrah of Naḥl arranges a community's duties, and the last clause states the purpose of the whole instruction: that they should remember. The classical commentators read the verse as the sūrah's summary of the law's intent.

**The Verse's Standing Among the Early Muslims**

Commentators report that ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd called this the most comprehensive verse in the Book for what it orders and forbids, and that the Prophet recited it in sermons — the sūrah's own close gives it the same weight. The verse contains three commands and three prohibitions, and each pair has been worked out in the law: justice and generosity in dealings (4:58 — *“Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners; and when you judge between people, judge with fairness. What a noble commandment from Allah to you! Surely Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing”*; 5:8 — *“O believers! Stand firm for Allah and bear true testimony. Do not let the hatred of a people lead you to injustice. Be just! That is closer to righteousness. And be mindful of Allah. Surely Allah is All-Aware of what you do”*), kindness to relatives as a debt and not a favour, and the ban on indecency, on what sound minds reject, and on aggression that takes what is another's. The Book sets the same list in other places as the substance of the covenant: the commands of Sūrah al-Anʿām, and the verse that names the most honoured as the most mindful (6:151 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Come! Let me recite to you what your Lord has forbidden to you: do not associate others with Him ˹in worship˺. ˹Do not fail to˺ honour your parents. Do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for you and for them. Do not come near indecencies, openly or secretly. Do not take a ˹human˺ life—made sacred by Allah—except with ˹legal˺ right. This is what He has commanded you, so perhaps you will understand”*; 49:13 — *“O humanity! Indeed, We created you from a male and a female, and made you into peoples and tribes so that you may ˹get to˺ know one another. Surely the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous among you. Allah is truly All-Knowing, All-Aware”*). The verse closes by telling the hearers why they were given all of it — so that they would remember — and the verse after it turns that memory into a duty, commanding them to keep the covenant of God they have just been reminded of (16:91 — *“Honour Allah’s covenant when you make a pledge, and do not break your oaths after confirming them, having made Allah your guarantor. Surely Allah knows all you do”*).
verses.91:
> Honour Allah’s covenant when you make a pledge, and do not break your oaths after confirming them, having made Allah your guarantor. Surely Allah knows all you do

The verse commands the honouring of a covenant and prohibits the breaking of oaths after they have been confirmed, on the ground that God has been made guarantor over them. The Arabic *ʿahd* is the pledge taken with God as witness, so the verse's argument is that a broken oath is not merely a broken promise to a person but a claim filed against the swearer with the One in whose name it was made. The Book restates this duty in the passage on the community that asks how it can break its treaty with those who broke theirs first (9:4 — *“As for the polytheists who have honoured every term of their treaty with you and have not supported an enemy against you, honour your treaty with them until the end of its term.”*, 9:7 — *“How can such polytheists have a treaty with Allah and His Messenger, except those you have made a treaty with at the Sacred Mosque?”*), and it orders fidelity to treaties even where the other side is difficult, as long as they are straight with the community. The sūrah then devotes four more verses to the same instruction, because the subject is the community's credibility.

---

The commentators attached the verse to the pledges the community had made to the Prophet ﷺ — the covenants of ʿAqabah, and the general undertakings given when the community was organised in Madinah — and read the words as a rule for every binding promise: an oath sworn with God as witness is not the speaker's to break at convenience. The Book repeats the command in several places, including the direct warning not to violate the pledge (17:34 — *“Do not come near the wealth of the orphan—unless intending to enhance it—until they attain maturity. Honour ˹your˺ pledges, for you will surely be accountable for them”*) and the oath law of the sūrah of the Table, which provides expiation for a broken oath (5:89 — *“This is the penalty for breaking your oaths.”*). The verse's closing reminder, that God knows what they do, is what makes the covenant a matter of standing rather than of words.
verses.92:
> Do not be like the woman who ˹foolishly˺ unravels her yarn after it is firmly spun, by taking your oaths as a means of deceiving one another in favour of a stronger group. Surely Allah tests you through this. And on the Day of Judgment He will certainly make your differences clear to you

The comparison is domestic and unforgettable: a woman who spins her yarn firmly and then unravels it thread by thread. That is what the community does when it makes oaths a means of deceiving one another, gaining an advantage by swearing and then swearing the opposite when a better offer appears. The verse states the reason God is testing them in this: the oaths become the test of whether the community can be trusted with its own word, and the Book states elsewhere that a promise given and broken is not a private matter but a public one (17:34 — *“Do not come near the wealth of the orphan—unless intending to enhance it—until they attain maturity. Honour ˹your˺ pledges, for you will surely be accountable for them”*). The sūrah's closing statement on the subject is that whatever the world offers in exchange for the covenant, what God has is better.

---

**The Word for the Loophole**

The verse supplies the term for the practice it forbids: *dakhalan*, something smuggled inside a thing to spoil it, the flaw a man introduces into his own case. The oaths were honest in form and rotten inside, because the swearer was not binding himself; he was keeping a door open to the better offer. The sūrah pairs the image with the community as a single body: tribal numbers were the currency of power in Arabia, so a group could gain by making a treaty and then taking a more favourable one when the balance shifted.
**What the Verse Says Will Happen**

The end of the verse answers the man who thinks an unkept promise costs nothing but words: *God will surely test you with it and will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that wherein you differed*. The test is in this life, where the bargain looks like a gain; the clarification is on the Day, when the ledger is opened. The verse that follows adds the reason none of it can be hidden: had God willed, He could have made the whole of mankind one community, and it is by His leave that they are not (16:93 — *“Had Allah willed, He could have easily made you one community ˹of believers˺, but He leaves to stray whoever He wills and guides whoever He wills.”*).
verses.93:
> Had Allah willed, He could have easily made you one community ˹of believers˺, but He leaves to stray whoever He wills and guides whoever He wills. And you will certainly be questioned about what you used to do

The verse answers the argument that division in the community is God's doing. It states the limit of that claim in the same line: if God willed, He could have made all of them one community, but He leaves to stray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, and He will question every one of them about what they were doing. The Book states the same in Sūrah al-Māʾidah, where God could have made a single community but did not, and in Sūrah Yūnus, where the people are told that if God willed, everyone on earth would have believed (10:99 — *“Had your Lord so willed ˹O Prophet˺, all ˹people˺ on earth would have certainly believed, every single one of them! Would you then force people to become believers”*). The verse therefore does not absolve the community: the questioning in its final clause belongs to those who were given a choice, and the sūrah's next verses name the oath-making that brought it about.

**What the Verse Does Not Say**

The sentence *He leaves to stray whom He wills and guides whom He wills* is the hardest kind of statement in the Book to handle, and the verse itself sets its own limit. The line does not end there; it ends with *and you will surely be questioned about what you were doing*. The two halves have to be read together: if the guidance and the straying were the whole story, there would be nobody left to question. The Book states the same pairing in the sūrah of the Table, where God could have made humankind one community and did not (5:48 — *“If Allah had willed, He would have made you one community, but His Will is to test you with what He has given ˹each of˺ you.”*), and in the sūrah of Jonah, where the Prophet is told that if God willed, everyone on earth would believe (10:99 — *“Had your Lord so willed ˹O Prophet˺, all ˹people˺ on earth would have certainly believed, every single one of them! Would you then force people to become believers”*) — and then told not to grieve himself over the people who will not.
**What the Verse Is Answering**

The sūrah has just described the community that broke its oaths and unraveled its own weaving (16:92 — *“Do not be like the woman who ˹foolishly˺ unravels her yarn after it is firmly spun, by taking your oaths as a means of deceiving one another in favour of a stronger group.”*), and this verse refuses the excuse they were reaching for: that their division was God's doing, since He could have made them one community if He had wanted. The Book grants the premise and rejects the conclusion. The existence of the choice is what makes the questioning possible, and the next verses name the oath-breaking that produced the division — the deceit, the trade of God's covenant for a small price, the slipping of a foot after it had been planted — as the thing the community itself did. The verse is an answer to a very old human move: blaming the arrangement for what the hand did with it.
verses.94:
> And do not take your oaths as a means of deceiving one another or your feet will slip after they have been firm. Then you will taste the evil ˹consequences˺ of hindering ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah, and you will suffer a tremendous punishment

The warning is built on the image of feet slipping after they were firm: the community holds its footing through the credibility of its word, and oath-breaking removes the ground. The verse's ending names the consequence in the next world — a taste of evil for having turned others away from the path of God, and great punishment. The Book uses the same picture of firm footing for the community's state after the treaty at Ḥudaybiyah, where the believers are said to have been sent serenity so that their feet might be fixed (48:4 — *“He is the One Who sent down serenity upon the hearts of the believers so that they may increase even more in their faith.”*, 48:26 — *“˹Remember˺ when the disbelievers had filled their hearts with pride—the pride of ˹pre-Islamic˺ ignorance—then Allah sent down His serenity upon His Messenger and the believers, inspiring them to uphold the declaration of faith, for they were better entitled and more worthy of it.”*), and it warns elsewhere against the deeper slip that follows a broken pledge (3:102–103 — *“And hold firmly to the rope of Allah and do not be divided.”*). The sūrah places this warning after the parable of the yarn, so that the moral and the metaphor arrive together.

---

**The Covenant and the Small Price**

The warning in this verse is followed by the verse that explains the trade-off: *and do not exchange the covenant of God for a small price; what is with God is better for you, if you only knew* (16:95 — *“And do not trade Allah’s covenant for a fleeting gain. What is with Allah is certainly far better for you, if only you knew”*). The buyers in this market were powerful tribes offering protection, alliance or a share of the caravan; the price paid was the community's word. The Book calls this small — not because the money was small in any man's hand, but because it was being weighed against what God has, and the comparison is what the verse insists on.
**The Marks of the Same Weakness**

The Prophet described the conduct of a person whose word is not a word, in a report that has reached us on several chains: the marks of the hypocrite are three — when he speaks he lies, when he makes a promise he breaks it, when he is trusted he betrays the trust (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 33). The verse's image of the foot that slides is that same diagnosis in a different register: what is shaken by the breaking of an oath is not only a contract but a person's whole footing, in this life and after it.
verses.95:
> And do not trade Allah’s covenant for a fleeting gain. What is with Allah is certainly far better for you, if only you knew

The verse states the exchange the community is being offered and refuses it on the community's behalf: do not trade the covenant of God for a small price, because what is with God is far better, if they only knew. The Book uses the same measure for the world in Sūrah al-Shūrā, where the provision of God is better and more lasting (42:36 — *“But what is with Allah is far better and more lasting for those who believe and put their trust in their Lord”*), and it names the price of a religion sold cheap in Sūrah al-Baqarah, where the traders of the covenant are described (2:79 — *“So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, “This is from Allah”—seeking a fleeting gain! So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they have earned”*). The clause "if only you knew" is the sūrah's standing way of pointing at the gap between what a person sees and what is in front of him, and it is repeated at 16:96 — *“Whatever you have will end, but whatever Allah has is everlasting. And We will certainly reward the steadfast according to the best of their deeds”* and 16:97 — *“Whoever does good, whether male or female, and is a believer, We will surely bless them with a good life, and We will certainly reward them according to the best of their deeds”* in the same passage.

---

The trade described is the sale of one's pledge for a price in this life, and the Book states the same bargain in the sūrah of the Family of ʿImrān, where those who sell the covenant and their oaths for a small gain have no share in the Hereafter (3:77 — *“Indeed, those who trade Allah’s covenant and their oaths for a fleeting gain will have no share in the Hereafter.”*), and in the sūrah of the Heifer, where the scribes who wrote their own book for a price are warned with the same words (2:79 — *“So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, “This is from Allah”—seeking a fleeting gain! So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they have earned”*). The verse's reasoning — that what is with God is better for them if they knew — is the sūrah's recurring argument against the Makkans' calculation, which the next verse states in full: what you have comes to an end and what God has is lasting.
verses.96:
> Whatever you have will end, but whatever Allah has is everlasting. And We will certainly reward the steadfast according to the best of their deeds

The verse completes the exchange with the plainest arithmetic in the Book: what you have will end, and what God has is everlasting. Then it adds the promise to those who are patient — the reward given according to the best of what they did, not according to the total of it. The Book repeats the same measure in Sūrah al-Zumar, where the reward is the best of what people did (39:35 — *“As such, Allah will absolve them of ˹even˺ the worst of what they did and reward them according to the best of what they used to do”*), and in Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt, where the patient are paid without measure (29:58; see also 39:10). The pairing matters for the sūrah's audience: the goods they gamble their oaths for are the very things that run out, and the patience the verse asks for is the discipline of holding on to what does not.

---

The verse states the exchange as a matter of fact: what the hearers possess is subject to ending, and what God holds does not end, and the reward is then attached to patience — *ṣabirūn*, the steadfast — measured by the best of what they did rather than by the sum. The Book states the same pair in the sūrah of the Cave, where the enduring good works are better with the Lord and better in hope (18:46 — *“Wealth and children are the adornment of this worldly life, but the everlasting good deeds are far better with your Lord in reward and in hope”*), and urges the same calculation in the sūrah of the Nights, where the life to come is better and more lasting (87:16–17 — *“even though the Hereafter is far better and more lasting”*). The verse's phrase about the best of their deeds is the measure the Qur'an applies to the reward in other places too (39:35 — *“As such, Allah will absolve them of ˹even˺ the worst of what they did and reward them according to the best of what they used to do”*; 29:7 — *“As for those who believe and do good, We will certainly absolve them of their sins, and reward them according to the best of what they used to do”*).
verses.97:
> Whoever does good, whether male or female, and is a believer, We will surely bless them with a good life, and We will certainly reward them according to the best of their deeds

The verse states the reward in terms that suit both halves of the audience: whoever does good, male or female, and is a believer, then a good life and a wage measured by the best of their deeds. The condition of faith is placed between the deed and the reward, so the sūrah is not describing a moralism that ignores belief; and the phrase "male or female" is repeated by the Book wherever it wants it understood that the reward does not depend on gender (3:195 — *“So their Lord responded to them: “I will never deny any of you—male or female—the reward of your deeds.”*; 4:124 — *“But those who do good—whether male or female—and have faith will enter Paradise and will never be wronged ˹even as much as˺ the speck on a date stone”*; 33:35 — *“Surely ˹for˺ Muslim men and women, believing men and women, devout men and women, truthful men and women, patient men and women, humble men and women, charitable men and women, fasting men and women, men and women who guard their chastity, and men and women who remember Allah often—for ˹all of˺ them Allah has prepared forgiveness and a great reward”*). The "good life" the verse promises is read by the commentators in two ways — provision in this world and contentment of heart, and contentment in the Hereafter — and the wage that follows is for the deeds themselves.

---

The same promise is given in the sūrah of the Women with nearly identical words — that the doer of good, male or female, with faith will enter the Garden and not be wronged by a date-stone's thread (4:124 — *“But those who do good—whether male or female—and have faith will enter Paradise and will never be wronged ˹even as much as˺ the speck on a date stone”*) — and it answers a question the community raised about whether women's good deeds would be rewarded as men's. The commentators differed over what the good life means: a sufficient living in this world, contentment with what God provides, or the life of the Garden itself, with most holding that the two belong together. The verse's condition of faith is what distinguishes the promise from a general optimism about good deeds, since the sūrah has already tied the benefit of deeds to belief.
verses.98:
> When you recite the Quran, seek refuge with Allah from Satan, the accursed

The instruction is attached to a specific act: when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge with God from Satan the accursed. The Book orders the same in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf, where the Prophet is told to say when a whisper from Satan reaches him that he seeks refuge with God, who is Hearing and Knowing (7:200 — *“If you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah. Surely He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing”*). In Sūrah Fuṣṣilat, where the answer to an evil suggestion is to seek refuge with the One who hears and knows (41:36 — *“And if you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah. Indeed, He ˹alone˺ is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing”*). The formula *aʿūdhu bi-llāh*, said before the recitation, is the practice the verse establishes, and the sūrah explains in the next two verses why the refuge works: the accursed has no authority over those who believe and rely on their Lord.

---

The command belongs to the etiquette of recitation, and the Book orders the same resort in the sūrah of the Heights, where the Prophet is told that if a whisper from Satan comes he should seek refuge with God, who is Hearing and Knowing (7:200 — *“If you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah. Surely He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing”*), and in the sūrah of Fussilat with the same instruction (41:36 — *“And if you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah. Indeed, He ˹alone˺ is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing”*). The scholars held that the seeking of refuge is recommended before recitation rather than part of the recitation itself, and they read the order of the sūrah's verses as deliberate: the passage on revelation and its carrier (16:102 — *“Say, “The holy spirit has brought it down from your Lord with the truth to reassure the believers, and as a guide and good news for those who submit ˹to Allah˺.””*) is followed by the protection requested for the act of reading.
verses.99:
> He certainly has no authority over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord

The verse states the limit of the enemy's power in terms of trust: he has no authority over those who believe and put their reliance on their Lord. The Book makes the same claim in Sūrah al-Ḥijr, where the answer to Satan's boast is that God's sincere servants are beyond him (15:40–42 — *“you will certainly have no authority over My servants, except the deviant who follow you”*), and in Sūrah al-Isrāʾ, where his power is described as sufficiency for those he drags away but not authority over the ones who take refuge (17:65 — *“˹Allah added,˺ “You will truly have no authority over My ˹faithful˺ servants.” And sufficient is your Lord as a Guardian”*). This is the answer to the previous verse: the refuge works because the refuge-taker belongs to God, and the whisperer's influence stops at the boundary of reliance. The next verse names the people over whom he does have authority.
verses.100:
> His authority is only over those who take him as a patron and who—under his influence—associate ˹others˺ with Allah ˹in worship˺

The verse names the people the enemy does work on: those who take him as a patron, and under his influence associate others with God. The willingness is stated first — adopting him as a protector — and the consequence follows, which is the sūrah's consistent order: the whisper is not compulsion but an opening that a person gives. The Book uses the same word, *tawallā*, for adopting the enemy as a friend, and it warns elsewhere that whoever takes the devil as an ally will be misled and left with a delusion (4:119–120 — *“And whoever takes Satan as a guardian instead of Allah has certainly suffered a tremendous loss”*; 18:50 — *“Would you then take him and his descendants as patrons instead of Me, although they are your enemy?”*). The verse therefore closes the pair that began with the command to seek refuge by describing who the refuge protects: not those who claim it while walking with the enemy, but those who rely on God alone.
verses.101:
> When We replace a verse with another—and Allah knows best what He reveals—they say, “You ˹Muḥammad˺ are just a fabricator.” In fact, most of them do not know

The verse answers a specific complaint. When a verse was replaced by another — a ruling adjusted, or a passage exchanged for one more suitable to the community's stage — the opponents seized on the change as proof that the Prophet was inventing the text as he went. The Book's answer is that God knows best what He reveals, and it adds that most of the accusers do not know what they are talking about: *bal aktharuhum lā yaʿlamūn*. The same objection is answered elsewhere with the reminder that the One who sent the Book down can replace it, since the revelation is His to give in the measure He decides (2:106 — *“If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything”*; 13:39 — *“Allah eliminates and confirms what He wills, and with Him is the Master Record”*). The verse's purpose in the sūrah is to show that the accusers were not weighing the content of what came but the fact that anything came at all.

**The Complaint About Changing Verses**

The verse reports an objection that had a practical cause. When a ruling was replaced by another — a verse of the Qur'an set aside and a new one sent in its place — the mockers in Makkah treated it as proof that the recitation was being made up as it went along. The Book answers the charge by stating who owns the process: God knows best what He sends down and when. The Sūrah of the Cow gives the rule in full, saying that when a verse is replaced God brings one better than it or like it (2:106 — *“If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything”*), and the change of the direction of prayer, the rulings on intoxicants and some of the rules on marriage and waiting are the clearest cases where the community watched this happen.
**Why the Teachings Came in Stages**

The Book gives the reason in more than one place, and the clearest is in the way the prohibition of wine arrives: first named as a thing with more harm than good (2:219 — *“They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about intoxicants and gambling. Say, “There is great evil in both, as well as some benefit for people—but the evil outweighs the benefit.” They ˹also˺ ask you ˹O Prophet˺ what they should donate. Say, “Whatever you can spare.” This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you ˹believers˺, so perhaps you may reflect”*), then forbidden close to the prayer (4:43 — *“O believers! Do not approach prayer while intoxicated until you are aware of what you say, nor in a state of ˹full˺ impurity—unless you merely pass through ˹the mosque˺—until you have bathed. But if you are ill, on a journey, or have relieved yourselves, or been intimate with your wives and cannot find water, then purify yourselves with clean earth, wiping your faces and hands. And Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving”*), then forbidden outright (5:90-91 — *“O believers! Intoxicants, gambling, idols, and drawing lots for decisions are all evil of Satan’s handiwork. So shun them so you may be successful Satan’s plan is to stir up hostility and hatred between you with intoxicants and gambling and to prevent you from remembering Allah and praying. Will you not then abstain”*). A community being built out of a society that had known none of this was taught in steps, and the steps are the mercy the verse's hearers were calling forgery. The verse closes by saying that most of them do not know — not that they are lying, but that they have not understood what they are looking at. The next verse names the tongue of the recitation itself as the answer.
verses.102:
> Say, “The holy spirit has brought it down from your Lord with the truth to reassure the believers, and as a guide and good news for those who submit ˹to Allah˺.”

The verse names the carrier of the revelation and the purpose of its coming down: the holy spirit brought it from your Lord with the truth, to reassure the believers, and as a guide and good news for those who submit. The Book names the same spirit as Gabriel in another place, where the Book says he brought it down on the Prophet's heart by God's permission (2:97 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it—a guide and good news for the believers.””*; 26:193–194 — *“which the trustworthy spirit ˹Gabriel˺ brought down”*), so the verse answers the charge that a human teacher was dictating the text (16:103 — *“And We surely know that they say, “No one is teaching him except a human.” But the man they refer to speaks a foreign tongue, whereas this ˹Quran˺ is ˹in˺ eloquent Arabic”*) by naming the actual bringer. The purpose stated here — strengthening the believers — reappears wherever the Book describes what the revelation does for a community under pressure (8:2 — *“The ˹true˺ believers are only those whose hearts tremble at the remembrance of Allah, whose faith increases when His revelations are recited to them, and who put their trust in their Lord”*; 9:124–125 — *“Whenever a sûrah is revealed, some of them ask ˹mockingly˺, “Which of you has this increased in faith?” As for the believers, it has increased them in faith and they rejoice But as for those with sickness in their hearts, it has increased them only in wickedness upon their wickedness, and they die as disbelievers”*). The verse follows the accusation of fabrication in 16:101 — *“When We replace a verse with another—and Allah knows best what He reveals—they say, “You ˹Muḥammad˺ are just a fabricator.” In fact, most of them do not know”* and prepares the answer to the human teacher in the next verse, so the two verses answer one accusation between them.

---

The carrier is identified elsewhere in the Book: the faithful spirit who brings the revelation on the Prophet's heart by God's permission (26:193 — *“which the trustworthy spirit ˹Gabriel˺ brought down”*; 2:97 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it—a guide and good news for the believers.””*), and the same name is used in the sūrah of the Table for the support given to Jesus (5:110 — *“Remember My favour upon you and your mother: how I supported you with the holy spirit so you spoke to people in ˹your˺ infancy and adulthood.”*). The verse's three purposes — truth, reassurance for the believers, and good news for those who submit — match the sūrah's portrait of the revelation as guidance and healing (16:89 — *“We have revealed to you the Book as an explanation of all things, a guide, a mercy, and good news for those who ˹fully˺ submit”*), and the objection it answers is the Makkan charge that the Prophet was being taught by a human being, to which the sūrah's answer is that the message comes by the spirit from the Lord of the worlds.
verses.103:
> And We surely know that they say, “No one is teaching him except a human.” But the man they refer to speaks a foreign tongue, whereas this ˹Quran˺ is ˹in˺ eloquent Arabic

The verse is the sūrah's direct answer to the accusation that a man was teaching the Prophet: the person they point to speaks a foreign tongue, while this recitation is in clear Arabic. The Book records the same charge elsewhere and answers it the same way, by pointing to the language of the text and its content (44:14 — *“then they turned away from him, saying, “A madman, taught by others!””*; 26:195 — *“in a clear Arabic tongue”*), and it notes that the accusers did not need evidence because the point of the accusation was to avoid the conclusion that the recitation was from God. The verse's name for the text — *lisānun ʿarabiyyun mubīn*, a clear Arabic tongue — is one of the Book's own descriptions of itself, alongside the descriptions of it as a guide, a mercy, and a reminder. The next verse states the consequence for those who will not believe what they hear.

**What the Accusation Was and Why It Failed**

The charge was that a man was secretly teaching the Prophet what to say. The sūrah's answer is a fact anyone in Makkah could check: the man they were pointing at was not an Arabic speaker, and what they were being asked to disbelieve was recitation in the clearest Arabic, with the kind of structure no translated sentence could have carried. The Book makes the same point elsewhere when it answers the same charge — this is a lie, and the tongue in question is plainly foreign while the words are Arabic. The illiterate trader they were describing as a pupil could not have produced a single line of the thing his accusers were standing in the street to hear.
**What the Verse Calls the Text**

The last words of the verse are the Book's own name for itself: *a clear Arabic tongue* — *lisānun ʿarabiyyun mubīn*. The sūrah has just called the revelation a guidance, a mercy and a reminder in the verses before, and the word for the language is the one that carries the sense of making something plain. A reader who had heard the recitation knew what the words were and what they meant; the accusers' problem was not comprehension, and the sūrah is careful to say so. The next verse states plainly what happens to the people who refuse to believe what is presented to them in their own language: a punishment for those who turn away from the signs of God.
verses.104:
> Surely those who do not believe in Allah’s revelations will never be guided by Allah, and they will suffer a painful punishment

**Refusing the Signs Closes the Road**

The verse says that the people who do not believe in the signs of God will not be guided by Him, and that a painful punishment waits for them. The sentence is short, and it states a rule the whole Book repeats: guidance is given along the road a person walks, not handed out to the person who has already turned away.

**Why the Verse Follows the Argument About the Revelation**

The two verses before this one answered the accusation that a human being was teaching the Prophet what he recited. The Book showed the absurdity of it: the man they pointed to spoke a foreign tongue, and the revelation was in clear Arabic (16:103 states both — *“And We surely know that they say, “No one is teaching him except a human.” But the man they refer to speaks a foreign tongue, whereas this ˹Quran˺ is ˹in˺ eloquent Arabic”*). The verse in front of the reader states what happens to people who keep refusing once an answer like that is in front of them. It is the same sentence the sūrah gave when it described the men who were too proud to take what they were given: the gates of the garden stay shut for them as long as the camel cannot pass through the eye of a needle (7:40 states that image in the sūrah of the Heights, and 18:57 describes the men who turn away from the signs when they are reminded of them).

**What Guidance Means Here**

The Book does not teach that a person is blocked at random. It teaches that a person's choices train him, and that the road he keeps choosing becomes the road he can see. The same sūrah said that God does not guide a people who lie about Him, and it stated the rule the other way round for the men who do right: God guides them because they asked for the road. The sūrah of the Bee puts the principle in the middle of its own argument when it tells the reader that the blind and the seeing are not the same (16:76 draws the comparison, and the sūrah returns to it near its close). The verse in front of the reader therefore names a consequence and not an invitation that was refused for no reason.

**Where the Passage Goes Next**

The verse after this one names the real liars in the dispute, which is the answer to the accusation the passage has been handling (16:105 states it — *“No one fabricates lies except those who disbelieve in Allah’s revelations, and it is they who are the ˹true˺ liars”*). The sūrah's method in this section is to let each charge answer itself: the claim that the revelation was invented is met with the definition of who invents, and the refusal of the signs is met with the statement of where it leads. The chapter has already told the reader what to do with the message when it reaches him: the sūrah opened with the command to do good and to be fair, and it warned the men who turned away that their provision was settled either way (16:71 speaks of the gifts God has spread among people). The verse in front of the reader closes one door in the argument so that the reader may take the open one.
verses.105:
> No one fabricates lies except those who disbelieve in Allah’s revelations, and it is they who are the ˹true˺ liars

**Who Actually Invents Lies**

The verse answers the charge that the Prophet was making the revelation up by naming the people to whom invention belongs: nobody invents lies except the people who do not believe in the signs of God, and those people are the liars. The verse turns the accusation around and settles the argument with a definition.

**The Charge the Verse Is Answering**

The sūrah has been handling two accusations in the passage. One was that the Prophet was repeating old stories that other people had written down, and the Book answered by pointing out that the man they meant spoke a foreign language while the revelation was in clear Arabic (16:103 gives both parts of the answer — *“And We surely know that they say, “No one is teaching him except a human.” But the man they refer to speaks a foreign tongue, whereas this ˹Quran˺ is ˹in˺ eloquent Arabic”*). The other was that he had invented it himself, and the Book's answer is the verse in front of the reader: invention belongs to people who have no faith in God's signs, because a person who believes the signs are real has no reason to make one up and no room to do it. The Book states the same denial in other sūrahs, where it challenges the doubters to bring a chapter of their own if they think the Book is a forgery (10:37 records the challenge and the same sūrah calls them to bring a sūrah like it at 10:38, and 11:13 names the ten sūrahs they were invited to produce).

**What the Sūrah Has Said About Speech**

The chapter has been warning about words throughout the passage, and this verse is its sharpest statement on the subject. It told the community to speak the truth and to keep its promises when it said that whoever makes a promise to God must keep it (16:95 warns against trading a promise of God for a small price). It named the man who invents something and then lays it on someone else, though the Book's exact words on that belong to the sūrah of women (4:112 describes carrying the slander and the plain sin). The verse in front of the reader takes the accusation that had been thrown at the Prophet and attaches it to the men who threw it, which is the same movement the sūrah makes later when it warns about the tongue that says one thing and the heart that believes another.

**Why the Verse Ends With the Word Liars**

The Book uses the word liar for the people who shape the message to suit themselves, not for people who make mistakes. The sūrah has named several kinds of falsehood in its passage on the covenant: the people who sold what they had promised for a small gain, and the people who used an oath to cover a lie (16:94 describes the man who uses his oath as a trick, and 16:92 compares the community to a woman who unravels her spinning after it is spun). The liars the verse names are the men who knew what the revelation was and preferred their own version of events. The sūrah tells the reader what to do with that habit when it says that God commands justice and kindness and giving to relatives (16:90 states the whole instruction — *“Indeed, Allah commands justice, grace, as well as courtesy to close relatives.”*), and the verse in front of the reader closes the accusation with the plainest sentence in the passage.

**Where This Leaves the Reader**

The verse leaves two questions with the reader: what he believes about the signs he has heard, and what he does with his words. The sūrah has shown the first in the opening argument about the revelation and the second in its teaching about speech, and it will go on to describe the people who broke their covenant after it was made (16:95 gives the warning — *“And do not trade Allah’s covenant for a fleeting gain. What is with Allah is certainly far better for you, if only you knew”*). The same chapter had already told the community that God knows what the hearts hide and what they make public (16:19 says it, and the sūrah repeats the knowledge at 16:23). The verse in front of the reader names the men the argument had been pointing at all along, and it leaves the reader to decide which side of the sentence he stands on. The sūrah has already answered the charge that the Prophet was inventing the revelation when it named the verses that were replaced by others (16:101 speaks of the exchange of one verse for another and the objection it drew).
verses.106:
> Whoever disbelieves in Allah after their belief—not those who are forced while their hearts are firm in faith, but those who embrace disbelief wholeheartedly—they will be condemned by Allah and suffer a tremendous punishment

The verse treats a case the community would soon face: someone who disbelieves after believing. It makes an explicit exception for the one who is forced to deny while his heart remains firm in faith. It puts the condemnation on the person who opens his own breast to disbelief, of which the Book says the wrath of God is upon him and there is a great punishment. The verse is read against the reports of the companions who were tortured in Makkah for saying what they did not believe, and against the Sūrah al-Muʾminūn and Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt passages where the trial of faith is described. The sūrah's interest is the distinction between a tongue under duress and a heart that has turned, and the next verse states the motive for the second.

---
