The occasion the commentators give for the verse is the compulsion suffered by the early Muslims in Makkah, and the report of ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir is the one most often cited: made to utter the words of denial under torture while his heart remained with the faith, he came to the Prophet ﷺ distressed, and was met with the question of how he found his heart and told that if it happened again he should do the same. The verse is the sūrah's ruling on that case: the forced word is not the apostasy, and the offence belongs to those who embrace disbelief and open their hearts to it. The principle stated here is one the jurists kept, that intention and compulsion are weighed in the assessment of speech.
verses.107:
> This is because they prefer the life of this world over the Hereafter. Surely Allah never guides those who ˹choose to˺ disbelieve

**Why They Chose What They Chose**

The verse gives the reason for the unbelief it has been describing: these people preferred the life of this world over the life to come, and it adds that God does not guide the people who choose to reject Him. The verse states the motive and the consequence in one breath.

**The Preference Named**

The Book keeps naming this same preference as the root of refusal, and the sūrah has shown it in the passage before: the men who broke a promise to God for a small price (16:95 warns against exactly that trade — *“And do not trade Allah’s covenant for a fleeting gain. What is with Allah is certainly far better for you, if only you knew”*), the men who used an oath as a cover (16:94 describes the trick — *“And do not take your oaths as a means of deceiving one another or your feet will slip after they have been firm. Then you will taste the evil ˹consequences˺ of hindering ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah, and you will suffer a tremendous punishment”*), and the men who turned away when the message asked something of them (16:103 records the accusation they made against the Prophet instead of listening). The Book names the same motive in the sūrah of the Heights, where it says of such people that they know the outside of this life and are careless of the next (30:7 states it, and the sūrah of the Cave names the man who preferred his garden to his Lord at 18:32).

**The Order in the Sentence**

The verse puts the preference first and the withholding of guidance second, and that order is the point the teachers of the community drew attention to. A person is not taught by the verse to blame God for his own decision: he chose, and the guidance that comes with the choice is that he no longer sees the road he walked away from. The sūrah has stated the same rule in the negative when it said that God guides the people who ask to be guided and that He increases the guidance of the men who are already on the road (the sūrah of Muhammad states the second half at 47:17 — *“As for those who are ˹rightly˺ guided, He increases them in guidance and blesses them with righteousness”*, and this sūrah tells the reader that the blind and the seeing are not the same at 16:76 — *“And Allah sets forth a parable of two men: one of them is dumb, incapable of anything. He is a burden on his master. Wherever he is sent, he brings no good. Can such a person be equal to the one who commands justice and is on the Straight Path”*). The verse in front of the reader is a statement of fact about how a person's direction settles.

**What the Sūrah Has Put in Front of Them**

The passage has been showing the readers what is being preferred to what: it named the signs in the sky and the earth, the provision that arrives without anyone's planning, the bee that produces a healing honey, and the human being who was made from a drop and then argues openly (16:4 describes the man who argues, and the sūrah keeps the contrast between the gift and the ingratitude through the passage). The Book says in the same sūrah that whoever does right, male or female, and has faith will be given a good life and a reward better than what he did (16:97 states the promise — *“Whoever does good, whether male or female, and is a believer, We will surely bless them with a good life, and We will certainly reward them according to the best of their deeds”*), and it says that the world's goods vanish while what God gives remains (16:96 makes that promise — *“Whatever you have will end, but whatever Allah has is everlasting. And We will certainly reward the steadfast according to the best of their deeds”*). The verse in front of the reader names the choice that produces the loss, and it names it plainly so that no reader can claim he did not know he was choosing.
verses.108:
> They are the ones whose hearts, ears, and eyes are sealed by Allah, and it is they who are ˹truly˺ heedless

**What the Refusal Produces**

The verse lists what follows from refusing the truth after it has been made clear: God seals their hearts, their hearing and their sight. This is not an arbitrary punishment dropped onto people who simply could not see. The sūrah has just described the people who opened their chests to disbelief after believing, and the one who is forced to deny while his heart stays settled in faith and is therefore not blamed (16:106 makes that distinction — *“Whoever disbelieves in Allah after their belief—not those who are forced while their hearts are firm in faith, but those who embrace disbelief wholeheartedly—they will be condemned by Allah and suffer a tremendous punishment”*). What this verse describes is the other case entirely: the deliberate exchange of faith for disbelief, made by a person who knew what he was doing.

**The Same Image Elsewhere**

The Book uses the same picture at the head of the sūrah of the Cow, where God says that He sealed the hearts of those who disbelieve and placed a cover over their sight (2:7 states both — *“Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and their sight is covered. They will suffer a tremendous punishment”*). It appears again in the sūrah of the Kneeling, where the man who takes his own desire as his god is left with a seal on his hearing and his heart and a cover over his sight (45:23 describes him — *“˹And so˺ Allah left them to stray knowingly, sealed their hearing and hearts, and placed a cover on their sight.”*). The image is consistent wherever it appears: the person chose first, and the sealing confirms the choice.

**Why These Three Organs**

The three organs named here are the ones the Book names as the means of understanding. Ears carry the message in. Eyes examine the signs. The heart is where evidence becomes conviction, since the Qur'an's heart is the organ of knowledge and decision rather than only of feeling. So the loss described is the loss of the very faculties by which the message would have reached them. Nothing has been taken that was not already being refused.

**The Word the Verse Ends On**

The verse ends with the word that fits the state: they are the heedless. The Arabic word describes people who fail to take notice of what concerns them, people who let what matters slip past while paying close attention to what does not. It is the exact opposite of the attention the sūrah has been asking for through every sign it has listed, from the rain that brings dead land to life to the honeybee and the shade. The chapter closes the account of this group with a single word, and it is not a word about intelligence. It is a word about care.

**What This Verse Is Not**

The verse should not be used to tell a struggling believer that his heart is sealed, that his questions are proof of ruin, or that his slips mean hope is over. The house of mercy stands open in the same Book, and the sūrah itself records the door of turning back in the verse before this one's subject. What is described here is the settled exchange of belief for unbelief by a person who has seen and understood. A person still asking, still fearing, still wanting to do better is doing the opposite of what this verse describes.
verses.109:
> Without a doubt, they will be the losers in the Hereafter

The verse draws the conclusion in the plainest form: without a doubt, they will be the losers in the Hereafter. The Book uses the same verdict at the close of Sūrah al-Baqarah, where those who trade guidance for error lose the bargain (2:16 — *“They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance. But this trade is profitless, and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided”*), and in Sūrah al-Zumar, where the losers on the Day of Resurrection are named as those who lose themselves and their families (39:15 — *“Say, “The ˹true˺ losers are those who will lose themselves and their families on Judgment Day.”*). The sūrah places the sentence here to close the passage on the sealed organs and to prepare the contrast that follows, where those who emigrated, struggled and persevered are given the promise of forgiveness and mercy in the same terms.
verses.110:
> As for those who emigrated after being compelled ˹to renounce Islam˺, then struggled ˹in Allah’s cause˺, and persevered, your Lord ˹O Prophet˺ is truly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful after all

The verse marks a change of case, and it is the hope that the previous verses left open. Those who emigrated after being put to trial, then struggled and were patient: for them the Lord is Forgiving and Merciful. The Book tells the same story in Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt, where the Mecca community is promised that their dwelling after migration will be better (29:56–58 — *“O My believing servants! My earth is truly spacious, so worship Me ˹alone˺ Every soul will taste death, then to Us you will ˹all˺ be returned ˹As for˺ those who believe and do good, We will certainly house them in ˹elevated˺ mansions in Paradise, under which rivers flow, to stay there forever. How excellent is the reward for those who work ˹righteousness!˺”*), and it repeats the combination of trial, migration and patience in Sūrah al-Naḥl's own later passage. The sūrah's structure is deliberate: the sealed hearts of the heedless are stated, and immediately after them the open door that those same hearts could have taken, with the cost measured honestly — migration, struggle, patience.

**Who the Verse Is About**

The verse follows a passage on those whose hearts were sealed and on the one who was forced to deny his faith while his heart stayed at peace (16:106-109 — *“They are the ones whose hearts, ears, and eyes are sealed by Allah, and it is they who are ˹truly˺ heedless”*). It is read as the promise given to the believers who were taken and tortured in Makkah and then left — first to Abyssinia, then to Madinah — and the words are chosen for that experience: they were put to trial, then they migrated, then they struggled, then they were patient, and after all of it the verse gives them forgiveness and mercy rather than a list of what they owed. Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt speaks to the same people in the same order, promising that the home they go to will be better than the home they left (29:56-58 — *“O My believing servants! My earth is truly spacious, so worship Me ˹alone˺ Every soul will taste death, then to Us you will ˹all˺ be returned ˹As for˺ those who believe and do good, We will certainly house them in ˹elevated˺ mansions in Paradise, under which rivers flow, to stay there forever. How excellent is the reward for those who work ˹righteousness!˺”*), and the Sūrah of the Spoils puts migration and struggle together among the things that raise a person's rank (8:72 — *“But if they seek your help ˹against persecution˺ in faith, it is your obligation to help them, except against people bound with you in a treaty.”*; 9:20 — *“Those who have believed, emigrated, and strived in the cause of Allah with their wealth and their lives are greater in rank in the sight of Allah. It is they who will triumph”*). The sūrah deliberately sets the sealed hearts of the heedless first and this verse immediately after, so the reader sees the same circumstances and the two possible ends.
verses.111:
> ˹Consider˺ the Day ˹when˺ every soul will come pleading for itself, and each will be paid in full for what it did, and none will be wronged

The scene of the Day is stated in one line: every soul comes pleading for itself, and every soul is paid in full for what it did, and none is wronged. The Book uses the same words in Sūrah al-Muʾmin, where the Day is described as the day every soul is repaid for what it earned, with no injustice and no intercession and no ransom (40:17–18 — *“Today every soul will be rewarded for what it has done. No injustice Today! Surely Allah is swift in reckoning.””*). In Sūrah Luqmān, where the promise is that nothing is hidden and every deed is brought forward (31:16 — *“˹Even˺ if a deed were the weight of a mustard seed—be it ˹hidden˺ in a rock or in the heavens or the earth—Allah will bring it forth.”*). The word for the pleading, *tujādilu ʿan nafsihā*, describes an argument a person makes on his own behalf — the same habit that filled a lifetime of debate — now reduced to a single case with no time for excuses.

**The Day the Argument Belongs to One Party**

The verse's Day is the Day every soul comes to plead, and the pleading has a history behind it: the people who spent a lifetime arguing against the messengers will find that on that Day the argument serves their own account and nothing else. The Book describes the shape of that pleading elsewhere: the wrongdoer bites his hands and wishes he had taken the path with the Messenger (25:27-29 — *“And ˹beware of˺ the Day the wrongdoer will bite his nails ˹in regret˺ and say, “Oh! I wish I had followed the Way along with the Messenger”*), the follower wishes he were as far from his leader as the two ends of the earth (2:166-167 — *“˹Consider the Day˺ when those who misled others will disown their followers—when they face the torment—and the bonds that united them will be cut off”*), and the one who was led blames the one who led. None of it delays the payment. Every soul is repaid in full for what it earned, and no soul is wronged (2:281 — *“Be mindful of the Day when you will ˹all˺ be returned to Allah, then every soul will be paid in full for what it has done, and none will be wronged”*; 21:47 — *“We will set up the scales of justice on the Day of Judgment, so no soul will be wronged in the least.”*; 45:22 — *“For Allah created the heavens and the earth for a purpose, so that every soul may be paid back for what it has committed. And none will be wronged”*). What the verse leaves out speaks as loudly as what it says: it names no advocate, no appeal and no postponement for a life that never asked for forgiveness.

**Where the Verse Stands in the Sūrah**

The verses before it describe the community's trial: those who emigrated after being made to suffer, who then struggled and endured, and whose Lord is forgiving and merciful (16:110 — *“As for those who emigrated after being compelled ˹to renounce Islam˺, then struggled ˹in Allah’s cause˺, and persevered, your Lord ˹O Prophet˺ is truly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful after all”*). The verse in front of us is the horizon of that endurance. The men who lost their homes for the faith are told of a Day when the whole account is settled by the God who saw the patience when nobody else did. The sūrah then returns to the command to call people to the way of the Lord with wisdom and fair preaching (16:125 — *“Invite ˹all˺ to the Way of your Lord with wisdom and kind advice, and only debate with them in the best manner.”*), and it closes with patience and the reminder that God is with those who are mindful of Him and who do good (16:127-128 — *“Be patient ˹O Prophet˺, for your patience is only with Allah’s help. Do not grieve over those ˹who disbelieve˺, nor be distressed by their schemes Surely Allah is with those who shun evil and who do good ˹deeds˺”*). The placement shows the link between what a believer does in a hard season and what is counted for him at the end of the road.
verses.112:
> And Allah sets forth the example of a society which was safe and at ease, receiving its provision in abundance from all directions. But its people met Allah’s favours with ingratitude, so Allah made them taste the clutches of hunger and fear for their misdeeds

The parable describes a town that was safe and at ease, receiving its provision in abundance from every direction, and then denied the favours of God and was clothed by God in hunger and fear for what its people had been doing. The place is understood by the commentators to be Makkah, which the Book elsewhere names as the sanctuary where people find safety while others are being carried off (29:67 — *“Have they not seen how We have made ˹Mecca˺ a safe haven, whereas people ˹all˺ around them are snatched away?”*; 106:1–4 — *“Who has fed them against hunger and made them secure against fear”*), and the parable is a warning to the same city: the safety it lives in is a gift, and the gift came with a condition. The Book finishes the thought in the next verse by naming the messenger who actually came to that town and was denied, and the torment that followed while they were wrongdoers.

---

The commentators identified the town of the parable with Makkah in most of the reports, since it was secure, well-supplied by caravans from every direction, and then met hunger and fear after it had denied the messenger raised among it. The same description appears in the sūrah of the Stories, where the sanctuary is called a place of safety and the provision is brought together there (28:57 — *“Have We not established for them a safe haven ˹in Mecca˺ to which fruits of all kinds are brought as a provision from Us?”*), and the sūrah's closing account of the Quraysh's security in the sūrah of Quraysh (106:3–4 — *“Who has fed them against hunger and made them secure against fear”*) states the same favour in the positive. The verse's point is the exchange: a community that treats God's provision as its own achievement loses the thing it took for granted, and what it is then clothed in is stated with the same physical word — hunger and fear.

**The Famine Behind the Parable**

The town the verse describes is the city of the Prophet himself, and the reports tell of the day the description became experience. The Prophet prayed against the Quraysh when they refused, asking God to send on them years of hunger like the years of Joseph, and the famine came on them until they ate carrion and bones. The Book's answer to the men who then begged for relief is the passage about the smoke that will cover the sky and the plea for it to be lifted, with the sentence that they will return to what they were doing (44:10-15 — *“Wait then ˹O Prophet˺ for the day ˹when˺ the sky will be veiled in haze, clearly visible”*). The verse in front of us was revealed among the same years, and its parable reads the famine back onto the safety that had come before it. A town that knows where its food comes from cannot be surprised by the cost of denying it.

**The Twin Parable of Sabaʾ**

The Book tells the same story of a favoured people who lost their provision in the sūrah of Sabaʾ. Two gardens stood on the right and the left of the people, and the Book said to them: eat of your Lord's provision and give thanks to Him, for a good land and a forgiving Lord (34:15 — *“˹Yours is˺ a good land and a forgiving Lord.””*). When they turned away, God sent on them the flood that broke their dam and gave them, in place of the two gardens, fruit that was bitter and trees that bore little (34:16 — *“But they turned away. So We sent against them a devastating flood, and replaced their orchards with two others producing bitter fruit, fruitless bushes, and a few ˹sparse˺ thorny trees”*), and the verse closes with the rule the parable exists to teach: that is how We repaid them for their unbelief, and do We repay anyone but the ungrateful (34:17 — *“This is how We rewarded them for their ingratitude. Would We ever punish ˹anyone in such a way˺ except the ungrateful”*). The Book states the same law in the positive elsewhere, when it says that if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of God, He would have opened on them blessings from the sky and the earth (7:96 — *“Had the people of those societies been faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, We would have overwhelmed them with blessings from heaven and earth.”*). Gratitude and ingratitude are not private feelings in these passages. They are the hinge on which the provision of a community turns.
verses.113:
> A messenger of their own actually did come to them, but they denied him. So the torment overtook them while they persisted in wrongdoing

The verse identifies the messenger as one of their own — *rasūlan minhum* — and the phrase removes the excuse that the messenger was a stranger with foreign claims, which the Book answers elsewhere by saying that every messenger was sent in the language and the community of his people (14:4 — *“We have not sent a messenger except in the language of his people to clarify ˹the message˺ for them.”*). The denial is followed immediately by the consequence, and the Book states this pattern in Sūrah al-Baqarah, where a sending and a denial are followed by the taking of the town (2:87–90 — *“Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers.”*). The verse also ends the sūrah's sequence on ingratitude: the town knew its safety, was reminded by one of its own sons, and lost both.

---

The verse's phrase, that the messenger came from among them, answers the accusation recorded earlier in the sūrah that the Prophet was taught by a foreigner (16:103 — *“And We surely know that they say, “No one is teaching him except a human.” But the man they refer to speaks a foreign tongue, whereas this ˹Quran˺ is ˹in˺ eloquent Arabic”*); the same defence is made in the sūrah of Joseph, where the messengers are said to have been men from the towns they addressed (12:109 — *“We only sent before you ˹O Prophet˺ men inspired by Us from among the people of each society.”*), and in the sūrah of the Bee at 16:43 — *“We did not send ˹messengers˺ before you ˹O Prophet˺ except mere men inspired by Us.”*. The warning that follows — that the torment overtook them while they were wrongdoers — is the sūrah's own summary of what happened to the towns of the past, and the passage closes the account of the town with the same verdict it gave to them.
verses.114:
> So eat from the good, lawful things which Allah has provided for you, and be grateful for Allah’s favours, if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺

The command is to eat what is lawful and good from what God has provided, and to be grateful for His favours if He is the one being worshipped. The verse links the legal and the devotional: gratitude is named as the proper proof of worship, and the sūrah places the command just before the list of what has actually been forbidden. The Book states the same in Sūrah al-Māʾidah, where the command to eat of the good things provided is joined to the duty to be mindful of God, in whom the believers trust (5:88 — *“Eat of the good, lawful things provided to you by Allah. And be mindful of Allah in Whom you believe”*). The form of the verse is worth noting: permission comes before prohibition in this sūrah, which is the Book's habit when it addresses a community free to choose.

---

The command repeats what the sūrah of the Heifer states to the whole of humanity: eat of what is lawful and good on the earth, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan (2:168 — *“O humanity! Eat from what is lawful and good on the earth and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy”*), and what the sūrah of the Table gives the believers in the same form (5:88 — *“Eat of the good, lawful things provided to you by Allah. And be mindful of Allah in Whom you believe”*). The pairing of the two commands in this verse — eat what is lawful, and be grateful — is the sūrah's method throughout: the legal permission and the devotional response are one act, since the lawful food is taken as provision from God rather than as an entitlement. The verse's condition, that the gratitude is owed if it is God alone who is worshipped, ties the diet to the doctrine the sūrah has been establishing.
verses.115:
> He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

The verse lists the four prohibitions — carrion, blood, the flesh of swine. What has been slaughtered in the name of anything other than God — and then states the exception for the one driven by necessity, neither desiring nor going to excess, with the note that God is Forgiving and Merciful. The Book repeats the list in Sūrah al-Baqarah, with an extra clause on the one who is compelled, and in Sūrah al-Māʾidah, where the flaunting of the same items is linked to the corruption of the markets (2:173 — *“He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah.”*; 5:3 — *“But whoever is compelled by extreme hunger—not intending to sin—then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*). The sūrah's treatment keeps the two ends together: the rule is stated plainly, and the door of necessity is left open by the same verse, which is the Book's usual way with legal burdens.

---

The same four prohibitions are listed in the sūrah of the Heifer (2:173 — *“He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—they will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*), the sūrah of the Table (5:3 — *“Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, and swine; what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah; what is killed by strangling, beating, a fall, or by being gored to death; what is partly eaten by a predator unless you slaughter it; and what is sacrificed on altars.”*) and the sūrah of the Cattle (6:145 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to eat except carrion, running blood, swine—which is impure—or a sinful offering in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—then surely your Lord is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.””*), with the last of these adding the flesh of an animal slaughtered in the name of other than God to the same list. The exception stated here — for the one driven by hunger, neither desiring the forbidden nor going beyond what is needed — is the basis of the juristic rule of necessity, which the scholars applied to food, drink and medicine in a case of danger to life. The verse's closing pair, that God is Forgiving and Merciful, is attached to the concession rather than to the offence.

**How Much the Starving Man May Take**

The verse's two conditions — that a person is driven to the forbidden food, not desiring it and not going past what the need requires — became the ground of the rules the jurists set for necessity. The permission is for the one who fears death or real harm, and the amount allowed is what keeps him alive and no more; the schools discussed whether he may eat his fill, whether he may carry any of it away, and whether he is obliged to eat when refusing would kill him, and their answers all work from the words of the verse rather than from its list. The same two conditions are repeated where the list is repeated, in the sūrah of the Cow and the sūrah of the Cattle (2:173 — *“But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—they will not be sinful.”*; 6:145 — *“But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—then surely your Lord is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.””*), and the Book leaves the reader with the pairing it uses here: the rule is stated in full, and the door is opened by the same verse that closes it. The two names at the end, Forgiving and Merciful, hang over the concession rather than the offence, which is the Book's way of signalling which of the two it expects to be used.

**Why the Rule Is Repeated Across the Sūrahs**

The list of forbidden foods appears in the Sūrah of the Cow, this sūrah, the Sūrah of the Table and the Sūrah of the Cattle, and the repetition is worth a moment. Each passage adds something the others leave out: the Table adds the animals killed by violence and the arrows of divination (5:3 — *“Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, and swine; what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah; what is killed by strangling, beating, a fall, or by being gored to death; what is partly eaten by a predator unless you slaughter it; and what is sacrificed on altars.”*), the Cattle adds the note that the blood meant is blood poured out and that no blame falls on a person for what he does in ignorance (6:145 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to eat except carrion, running blood, swine—which is impure—or a sinful offering in the name of any other than Allah.”*), and this verse keeps the list short and puts the weight on the exception. The Book's habit of repeating a law with a new edge is a mercy in itself: a community that hears the same rule in several places cannot claim to have missed it, and the differences between the passages are where the jurists found the room they needed to answer questions the first list did not address.
verses.116:
> Do not falsely declare with your tongues, “This is lawful, and that is unlawful,” ˹only˺ fabricating lies against Allah. Indeed, those who fabricate lies against Allah will never succeed

The verse forbids a specific practice: declaring things lawful or unlawful with nothing but the tongue, and attaching the declaration to God. The Book elsewhere condemns the same habit among those who invented religious rules — the practice of setting aside animals and crops as offerings in God's name while treating them as forbidden (6:136–138 — *“The pagans set aside for Allah a share of the crops and cattle He created, saying, “This ˹portion˺ is for Allah,” so they claim, “and this ˹one˺ for our associate-gods.””*), and the claim that certain things were permitted to one group and not another without proof. The verse's closing clause states the outcome: those who fabricate lies against God will never succeed, and the next verse adds what their fabrication converts into — a brief enjoyment, and then the painful punishment. The scholars read the verse as a standing warning against ruling on religious matters without evidence, applied in every age.

---

The practice the verse forbids is the invention of food laws and the attribution of them to God, which the sūrah of the Cattle describes at length in the catalogue of the bahīrah, sāʾibah, waṣīlah and ḥām (5:103 — *“Allah has never ordained the ˹so-called˺ baḥîrah, sâ'ibah, waṣîlah, and ḥâm camels.”*), and which the sūrah of Jonah condemns when it asks whether God has permitted what they make unlawful (10:59 — *“Ask ˹the pagans, O Prophet˺, “Have you seen that which Allah has sent down for you as a provision, of which you have made some lawful and some unlawful?””*). The offence is placed among the great sins because it puts a human decision in the place of revelation, and the Book attaches the same warning to any who conceal or invent what they have not been given (2:79 — *“So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, “This is from Allah”—seeking a fleeting gain! So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they have earned”*). The verse's ending states the consequence in the plainest terms: those who fabricate lies against God will not prosper.
verses.117:
> ˹It is only˺ a brief enjoyment, then they will suffer a painful punishment

The verse answers the forgery of the previous one with the shortest possible account of what it buys: a brief enjoyment, and then a painful punishment. The two-word summary of worldly gain — *matāʿun qalīl* — is one of the Book's standing measures of everything that is traded for the truth, used for the price the disbelievers accept in Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān and for the provision of this life generally (3:197 — *“It is only a brief enjoyment. Then Hell will be their home—what an evil place to rest”*; 9:38 — *“Do you prefer the life of this world over the Hereafter?”*). The sūrah has just described people inventing a ruling of their own and attributing it to God, and the verse states the outcome without ornament: the enjoyment is short, and the punishment is not. The next verse turns to the community that was given restrictions already, and explains that the restrictions were not a wrong done to them.

**The Forgery and Its Price**

The verse before this one describes people who invent a ruling and then attach it to God, and the same sūrah states elsewhere who does that: it is those who do not believe in the signs of God who invent falsehood about Him (16:105 — *“No one fabricates lies except those who disbelieve in Allah’s revelations, and it is they who are the ˹true˺ liars”*). What the verse gives them is a measured account of the bargain rather than a threat in general terms. The enjoyment is small and short, and the punishment is described as painful. The Book measures this life in the same few words every time it is put against the reward: a passing enjoyment, a small provision, a bloom that withers (3:197 — *“It is only a brief enjoyment. Then Hell will be their home—what an evil place to rest”*; 57:20 — *“And in the Hereafter there will be either severe punishment or forgiveness and pleasure of Allah, whereas the life of this world is no more than the delusion of enjoyment”*). The Sūrah of Repentance puts the same choice in front of the believers rather than the deniers, asking what they preferred the life of this world for, since its enjoyment is so little (9:38 — *“Do you prefer the life of this world over the Hereafter?”*). The verse, in short, is not an outburst. It is an accounting, and the person reading it is invited to check his own scale.
verses.118:
> To the Jews, We have forbidden what We related to you before. We did not wrong them, but it was they who wronged themselves

The verse speaks to the objection raised by the Jews of Madinah about the food laws, and it states the matter in two parts: what was forbidden was related in the Book before, and God did not wrong them — they wronged themselves. The sūrah refers to the passage in Sūrah al-Anʿām where the restrictions are listed and explained as a penalty for their own transgressions (6:146 — *“For those who are Jewish, We forbade every animal with undivided hoofs and the fat of oxen and sheep except what is joined to their backs or intestines or mixed with bone. In this way We rewarded them for their violations. And We are certainly truthful”*), and it refers elsewhere to the breaking of the Sabbath and the violations that followed. The verse's function in this sūrah is to separate two things that were being merged in the argument: the laws of the earlier community, which were a response to their conduct, and the law of the new community, which the sūrah states in the verses just before. The next verse opens the door of repentance to the same people.

**The Restrictions Were Not an Injustice**

The verse returns to the food laws that have been argued over a few verses earlier, and it says again that what was forbidden for the Jews was stated before (16:115-116 — *“He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful Do not falsely declare with your tongues, “This is lawful, and that is unlawful,” ˹only˺ fabricating lies against Allah. Indeed, those who fabricate lies against Allah will never succeed”*). The Book gives the list in the Sūrah of the Cattle: every animal with claws, the fat of cattle and sheep with the exceptions named, and other restrictions placed on them for their own transgression (6:146 — *“For those who are Jewish, We forbade every animal with undivided hoofs and the fat of oxen and sheep except what is joined to their backs or intestines or mixed with bone.”*). What the verse adds here is the verdict on that legislation: We did not wrong them; they were wronging themselves. The restriction was a consequence of their history and not an arbitrary punishment, and the Sūrah of Āl-ʿImrān makes the same point about Israel, saying that all food was lawful to him except what he forbade himself before the Torah came (3:93 — *“All food was lawful for the children of Israel, except what Israel made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed.”*).
**What This Means for the New Community**

The passage is building toward the close of the sūrah and its argument with the People of the Book, so the point here is not merely historical. The rules of the earlier communities were given for their circumstances, and the community receiving this recitation is told that its own laws come from the same Giver with the same justice. The verses that follow move from the food laws to the call to Abraham's way, and the whole passage answers the charge that the new teaching was either a copy or a contradiction of what came before.
verses.119:
> As for those who commit evil ignorantly ˹or recklessly˺, then repent afterwards and mend their ways, then your Lord is surely All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**The Door for the One Who Comes Back**

The verse says that the people who do evil out of ignorance, and then turn back and put their conduct right afterwards, will find their Lord forgiving and merciful. The verse follows the passage that named the men who did wrong and then were lost in their preference for this life (16:107 — *“This is because they prefer the life of this world over the Hereafter. Surely Allah never guides those who ˹choose to˺ disbelieve”*), and it keeps the door open for the reader who recognizes himself in the earlier verses.

**What Ignorance Means Here**

The word does not describe a person who never knew anything; it describes the state in which a person acts, which is the state of everyone who falls into sin. The Book uses the same phrase in the sūrah of the women, where the verse says that God accepts the turning back of people who do wrong out of ignorance and put the matter right quickly, and it says that He does not accept the turning of those who keep at it until death arrives (4:17 gives the first half and 4:18 gives the second). Ignorance here means the moment of appetite rather than a lifetime of being uninformed, which is why the verse attaches the mending of conduct to the turning back. The sūrah of the Throngs gives the same invitation in the widest words when it tells people who have gone too far against themselves not to despair of God's mercy (39:53 states it — *“Do not lose hope in Allah’s mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins.”*).

**Why the Verse Sits in This Sūrah**

The passage before it discusses the community that broke its covenants and reached the point of arguing with God's messenger (16:103 names the accusation, and 16:112 tells the story of the town that was given provision and then denied it). The verse in front of the reader does not let the reader conclude that the people in those stories were beyond return, and the chapter's own habit confirms it: it names the wrong and then names the way back. The Book says in the same sūrah that God commands justice and kindness and giving to relatives, and that He forbids indecency, wrong and rebellion (16:90 states the whole command — *“He forbids indecency, wickedness, and aggression.”*), which means the man who has fallen can measure himself against the command and get up.

**What the Two Names at the End Mean**

The verse closes with the forgiving and the merciful, the pair the Book attaches to the moment of return rather than to the person who never made a mistake. The sūrah of the women used the same two names when it promised the man who asks forgiveness that he would find God forgiving and merciful (4:110 states it — *“Whoever commits evil or wrongs themselves then seeks Allah’s forgiveness will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*), and the sūrah of the Crowd used them for the servant who has harmed his own soul and then learns that the one who forgives is the one who forgave him (39:53 again in that sūrah's own call — *“He is indeed the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*). The verse in front of the reader turns the warning of the passage back into an invitation, and it does so with the two names that describe what God does with a person who comes back.

**What the Reader Is Asked to Do**

The verse gives three movements: recognize the wrong, turn back from it, and put the conduct right. The middle word is the one the Book uses for the turning of the whole person, and the third one means the repair that shows in what a person actually does. The sūrah has described that repair in its teaching about speech and honesty, and it will go on to tell the reader what will happen to the people who keep going the other way (16:106 describes the man who turns back from his faith after having believed). The verse in front of the reader keeps the road open for anyone reading the passage and finding his own story in it, and it says that the two names of God are waiting at the end of the road.
verses.120:
> Indeed, Abraham was a model of excellence: devoted to Allah, ˹perfectly˺ upright—not a polytheist—

The verse names Abraham as a model — *ummah*, a community in himself, the word the Book uses for a people and here for a single man — and it describes him with three qualities: devoted, upright, and not of the polytheists. The Book gives him the same title in Sūrah al-Baqarah, where he is called an upright community obedient to God (2:120–121 in some renderings — *“Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith. Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.” And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against Allah Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed. It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it. As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers”*), and it states his standing as a friend of God in Sūrah al-Nisāʾ (4:125 — *“And who is better in faith than those who ˹fully˺ submit themselves to Allah, do good, and follow the Way of Abraham, the upright? Allah chose Abraham as a close friend”*). The verse's purpose in the closing argument of this sūrah is to give the community a single ancestor of the faith rather than a lineage, and the next verse names the gratitude for which God chose him.

---

The word *ummah* applied to a single man is read by the commentators as describing Abraham as a community in himself — a whole people's worth of faith, guidance and gratitude — and the verse then names his three marks: devoted, upright, and free of polytheism. The Book gives him the same standing elsewhere: he was tried by his Lord with words and fulfilled them, and was made a leader of the people (2:124 — *“˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments, which he fulfilled.”*); he was not a Jew nor a Christian but upright and submissive (3:67 — *“Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian; he submitted in all uprightness and was not a polytheist”*); and he was taken as a friend by God (4:125 — *“And who is better in faith than those who ˹fully˺ submit themselves to Allah, do good, and follow the Way of Abraham, the upright? Allah chose Abraham as a close friend”*). The verse's mention of gratitude is the reason for his praise in the same passage: the favours were given and he answered them with thanksgiving.
verses.121:
> ˹utterly˺ grateful for Allah’s favours. ˹So˺ He chose him and guided him to the Straight Path

The verse states what God did in return for Abraham's gratitude: He chose him and guided him to a straight path. The order is the sūrah's order throughout — the response of the servant, then the gift — and the Book tells the same story of the choice in Sūrah al-Baqarah, where Abraham is told that God has made him a leader of people (2:124 — *“˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments, which he fulfilled. Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model for the people.” Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?” Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.””*). In Sūrah al-Nisāʾ, where he is described as submitted to God and doing good. The gratitude named here is the same virtue the sūrah has been asking of its audience since the section on blessings began, so the verse presents Abraham as the model who did what the community was being told to do.

**The Model the Sūrah Was Reaching For**

The verse is part of the passage that closes the sūrah's argument with the People of the Book, and Abraham is placed at its centre: a nation in himself, devout, never an idolater, grateful for God's gifts (16:120-121). The choice by God is stated in the Sūrah of the Cow as well, where Abraham is told he will be made a leader of people (2:124 — *“˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments, which he fulfilled. Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model for the people.” Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?” Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.””*), and in the Sūrah of Women, where the Book says God took him as a friend (4:125 — *“And who is better in faith than those who ˹fully˺ submit themselves to Allah, do good, and follow the Way of Abraham, the upright? Allah chose Abraham as a close friend”*). The Book also settles the claims made about him by the two later communities: he was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but one who submitted (3:67 — *“Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian; he submitted in all uprightness and was not a polytheist”*). Gratitude is the quality singled out here, and it is the same quality the sūrah has been asking of its own audience since the section on blessings began, so that the ancestor it points to is the man who actually did what the hearers were being told to do.
verses.122:
> We blessed him with all goodness in this world, and in the Hereafter he will certainly be among the righteous

The verse gives Abraham the two rewards together: good in this world, and a place among the righteous in the Hereafter. The Book gives him the same double portion in Sūrah al-Baqarah, where the good he is given is named as the honourable mention that follows him among later peoples (2:129–130 in the sense of his prayer and its answer — *“And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool! We certainly chose him in this life, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous”*). In Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt, where the reward of the upright is stated in the same pattern. The sūrah puts the two worlds side by side for a community that had been arguing about lineage and law, and it makes the man on whom they all agreed the example of what it was arguing about.

**The Two Rewards and the Closing Command**

The verse gives Abraham both halves of the promise: a good name in this world, and a place among the righteous in the next. The Sūrah of the Cow gives the same double gift in the answer to his prayer for his descendants — guidance and the honourable mention that follows him among later peoples (2:129-130 — *“And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool! We certainly chose him in this life, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous”*). The sūrah then turns from the ancestor to the Prophet and gives the command that closes the whole argument: follow the religion of Abraham, the upright, and he was not of the idolaters (16:123 — *“Then We revealed to you ˹O Prophet, saying˺: “Follow the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not one of the polytheists.””*). The order matters. The community that had been arguing about lineage and law is shown the one man all parties claimed, and then told that the way to belong to him is not descent but the same gratitude and submission he showed. It is the point the Book makes about him elsewhere too: whoever turns away from his religion has made a fool of himself (2:130 — *“And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool! We certainly chose him in this life, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous”*).
verses.123:
> Then We revealed to you ˹O Prophet, saying˺: “Follow the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not one of the polytheists.”

The verse gives the Prophet the command that settles the argument of the passage: follow the faith of Abraham, who was upright and not of the polytheists. The same instruction appears at the head of the sūrah of the Bee's later argument and in Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān, where the Book rejects the claim of Abraham for Jews and Christians and assigns it to the one who follows his way (3:67–68 — *“Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian; he submitted in all uprightness and was not a polytheist”*). The command is followed in the next verse by the statement about the Sabbath, which fixes the difference between the community of Abraham and the communities that disputed over their laws. The sūrah's closing passage therefore gives the community one ancestor in faith, one clear path, and a method of inviting others to it.

---

The command to follow the faith of Abraham is given twice in the sūrah of the Family of ʿImrān — "say: Allah has spoken the truth, so follow the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not of the polytheists" (3:95) — and it settles the argument with both the Jews and the Christians, since each claimed him. The sūrah of the Cattle gives the Prophet the same declaration (6:161 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Surely my Lord has guided me to the Straight Path, a perfect way, the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not one of the polytheists.””*), and the command here has a particular force in the sūrah of the Bee because it arrives after the passage on the food laws and the sabbath, where the community is warned not to adopt the disputes of the earlier communities about what was permitted to them.
verses.124:
> ˹Honouring˺ the Sabbath was ordained only for those who disputed about Abraham. And surely your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their disputes

The verse answers the dispute about the Sabbath by narrowing it: the Sabbath was ordained only for those who differed over it, which is to say that the obligation grew out of the dispute and the divisions of the community that received it. It did not belong to Abraham, whose path the sūrah has just commanded the Prophet to follow (16:123 — *“Then We revealed to you ˹O Prophet, saying˺: “Follow the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not one of the polytheists.””*). The Book makes the same point in Sūrah al-Baqarah, where the strictness of the Sabbath is tied to the community's own conduct (2:65 — *“You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath. We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!””*), and in Sūrah al-Nisāʾ, where the punishment of that community is described. The verse ends by handing the judgement back to God on the Day of Resurrection, which is the sūrah's answer to every argument about the laws of the previous communities.

**What the Sabbath Was and for Whom**

The verse closes a passage that has been arguing with the people of the Book about their own laws, and it does two things in one sentence. It states that the Sabbath was only made obligatory for the people who differed about it — the children of Israel who disputed among themselves what the day required and why it had been given to them — and it says the community of the Prophet is not under that law. The sūrah has already named the day in its list of the blessings given to Israel, and it has already told the Muslims that they follow the way of Abraham, who was neither Jew nor Christian and who was not among those who associated partners with God (16:120-123, and see 3:67). The ruling is a boundary: the religious law given to Muḥammad neither picks up the whole of the earlier law nor abolishes the earlier communities' obligations for the sake of it.
**What the Disagreement Was**

The Qur'an uses the disagreement about the Sabbath as the reason it had to be laid down so firmly for the people who received it. Some of them kept the day and some of them did not; the Book reports on more than one occasion that a group of them were transformed for the violation. The verse does not go into those accounts here — it leaves them to the sūrahs that tell the story — and keeps to the point the argument needs: the differences the community inherited are for God to settle on the Day of Resurrection, and the reader is told twice in the passage that the return and the judgment are His, not the community's to carry out on anyone's behalf.
verses.125:
> Invite ˹all˺ to the Way of your Lord with wisdom and kind advice, and only debate with them in the best manner. Surely your Lord ˹alone˺ knows best who has strayed from His Way and who is ˹rightly˺ guided

The verse states the method of the invitation: wisdom, good advice, and debate in the best manner, with the reminder that the Lord knows best who has strayed and who is guided. The Book states the same in Sūrah Ṭā-Hā, where Moses and Aaron are told to speak gently to Pharaoh (20:44 — *“Speak to him gently, so perhaps he may be mindful ˹of Me˺ or fearful ˹of My punishment˺.””*), and in Sūrah al-ʿAnkabūt, where discussion with the People of the Book is to be conducted with what is best. The last clause removes the pressure of results from the man who conveys: the knowledge of who will respond belongs to God, so the method does not need to be replaced by force. The sūrah places the instruction at the point where the argument has finished, so that the method is stated after the case has been made.

---

The method named in this verse is one of the Book's clearest statements on how the invitation is to be made, and the sūrah of the Spider adds the rule for argument with the People of the Book: argue in the best manner, except with those who do wrong, and say that the community believes in what was revealed to it and to them (29:46 — *“Do not argue with the People of the Book unless gracefully, except with those of them who act wrongfully.”*). The sūrah of Ṭā Hā applies the same principle to the hardest case of all, when Moses and Aaron are told to speak gently to Pharaoh so that he may remember and fear (20:43–44 — *“Speak to him gently, so perhaps he may be mindful ˹of Me˺ or fearful ˹of My punishment˺.””*). The closing words of the verse return the outcome to God, who knows best who has strayed from His path and who is guided, which is the same limit the sūrah placed on the messenger's duty at 16:82 — *“But if they turn away, then your duty ˹O Prophet˺ is only to deliver ˹the message˺ clearly”*.
verses.126:
> If you retaliate, then let it be equivalent to what you have suffered. But if you patiently endure, it is certainly best for those who are patient

The verse states the limit on retaliation and then names the better course: if you retaliate, let it be exactly equivalent, and if you patiently endure, it is certainly better for those who are patient. The Book states the same principle of equivalence in Sūrah al-Baqarah with the law of retribution and the permission of pardon (2:178 — *“O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set for you in cases of murder—a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female.”*; 5:45 — *“We ordained for them in the Torah, “A life for a life, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, a tooth for a tooth—and for wounds equal retaliation.” But whoever waives it charitably, it will be atonement for them. And those who do not judge by what Allah has revealed are ˹truly˺ the wrongdoers”*), and it records the occasion of this verse in the Prophet's own grief after the battle of Uḥud. The permission is not withdrawn; the preference is stated, and the preference is attached to the patience named in the next verse as possible only with God's help.

---

The permission to retaliate on equal terms is stated in the sūrah of the Heifer as the law of retribution (2:178 — *“O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set for you in cases of murder—a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female. But if the offender is pardoned by the victim’s guardian, then blood-money should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously. This is a concession and a mercy from your Lord. But whoever transgresses after that will suffer a painful punishment”*) and in the sūrah of the Pilgrimage with the same condition of equivalence (22:60 — *“That is so. And whoever retaliates in equivalence to the injury they have received, and then are wronged ˹again˺, Allah will certainly help them. Surely Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving”*), while the better course named here is repeated in the sūrah of Consultation, where the recompense of an evil is an evil like it, but whoever forgives and reconciles has his reward with God (42:40 — *“The reward of an evil deed is its equivalent. But whoever pardons and seeks reconciliation, then their reward is with Allah. He certainly does not like the wrongdoers”*). The reports connect the verse to the treatment of the Prophet's uncle Ḥamza after Uḥud and to the grief of the community, which is why the next verse addresses the Prophet's own patience directly. The sūrah's order is the teaching: the limit is preserved, and the preference for patience is named without abolishing the right.
verses.127:
> Be patient ˹O Prophet˺, for your patience is only with Allah’s help. Do not grieve over those ˹who disbelieve˺, nor be distressed by their schemes

The verse addresses the Prophet directly and gives the command with the reason attached: be patient, and your patience comes only with the help of God. It then removes two weights from him: do not grieve over the people who refuse, and do not be distressed by their plotting. The Book comforts the Prophet in the same terms elsewhere, where it says that no soul will believe except by God's permission and following the plot of those who refuse is pointless (10:100–101 — *“It is not for any soul to believe except by Allah’s leave, and He will bring His wrath upon those who are unmindful”*). The command is followed by the promise in the next verse, which closes the sūrah on the support rather than the hardship.

---

The two griefs the verse removes are the same two the sūrah named at the opening of its address to the Prophet: the refusal of the people and the plotting of those who deny (16:127; compare 15:97). The Book repeats the counsel in the same form in the sūrah of the Family of ʿImrān, where the Prophet is told not to grieve for the disbelievers (3:176 — *“˹O Prophet!˺ Do not grieve for those who race to disbelieve—surely they will not harm Allah in the least.”*), and in the sūrah of the Cave. The verse's closing note, that God is with those who are mindful and those who are doers of good, is the promise the passage ends on, and the sūrah's next verse adds the command to patience with the community's own conduct (16:128 — *“Surely Allah is with those who shun evil and who do good ˹deeds˺”*).
verses.128:
> Surely Allah is with those who shun evil and who do good ˹deeds˺

The sūrah ends with the ground of the command it has just given: God is with those who shun evil and who do good. The Book closes several of its addresses on the same note, and the two words at the end are the summary of the whole sūrah's teaching — *ittaqā*, to be mindful of God and guard against doing wrong, and *muḥsinūn*, those who do good. The sūrah that began with the command to be grateful and the warning against ingratitude ends with the presence of God promised to the people who followed its instruction, and it leaves the reader with the pair of virtues the earlier verses have been asking for from the beginning.
